modules.title: Welcome to Station
modules.outcome: Say in one breath what Station does, who it's for, and what your job is (and isn't).

lessons.title: The gap
lessons.goal: Explain what Station does in one sentence any owner understands.
film: Black. A phone buzzes on a bare floorboard, screen lit: "Unknown caller". A gloved hand reaches for it; the buzzing stops just before he gets there.
Under a house, in a crawlspace, a plumber hears his phone ring.
Hard cut to paper. Headline types in, Archivo heavy: "Missed call." Beneath it, three grey ticks fill in one by one.
By the time he climbs out, that caller has already rung the next plumber on Google.
The headline slides up and two more lines stack under it: "The follow-up nobody sent." "The review nobody asked for."
That's the gap. Every local business has it: the call missed on a job, the lead you meant to chase, the happy customer you never asked for a review.
The three lines collapse into one hairline. The Station mark spins in at its centre. Wordmark: STATION.
Station fills the gap.
The real station.solutions/products/ shelf scrolls slowly inside a browser frame: 14 product tiles, each with its painting.
We sell fourteen simple products that answer calls, text back missed calls, chase leads, book appointments, earn reviews, keep a business visible on Google, and get it paid.
Three tags pop onto the shelf, blue: "We build it." "We host it." "We support it."
And Station does all the building, setup, hosting, billing and support. The owner never has to become a tech person.
A row of trades in big type, one after another on the beat: Plumbers. Roofers. Salons. Gyms. Clinics. Cleaners. Shops.
Who buys? Owners of small local service businesses. The ones who answer their own phone, work on jobs all day, and lose work in the gaps.
The one-sentence pitch builds word by word: "Station fills the gaps that cost local businesses work."
So here's the whole company in one sentence. Station fills the gaps that cost local businesses work.
Do-this-now card: "Say it out loud once." with a blue tick that lands when the voice stops.
Say that out loud once, right now. You'll be saying it a lot.
lessons.read_md:
**Station runs the front office for local service businesses.** We sell fourteen products that answer calls, text back
missed calls, chase leads, book appointments, earn reviews, keep a business visible on Google, and get the business paid.
One of the fourteen is a custom website, designed for each business.

The buyer is the owner of a small local service business: a plumber, roofer, HVAC company, cleaner, salon, gym, clinic,
contractor or shop. They answer their own phone, they're busy on jobs, they miss calls, they forget to follow up, and they
have too few reviews or a thin Google listing.

**Station does all the building, setup, hosting, billing and technical support.** The client gets their own Station
account, where they see their messages and bookings and can change the wording of every message their products send.

The whole company in one sentence: **Station fills the gaps that cost local businesses work.**

check.q: A friend asks what Station does. Which answer is closest?
options: It's an AI company that replaces a business's staff.
It's a marketing agency that guarantees more customers.
It fills the gaps that cost local businesses work, like missed calls, slow follow-up and missing reviews.
check.why: Station sells simple tools for specific gaps. It doesn't replace people and it never guarantees results.

check.q: Who sets up and supports a client's products?
options: Station, always.
You, the partner.
The client, from a how-to video.
check.why: Station builds, sets up, hosts, bills and supports everything. Your job is the relationship, not the setup.

lessons.title: Your job, in one picture
lessons.goal: Know exactly what a partner does and what they never do.
film: Split screen built from one hairline that drops down the middle. Left heading "You". Right heading "Station".
Here's the deal between you and Station, in one picture.
Left column fills on the beat: "Find the business." "Start the conversation." "Help them pick." "Close."
You find businesses and start conversations. You help the owner pick the one product that fixes what's hurting most, and you close.
Right column fills: "Build." "Set up." "Host." "Bill." "Support."
Station builds it, sets it up, hosts it, bills for it and supports it.
Left column adds: "Stay in touch with your clients." A small book icon slides under it labelled "Your book".
And once a client is yours, you stay in touch. They're in your book of business. You're the friendly face who checks in and suggests the next thing that would help.
A client chat bubble appears on the left: "My texts stopped sending." An arrow carries it across the hairline to Station's side, where it turns blue: "Handled."
When a client brings you a problem, any problem, you don't fix it. You tell them Station will handle it, and you pass it to Station the same business day.
A red rule strikes through four lines that try to slide into the left column: "Take payments." "Set prices or discounts." "Promise results." "Log into a client's account."
A few things you never do. You never take payments, never set a price or a discount, never promise results or dates, and never log into a client's account.
Title card: "Independent partner." Under it, smaller: "Not an employee. Commission only. No quota."
You're an independent partner, not a Station employee. You're paid commission only, and there's no quota.
Do-this-now: "Say: 'I'm an independent partner with Station.'"
Practise how you'll introduce yourself: "I'm an independent partner with Station."
lessons.read_md:
**You do:**
- Find businesses (Station sends you leads, and you can add ones you find yourself) and start the conversation.
- Help the owner pick the right product, answer questions, and close.
- Stay in touch with the clients in your book, including about adding Station products at published prices.
- Log every call and keep your notes and lead status current in Partner World.

**Station does:** all building, setup, hosting, billing and support.

**When a client brings you a question or a problem** (technical, their account, billing or a change), tell them Station
will handle it and pass it to Station **the same business day** with **Message Station**. Tell Station straight away if a
client wants to cancel, complains, or raises a refund, dispute or legal issue.

**You never:** build, fix or host anything; take payments; sign anything for Station; set prices or discounts; promise
results, custom work or timelines; log into a client's account or handle their passwords, bank details or ID.

You're an **independent contractor**, commission only, with no quota.

check.q: A client in your book emails you: "The booking page shows the wrong hours." What do you do?
options: Tell them to work it out from the help pages.
Tell them Station will handle it and pass it to Station the same business day with Message Station.
Ask for their login and fix the hours yourself.
check.why: All support is Station's. Your job is to make sure it reaches Station fast, so the client feels looked after.

check.q: How do you describe yourself to a business?
options: "I'm a Station account manager."
"I'm calling from Station's sales team."
"I'm an independent partner with Station."
check.why: You're independent, not an employee. Saying otherwise breaks the agreement and the trust.

check.q: An owner asks if you can do it for $50 less a month. You:
options: Agree, and ask Station later.
Say Station sets the prices and they're the same for everyone, then make sure they're on the right product.
Offer to give them part of your commission.
check.why: Partners never set prices, discounts or side deals. Sharing commission is a breach of the agreement.

lessons.title: How this course works
lessons.goal: Know the path from here to your first leads.
film: A single blue line draws left to right across paper, with fourteen small ticks on it. A dot sits at the start: "You are here."
This course is one road with fourteen stops.
The dot moves; stop labels flick past: "The money." "Who buys." "The shelf." "The software." "The call." "Closing."

You'll learn the money first, so you know what you're working for. Then who buys, every product on the shelf, the software you'll use and the software your clients get, how a call works, and how to close.
A lesson card zooms out of a tick: a film frame, a short text block, then three answer buttons; one lights blue.
Every lesson is a short film, a quick read, and two or three questions. Get them right and the lesson's done.
At the end of the line, a seal: "Certified". Two steps fade up under it: "Final quiz." "One practice call."
At the end there's a final quiz and one practice call. You record yourself pitching a business. A Station founder listens and gives you notes.
The seal turns into a key, and the key turns in a lock labelled "Your leads". The lock opens to Partner World's Calls tab.
Pass both, and your leads unlock. Station starts sending you businesses to call.
Do-this-now: "Start Module 1: The money." with a blue arrow.
Let's start with the part everyone wants to know. The money.
lessons.read_md:
The course is 14 modules. Every lesson has a short film, the same content to read, and two or three questions. Answer
them right and the lesson is done. Your progress is saved to your Partner World account, so you can stop and pick up on
any device.

**To unlock your leads:**
1. Finish every module.
2. Pass the final quiz.
3. Record one practice call (you pitching a business, using the script from Module 9) and send it in. A Station founder
   listens and either passes it or sends notes to try again.

Once you pass, Station starts sending you businesses to call. Until then, you can add businesses you've found
yourself to your list, so they're ready for the day you unlock.

check.q: What unlocks the leads Station sends you?
options: Finishing the course, passing the final quiz, and a practice call a founder passes.
Making ten calls from your own list.
Signing in to Partner World for the first time.
check.why: Station wants every partner who calls a business to be ready for it, first time.

modules.title: The money
modules.outcome: Work out, from a client's plan, what you earn in year one and after, and know every step from "yes" to money in your bank.

lessons.title: The deal: 40%, then 15%
lessons.goal: State the commission rule and do the arithmetic for one client.
film: A big green "40%" slams into the centre of paper and holds.
Let's talk about the money. Here's the headline.
The "40%" slides left. A timeline draws out of it: twelve month-ticks, labelled "Months 1–12".
For every client in your book, you earn 40% of what they pay Station, every month, for their first 12 months.
The timeline keeps going past month 12; the label changes to "15%, for as long as they stay" and the line runs off the right edge.
After that, you keep earning 15% of every payment for as long as they stay a client. No end date.
The real Frontdesk painting slides in behind a price tag: "Frontdesk · $397 a month".
Let's make it real. Say you sign up a plumber on Station's Frontdesk, the receptionist that answers every call. That's $397 a month.
Counter rolls up in green: "$158.80 a month". Twelve coins stack beside the timeline, one per month; a total ticks to "$1,905.60".
40% of that is $158.80 a month. Over the first twelve months, that's $1,905.60.
Past month twelve, the coins shrink a size and keep stacking: "$59.55 a month".
From month thirteen it's 15%: $59.55 a month, for as long as that plumber stays.
Small text drops under the counter, plain and calm: "Arithmetic, not a promise. Paid on what actually clears."
That's arithmetic, not a promise. You're paid on what the client actually pays, never on a list price or a guess.
The timeline collapses into a single line of type: "40% for 12 months. 15% after. Every client."
40% for the first 12 months, 15% after that, on every client in your book.
Do-this-now: "Open Products in Partner World. Find what you'd earn on Frontdesk."
Go to Products in Partner World and look at what each product pays. Next lesson: what counts, and what doesn't.
lessons.read_md:
For every client in your book of business:

- **Months 1 to 12:** you earn **40%** of what they pay Station.
- **After month 12:** you earn **15%** of every payment, for as long as they stay a client and
  your agreement is in effect.

The 12 months count from the client's **first payment that clears** (any free trial doesn't count).

**Example (arithmetic, not a forecast or a promise):** a client on Frontdesk at $397 a month earns you
$158.80 a month for their first 12 months ($1,905.60 in all), then $59.55 a month
after that. You're paid on what actually clears, after refunds and credits, never on a list price or a quote.

There's no bounty and no sign-up bonus. (The one way to keep 40% for good is in lesson 1.3.)

check.q: A client pays $397 a month for Frontdesk. What do you earn in their 5th month?
options: Nothing until they've been a client for a year.
check.why: Months 1 to 12 pay 40%. The 5th month is inside that window.

check.q: The same client is now in month 20. What do you earn that month?
options: Nothing, commission ends after a year.
check.why: After 12 months it drops to 15%, and keeps going as long as they stay (unless you've unlocked 40% for good, lesson 1.3).

check.q: Your commission is worked out on:
options: The list price on the website.
What the client actually paid and cleared.
The price you quoted on the call.
check.why: Commission is never on list price, quotes or projections. Refunds and credits come off.

lessons.title: What counts, and what doesn't
lessons.goal: Tell which payments earn you commission and which don't.
film: A receipt prints down the screen, line by line, like a till roll.
Not every dollar a client pays earns commission. Let's read a receipt.
Line 1 lands: "Frontdesk, monthly". A green tick stamps beside it.
Every product and every plan they pay for monthly: counts.
Line 2: "Custom website, setup fee". Green tick, small tag "once".
A custom website's setup fee: counts, 40%, once, when they pay it.
Line 3: "Keep-the-site buyout, $1,250". Green tick, tag "once".
If a client leaves and pays the one-time $1,250 to keep the website that came with their plan: counts, 40%, once.
Line 4: "Hosting & care, monthly". A grey dash instead of a tick.
Hosting and care, the monthly fee to keep a website online: doesn't count.
Lines 5 and 6: "Extra texts (over allowance)", "Top-up pack". Grey dashes.
Overage, when a client uses more than their allowance, and top-up packs: don't count.
Line 7: "Free website (included with plan)". Grey dash, tag "$0 setup".
The free website that comes with a plan has no setup fee, so there's nothing to earn on the build.
The receipt tears off. Two piles: green "Counts" and grey "Doesn't". The green pile sits heavier.
So: monthly products and plans, website setup fees, and the buyout count. Care, overage, top-ups and taxes don't.
Do-this-now: "Remember: never quote care, overage or a website price. Station quotes those."
And one more thing. You never quote a price for care or a custom website. Station quotes those, every time.
lessons.read_md:
**Earns commission:**
- Monthly payments for every Station product, collection and plan.
- A custom website's **setup fee**: 40%, once, when the client pays it.
- The one-time **$1,250 keep-the-site buyout** (a client leaving a plan pays it to keep the website that came with it): 40%, once.

**Earns nothing:**
- **Hosting & care** (the monthly fee that keeps a website online).
- **Overage** (usage over a product's monthly allowance) and **top-up packs**.
- The free Station-built website included with a plan (it has no setup fee).
- Other one-time fees, taxes, and amounts Station charges only to recover a third-party cost.
- Anything not yet paid and cleared.

If a client prepays (for example a year up front), your commission is paid in equal monthly instalments over the months
they prepaid, not in one lump.

**Never quote** a custom website price or a hosting & care price. Station quotes both, for each client.

check.q: A client on Pro uses more texts than their allowance and pays extra that month. You earn:
options: Your normal share of their Pro payment, and nothing on the extra texts.
Nothing that month.
Your share of the Pro payment and of the extra texts.
check.why: Overage and top-ups never earn commission.

check.q: A business wants Station to host and look after their new site. How much is it?
options: Whatever the last client paid.
$49 a month.
You don't quote it. You tell Station what they need with Message Station, and Station quotes them.
check.why: Hosting & care has no list price and earns no commission. Station always quotes it.

check.q: A client leaving their plan pays $1,250 to keep their website. You earn:
options: 15% of it.
Nothing, it's a one-time fee.
40% of it, once.
check.why: The keep-the-site buyout earns 40%, once, like a website setup fee.

lessons.title: Keep 40% for good
lessons.goal: Know the 10-client unlock and how you keep it.
film: Ten empty circles in a row.
There's one way to keep 40% on every client, for good.
Circles fill blue one by one on the beat, a business name appearing under each: "Dave's HVAC", "Rosa's Taqueria", ... to ten.
Get to 10 active, paying clients in your book...
A meter under the row fills in green to "$4,000 a month".
...whose payments to Station add up to at least $4,000 a month together...
Both bars complete; a lock icon above the row opens. Text: "40% on all of them. Every month."
...and you earn 40% on all of them, every month, including the ones past their first year.
One circle empties (a client leaves). A clock face appears beside the lock: "2 months grace".
Clients come and go. If you drop below, you get 2 months of grace to get back above the line before anything changes.
Clock runs out with the row still at nine; the lock clicks shut, the older clients' tags drop back to 15%.
If you're still below after 2 months, clients past their first year go back to 15%. Get back above the line and 40% returns.
Do-this-now: "Your progress to the unlock is on the Money tab."
Your count toward the unlock is on the Money tab.
lessons.read_md:
**The unlock:** when you have at least **10 active, paying clients** in your book **and** their payments to Station add
up to at least **$4,000 a month** together, you earn **40% on every client in your book**, including clients past
their first 12 months.

**If you drop below** either line, you have **2 months of grace** to get back above it. If you're still below after that, clients
past their first 12 months go back to 15% until you're above the line again.

Money shows how close you are.

check.q: You have 12 active clients paying Station $2,400 a month together. Are you unlocked?
options: No. You need $4,000 a month together as well as 10 clients.
Yes, once you've been a partner for a year.
Yes, you have more than 10 clients.
check.why: Both lines have to be met: 10 active clients and $4,000 a month together.

check.q: You're unlocked, then a client cancels and you drop to 9. What happens?
options: Nothing ever changes once you've unlocked.
Every client drops to 15% that day.
You have 2 months to get back to 10 before anything changes.
check.why: There's a 2 months grace period before older clients go back to 15%.

lessons.title: From "yes" to money in your bank
lessons.goal: Walk through every step between a client saying yes and the money reaching you.
film: Phone call ends; a speech bubble: "Let's do it." A blue path starts drawing from the bubble.
They said yes. Here's the road from that yes to money in your bank.
Stop 1 on the path: the real Partner World Calls card, cursor presses "Won: they're buying".
One. Mark them Won in Calls, and send your link so the signup is credited to you.
Stop 2: a checkout page in a browser frame; a "14-day free trial" ribbon on single products, none on a plan.
Two. They check out on station.solutions. Single products and collections start with a 14-day free trial. Nothing is earned during a trial.
Stop 3: a card payment ticks from "Processing" to "Cleared" in green.
Three. Their first real payment clears. That's when your commission starts.
Stop 4: a calendar with 30 days shaded: "On hold".
Four. A new client's first payment can be held up to 30 days after it clears. That's the refund and chargeback window. Renewals aren't held.
Stop 5: the real Money tab, its two setup steps: "Your tax form" and "Set up payouts with Stripe". Both tick green.

Five. Before Station can pay you anything, two setup steps. Upload your tax form, a W-9 if you're in the US, on the Money tab. And set up payouts with Stripe, where you type your bank details on Stripe's own site. Station never sees them.
Stop 6: the Money statuses roll past: "Ready for your next payout" → "Sent to your Stripe account" → "In your bank".
Six. Once it's ready and you're over the $50 minimum, Station pays it to your Stripe account, and Stripe pays it into your bank.
The path loops back to the start; small text "Smaller balances roll forward. They never expire."
Under $50? It rolls forward and never expires.
Do-this-now: "Do your two setup steps today: tax form + Stripe."
Do both setup steps today, before you need them. Then the first time a client pays, nothing's waiting on you.
lessons.read_md:
1. **Mark them Won** in Calls and send them your link, so the signup is credited to you. Tell Station what they're buying with
   **Message Station**, so the order can be accepted into your book.
2. **They check out on station.solutions.** Single products and collections start with a **14-day free trial**; nothing is
   earned during a trial. Plans (Core, Pro, Max) are billed at checkout.
3. **Their first real payment clears.** Your commission starts here, and the 12 months start counting.
4. **Hold:** a new client's first payment can be held up to **30 days** after it clears (the refund and chargeback window).
   Renewals aren't held.
5. **Your two setup steps** must be done before anything is paid: your **tax form** (W-9 for U.S. persons, W-8BEN outside the U.S.),
   uploaded on the Money tab, never emailed; and **Set up payouts with Stripe**, where you type your bank details on Stripe's site.
6. **Payout:** once it's ready and your balance is at least **$50**, Station pays it to your Stripe account and Stripe pays it
   to your bank. Smaller balances roll forward and never expire.

Station issues a Form 1099 where the law requires. Your income and self-employment taxes are your own responsibility.

check.q: A client starts a 14-day free trial on Lineback today. When does your commission start?
options: Today, when they sign up.
When the trial ends and their first real payment clears.
After the 30-day hold, whether or not they pay.
check.why: Nothing is earned during a free trial. It starts with the first payment that clears.

check.q: You've earned commission but haven't uploaded your W-9. What happens?
options: It builds up, but nothing is paid until your tax form is on file.
You lose it.
Station pays it anyway and you send the form later.
check.why: Commission can accrue first, but no payout is made until the form is on file.

check.q: Where do you send your W-9?
options: Upload it on the Money tab in Partner World.
Email it to main@station.solutions.
Send it through Message Station.
check.why: It carries your Social Security number, so it goes through the upload only, never email or messages.

lessons.title: What can take money back
lessons.goal: Know when commission is reversed or stops, so nothing surprises you.
film: A green commission line in the Money table. A rewind icon spins over it.
Now the part nobody likes, so you're never surprised.
The line flips to "Reversed". A card icon with a back-arrow: "Refund / chargeback".
If a client's payment is refunded or charged back, the commission on that payment comes back off your balance.
A client card fades to grey: "Cancelled". The month-ticks after it go empty.
When a client cancels, your commission stops once they stop paying. Money you've already earned stays yours.
A client card slides from your book to another partner's: "Reassigned".
Station can reassign a client: if the client asks, or if you're not looking after them after a warning and a chance to fix it.
A door closes: "If you leave". Text: "Paid on what cleared up to your end date. Nothing after."
If you leave the program, you're paid on payments that cleared up to your end date, and nothing after, even for clients you brought in.
A red strip: "Fake or self-referrals, spam, misrepresentation → removed, unpaid commission forfeited."
And if a partner is removed for cause, like fake or self-referrals, spam or lying to a business, unpaid commission can be forfeited.
Do-this-now: "Look after your book. It's your income."
The fix for almost all of this is simple. Look after your book.
lessons.read_md:
- **Refunds and chargebacks:** the commission on that payment is reversed from your balance or next payout. If no balance is
  left, Station may invoice you for the difference.
- **A client cancels within 30 days of paying:** Station may hold that commission until it's sure the payment is final.
- **A client cancels:** your commission stops once they stop paying. Tell Station right away if a client says they want to cancel.
- **Reassignment:** Station can move a client to another partner if the client asks, if you aren't looking after them (after notice and
  a chance to fix it), if you breach the agreement, or when it ends. Commission already earned stays yours.
- **If you leave:** either side can end the agreement by email. You're paid on what cleared up to the end date, and nothing after.
- **For cause** (fraud, fake or self-referrals, spam, misrepresentation, misuse of client data, brand damage): unpaid commission can be
  forfeited.
- **Never eligible:** your own business, your family's, or any your company's owners control.
- **Statements:** if a payout looks wrong, tell Station in writing within 60 days.

check.q: Your cousin owns a salon and wants Answer. Can she be your client?
options: No. Businesses you or your family own or control are never eligible.
Yes, as long as she pays.
Yes, if she uses your link.
check.why: Family and self-referrals are never eligible, and doing it anyway is grounds for removal.

check.q: A client you closed in March gets a refund for April. What happens to your April commission?
options: It's doubled next month.
You keep it, you earned it.
It's reversed from your balance or next payout.
check.why: Commission follows what Station actually keeps.

lessons.title: What one client is worth
lessons.goal: Compare what different products and plans pay you, so you pitch the right fit, not the biggest number.
film: Three columns rise like bars on a hairline grid: "Answer", "Frontdesk", "Core".
Here's what three different clients would earn you. Arithmetic only.
Answer bar labels in: "$297 a month → $118.80 a month, first year".
Answer collection, $297 a month: $118.80 a month for the first year, then $44.55.
Frontdesk bar: "$397 a month → $158.80 a month".
Frontdesk, $397 a month: $158.80, then $59.55.
Core bar, tallest: "$1,297 a month → $518.80 a month".
A hand tries to drag the Core bar onto a small detailer's card; the card shakes no.
Now, the trap. The biggest number isn't the best pitch. Offer Core to a one-man detailer and he hangs up.
The Answer bar slides onto the detailer's card; it ticks blue "Yes". Then, months later, a second product clicks onto it: "+ Frontdesk".
Sell the smallest thing that fixes his problem. A client who sees one product working adds more later, and you earn on every one.
Do-this-now: "Next: Module 2, Who buys."
So who buys what? That's next.
lessons.read_md:
Arithmetic only, not a forecast or a promise:

| Client on | They pay | You earn, months 1–12 | After that |
|---|---|---|---|
| Answer collection | $297 a month | $118.80 a month | $44.55 a month |
| Frontdesk | $397 a month | $158.80 a month | $59.55 a month |
| Core plan | $1,297 a month | $518.80 a month | $194.55 a month |

**Pitch the fit, not the biggest number.** Lead with the one product that fixes what's hurting most. A small owner who hears a
plan price first usually stops listening. A client who sees one product working adds more later, and you earn on each one.

check.q: A one-person mobile detailer misses DMs and calls at night. Which do you lead with?
options: Core, because it pays the most.
The Answer collection, the smallest thing that fixes the missed messages.
Every product, so they can choose.
check.why: Lead with the smallest fix. Big plans first lose small owners, and one product working leads to more.

modules.title: Who buys
modules.outcome: Recognise which of the ten Station buyers you're talking to within 20 seconds, and use their question, their line and their reply.

lessons.title: What a Station buyer is feeling
lessons.goal: Know the three things almost every owner feels when your call comes in, and open the call to fit them.
film: A van door slides shut. On the dash, a phone lights up: "Missed calls (3)". A hand in a work glove picks it up, thumb hovering.
It's four in the afternoon. The owner you're about to call has been on jobs since seven.
Hard cut to paper. Three words stack in Archivo heavy, one per beat: "Busy." "Behind." "Burned before."
Most Station buyers feel three things when your call comes in. They're busy. They're behind. And a lot of them have been burned by someone selling marketing.
"Busy." stays lit; small icons orbit it: a ringing phone, a DM bubble, a clipboard.
Busy means you're interrupting real work. So say who you are and ask if it's a good time, before anything else.
"Behind." lights; an unticked list writes itself under it: "Call back the Hendersons." "Ask for that review." "Fix the Google hours."
Behind means they already know about the gap. The missed calls, the follow-up they never sent. They don't need you to explain it. They need you to ask about it.
"Burned before." lights; a crumpled agency invoice drops in and a grey line strikes through "Guaranteed results".
Burned before means a fast pitch sounds like a scam. Slow down. Say you're an independent partner, and that you earn a commission.

Nobody on the other end wants software. They want to stop losing the job that went to whoever answered first.

So you open with a question about their week, not a list of products. The card gives you that question for every business.
Ten name tags slide onto a hairline, one per beat: Jaylen, Mr. Chen, Dave, Brianna, Karen, Marcus, Rosa and Javier, Linda, Tom, Priya.

lessons.read_md:
**Most Station buyers feel three things when you call:**
- **Busy.** You're interrupting real work. Say who you are and ask if you caught them at a bad time.
- **Behind.** They already know about the missed calls and the follow-up they never sent. Ask about it; don't lecture.
- **Burned before.** Plenty have paid for marketing that did nothing. Slow down, say you're an independent partner, and say
  you earn a commission.

**The habits that fit all three:**
- Start with what it costs them, not with the product. "When the phone rings and you can't get to it, what happens to that caller?"
- One problem, and the smallest thing that fixes it.
- Let them do the math on one job. Ask what a job is worth; never tell them they're losing a specific amount.
- Never promise a number of calls, jobs, reviews or a ranking. Never quote a statistic about other clients.

Partner World's **Who buys** (linked from Home and Products) has all ten buyers. The next four lessons group them by what's
hurting, so you learn four patterns, not ten scripts.

check.q: An owner picks up and you can hear a drill running. Your first move?
options: Say who you are and ask if you caught them at a bad time.
Tell them how many calls a business like theirs loses each week.
Go straight to the price so you don't waste their time.
check.why: Busy owners give you a few seconds. Earn them by being straight and polite. Never quote a loss or a statistic.

options: "Station has fourteen products. Can I run through them?"
"Businesses like yours get far more bookings with us."
"When the phone rings and you can't get to it, what happens to that caller?"
check.why: Start with what the gap costs them. A product list loses them, and a result you can't prove breaks the rules.

lessons.title: On the job: Dave, Rosa and Javier, Jaylen
lessons.goal: Work the three owners who miss calls because they're busy doing the work, and know who decides for each.
film: A crawlspace in torchlight. A phone face-down on the dirt buzzes, then stops. Name tag drops in: "Dave, 47. HVAC and plumbing, four techs."
Meet Dave. He's under a house most of the day, and a homeowner just told him, "I called you first and nobody answered."
Paper. Dave's question types in, big: "When you're under a house and the phone rings, what happens to that caller?"
Ask him exactly that. Then let him answer. He already knows.
The Answer collection card from the real products page slides in, then the Frontdesk painting beside it.

Then the line: "Station's Answer collection texts back anyone you miss, and Station's Frontdesk, the receptionist, can answer the call itself. You keep your own number, it just forwards. Which would help more, the text or the answering?"
A speech bubble from Dave: "Will it sound like a robot?" A second: "Does it work with Housecall Pro?"
You'll hear one of two worries. Is it a robot? And does it work with the software I already use?
Two answer cards flip over: "Automated. Answers from your facts. Always offers a person." and "Station can confirm. I won't guess."

Be honest. It's an automated assistant. It answers from his business facts, doesn't make up prices, and always offers to transfer the caller to a person. For his other software: Station can confirm how it fits. Don't guess.
A kitchen-table ledger with a second name on it. Tag: "Who decides: ask who does the books."
Before you finish, ask who handles the books. If it's his wife, include her. And say "forwards", never "port".
Cut to a taqueria at 12:15: tickets on a rail, a phone ringing behind the counter. Tag: "Rosa and Javier. Taqueria and catering."
Rosa and Javier run a family taqueria. In the lunch rush nobody can answer, and a catering order goes to voicemail.
Their line builds on paper: "...so a catering inquiry gets an answer. $297 a month, 14 days free." Then: "Who decides, you or Javier?"
"Station's Answer collection texts back every caller you miss, so a catering inquiry gets an answer. It's $297 a month with a 14-day free trial. Who decides about something like this, you or Javier?"
Bubble: "Do you take online orders?" A grey card answers: "Not a product I know of. I'll ask Station."
If they ask about online ordering, it isn't one of the products, so don't guess. Offer to ask Station, and set a time when both of them can listen.
A phone screen full of Instagram DMs, one reading "u still free sat?" sent 9 hours ago. Tag: "Jaylen, 24. Mobile detailer."
Jaylen runs his detailing business from his DMs. He just lost a job to someone who answered faster.
Jaylen's question types in: "When a customer messages you at night, how long before they hear back?" Then his worry: "I'm too small for this."
Ask how long a late message waits. When he says he's too small, that's what the free trial is for: 14 days, no contract, no setup fee.
A "Core" tag tries to slide onto Jaylen's phone and bounces off. The Answer card settles there instead.
And never lead with a plan. A new owner hears a big number and stops listening. Start with the smallest thing that fixes the missed message.

You get about twenty seconds before an owner decides whether to keep listening. Here's how to use them.
The real Calls card in a device frame. The cursor rings the trade, the city, the rating and "Why them".
Before you dial, read the card. The trade and the Why them line already tell you who you're probably calling. A plumber is likely a Dave. A salon, a Brianna.
The stopwatch ticks to 0:05. Clue 1 types in: "Who picked up?" Under it, flicking past: "The owner." "A family member." "A manager."
Then three clues. One: who picked up. The owner? A daughter or a husband? A practice manager who says her name and the office's?
0:10. Clue 2: "Where are they?" Sound cues as icons: a drill, a busy kitchen, a quiet office.
Two: where they are. A drill or a van means on the job. Clattering plates at noon means the rush. A quiet desk means someone who reads before they buy.
0:15. Clue 3: "What do they say first?" Bubbles pop: "Who is this?" "How much?" "I'm with a client."
Three: what they say first. "Who is this and who are you with?" is a Tom. "How much for three locations?" is a Priya. "I'm with a client, make it quick" is often a Brianna.
0:20. A matching table assembles row by row on paper (clue on the left, buyer and question on the right).
By twenty seconds, you've got a good guess. Ask that buyer's question, and listen.
A grey card: "Guessed wrong? The answer to your question tells you." The table re-sorts itself.
If you guessed wrong, their answer will tell you. That's why every buyer's line starts with a question.
Do-this-now: "On your next call, name the buyer in your head before you say your second sentence."
On your next call, name the buyer in your head before your second sentence.
lessons.read_md:
**Before you dial**, read the card: trade, city, rating and **Why them**. They tell you who you're probably calling.

**In the first 20 seconds**, listen for three clues:
1. **Who picked up?** The owner, a family member, a manager or staff.
2. **Where are they?** On a job, in a rush, or at a desk.
3. **What do they say first?** Suspicion, a price question, or "make it quick".

| What you notice | Probably | Ask |
|---|---|---|
| Plumbing, HVAC, roofing; a drill or a van | Dave | "When you're under a house and the phone rings, what happens to that caller?" |
| A restaurant, noise, around lunch | Rosa and Javier | Ask if it's a bad time, then "When the phone rings in the lunch rush, what happens?" |
| Young owner, mobile service, no website | Jaylen | "When a customer messages you at night, how long before they hear back?" |
| Slow careful English, or a family member answers | Mr. Chen | "Do you know what hours Google shows for your shop?" |
| "Dental office, this is Karen" | Karen | "When a patient doesn't rebook, does anyone follow up?" |
| Salon or spa; "I'm with a client" | Brianna | "When did you last reach out to clients who haven't been in for a while?" |
| Realtor or agent, out of the office | Linda | "When a new lead comes in while you're out, how soon do they hear back?" |
| Gym or studio running ads | Marcus | "When someone fills in a form at night, how soon do they hear from you?" |
| B2B trade; "Who is this? Who are you with?" | Tom | Say who you are and that you earn a commission, then "Have you worked with a marketing company before?" |
| Several locations; asks for a number | Priya | "How many locations, and does each have its own Google profile and phone line?" |

These are good guesses, not labels. Their answer to your first question tells you if you were right. If someone other than the owner
picks up, don't pitch them: get a name and the best time to reach the owner.

check.q: A woman answers, "Bright Smile Dental, this is Karen." What's your best move?
options: Ask to speak to the dentist and hang up if you can't.
Pitch Core, since a clinic can afford it.
Ask whether anyone follows up when a patient doesn't rebook, and later, who'd need to see the page.
check.why: A practice manager researches and the doctor approves. Use Karen's question, then get the page to whoever decides.

check.q: At 12:15, a taqueria picks up over clattering plates: "Hold on... yeah?" What do you do?
options: Leave the price and promise to email.
Pitch fast before they hang up.
Say who you are, ask if it's a bad time, and offer to call back after the rush.
check.why: You've caught Rosa and Javier mid-rush. A polite call-back time outside it is worth more than a rushed pitch.

check.q: The first thing an owner says is, "Who is this, and who are you with?" Which buyer is this most likely, and what's the move?
options: A Jaylen. Lead with the free trial.
A Priya. Give the total price.
A Tom. Say your name, that you're an independent partner with Station, and that you earn a commission.
check.why: Suspicion first means a burned buyer. Honesty about who you are and how you're paid is the pitch.

modules.title: The shelf
modules.outcome: Name every Station product by the job it does, and for each one say who it's for, what it costs, what Station needs, the question to open with, and what you never promise.

lessons.title: The shelf, by the job it does
lessons.goal: Sort every Station product into the job it does, so one answer from an owner tells you which shelf to reach for.
film: Morning, inside a contractor's truck. His phone on the dash lights up three times: "Missed call", "Form fill, 2 days ago", "Google: 3.9 stars".
One owner, one morning. A call he missed, a lead he never chased, and a Google listing that sells him short.
Hard cut to paper. The real station.solutions/products/ shelf scrolls in a browser frame; the tiles lift off and sort themselves into five short stacks.
Station's shelf looks like a lot of products. It isn't. It's a few jobs, and every product does one of them.
Heading "Answer" in Archivo. Five paintings slide in under it, each with its label: Frontdesk (day-night.webp), Lineback, Greet, Dial, Slate.

Job one: answer. Frontdesk answers the phone. Lineback texts back the calls you miss. Greet answers the chat on your website. Dial gives the business its own number. Slate lets customers book themselves, then reminds them to show up.
The heading morphs to "Follow up". Pursuit, Revive and Dispatch paintings slide in.
Job two: follow up. Pursuit chases every new lead until they reply. Revive wins back old customers. Dispatch sends email campaigns to the customer list.
Heading morphs: "Get found". Echo, Repute and Marquee paintings.
Job three: get found. Echo keeps the Google listing complete and active. Repute asks every customer for a review. Marquee keeps the social pages posting.
Heading morphs: "Get paid". The Tap painting, alone.
Job four: get paid. Tap takes card payments on the owner's own phone, or by a text link.
Heading morphs: "Find business customers". The Radar painting, with a hairline under it and two words: "Business customers only."
Job five is only for some businesses. Radar finds business customers, for trades and services that sell to other businesses. Nobody else.
Heading morphs: "Websites". The Storefront painting.
And websites. Station designs custom websites, priced to the project, after a free demo.

Three collection names stack beside their shelves: "Answer collection · $297 a month", "Get Found · $497 a month", "Follow Up · $427 a month". A small grey note under Radar: "Never in a collection or plan."
Three of those jobs also come as collections at one price: the Answer collection, Get Found and Follow Up. Radar is never in a collection or a plan.
The truck's three notifications return. Each turns blue and snaps onto a shelf: Missed call to Answer, Form fill to Follow up, 3.9 stars to Get found.
So when an owner tells you what hurts, you already know the shelf. Then you pick the one product on it that fits.
Do-this-now: "Open Products in Partner World. Find one product from each shelf."
Open Products in Partner World and find one product from each shelf. The next lessons take them one at a time.
lessons.read_md:
Every Station product does one job. Learn the jobs and the shelf gets short.

| Job | Product | In plain words |
|---|---|---|
| **Answer** | Frontdesk | An AI receptionist that answers every call, day or night |
| | Lineback | Texts back every call they miss |
| | Greet | Answers the chat on their website |
| | Dial | A business number with texting, so their own cell stops being the company line |
| | Slate | Customers book themselves, and reminders get them to show up |
| **Follow up** | Pursuit | Follows up on every new lead until they reply or book |
| | Revive | Wins back customers who've gone quiet |
| | Dispatch | Email campaigns to their own customer list |
| **Get found** | Echo | Keeps their Google listing complete, accurate and active |
| | Repute | Asks every customer for a review and drafts the replies |
| | Marquee | Social posting, ads and a brand board |
| **Get paid** | Tap | Card payments on their phone or by text link, straight to their bank |
| **Find business customers** | Radar | Finds and contacts the businesses they want as customers (business-to-business only) |
| **Websites** | Custom website | Designed from scratch, priced to the project after a free demo |

**Collections:** the Answer collection ($297 a month), Get Found ($497 a month) and Follow Up ($427 a month) put a shelf's
products together at one price. **Radar is never in a collection or a plan.**

Listen for the job first ("I miss calls", "leads go cold", "nobody can find us"), then offer the one product on that shelf
that fits. Every price is on station.solutions and in Products; check it before you quote.

check.q: An owner says, "I'm on a roof all day and I miss half my calls." Which shelf do you reach for?
options: Follow up: Dispatch.
Get found: Echo.
Answer: Lineback or Frontdesk.
check.why: Missed calls are an answering problem. Start there, with the one product that fits.

check.q: A house cleaner who only works for homeowners saw Radar on the site and wants it. You:
options: Sell it, but tell her to cancel if it doesn't work.
Tell her Radar is built only for businesses that want business customers, and ask what's costing her work.
Sell it. Every business wants more customers.
check.why: Radar is business-to-business only. Selling it to the wrong owner breaks the guide and loses the client.

check.q: A client on the Answer collection asks you to "turn on Radar, since it's part of the package." You:
options: Tell Station to switch it on at no extra cost.
Explain Radar isn't in any collection or plan; it's its own product at its own price, and only for business customers.
Say yes, it's included in every collection.
check.why: Radar is never included in a collection or plan.

lessons.title: Greet: the website that answers back
lessons.goal: Pitch Greet to an owner whose website gets visitors, and know what it never does.
film: 8:41 PM. A woman on her couch, phone in hand, on a plumber's website. She types into a box: "Do you do tankless?" Nothing comes back.
Eight forty-one at night. She has one question for a plumber. She's not going to call at this hour.
8:43 PM. She swipes to the next plumber's site. Text on paper: "Gone. The next site answered."
Two minutes later she's on the next site. That plumber never knew she existed.
The Greet painting fills the frame, then slides back into the real station.solutions/greet/ page in a browser frame, on the "same 8:41 PM visit, with and without it" story.
That's what Greet is for. Station's Greet is a chat assistant on the business's website.
The "With Greet" side plays: "We do. Want Thursday morning?" then "Name, number and the job, captured."
It answers from the owner's own business facts, asks the right questions, and drops the visitor's name, number and the job into their inbox. The owner can take over live any time.
Three price lines count in: "$79 a month · 250 chats", "Busy $149 a month · 750", "High Volume $249 a month · 1,750".
It's $79 a month for 250 chats a month. Busy is $149 a month, and High Volume is $249 a month. A chat is one visitor's conversation in a day.
A stopwatch: "Live in minutes." Under it: "Station built the site? Nothing needed. Otherwise: one line of code, added by Station."
It's live in minutes. If Station built the site, there's nothing to do. Otherwise Station adds one line of code, or the owner sends Station an invite to add it.
A split card. Left "For": a website that gets visitors. Right "Not for": an Instagram profile with no website.

It's for a business whose website gets visitors. No website? Greet has nowhere to live. Ask about the missed messages instead, and look at the Answer collection, which comes with a free Station-built website.
The real Partner World Greet cheat sheet; the opener highlights in blue: "When someone visits your website late at night with a question, what happens?"
Open with one question. When someone visits your website late at night with a question, what happens?
A red rule strikes three lines: "It's a real person." "It never makes a mistake." "It'll quote your prices."
Never say it's a person, never say it can't make a mistake, and never say it quotes prices. It only does that if the owner allows it, and it hands off when it's unsure.
Do-this-now: "Open greet in Products. Read the opener out loud."
Open Greet in Products and say the opener out loud once.
lessons.read_md:
**What it does.** Station's Greet is a chat assistant on the business's website. It answers visitors from the owner's business
facts (services, hours, service area), qualifies them, and captures name, number and the job into their inbox. The owner can
take over live. It never quotes prices unless the owner allows it, and it hands off when it's unsure.

**Who it's for:** any business whose website gets visitors, especially at night and on weekends.
**Not for:** an owner with no website. Ask about missed messages instead; the Answer collection includes Greet and a free
Station-built website.

**Price:** $79 a month for 250 chats a month. Busy $149 a month (750). High Volume $249 a month (1,750). A chat is one
visitor's conversation in 24 hours. It starts with a 14-day free trial.

**Live in:** minutes. **Station needs:** nothing if Station built the site; otherwise one line of code (Station adds it) or an
invite for Station to add it, plus the owner's common questions. You never handle their website login.

**Open with:** "When someone visits your website late at night with a question, what happens?"
**One-line pitch:** "Greet is a chat assistant on your website. It answers visitors from your own business facts, day or night,
and passes you their name, number and what they need. It's $79 a month."

**Never promise:** that it's a person, that it never makes mistakes, that it quotes prices, or a number of leads.

check.q: The owner asks, "Will it make up prices and promise my customers things?" You say:
options: "It quotes whatever prices it finds online, so customers get an answer."
"No. It answers from your business facts, doesn't quote prices unless you allow it, and hands off to you when it's unsure."
"It's never wrong, so you won't need to check it."
check.why: Greet answers from the owner's facts and hands off when unsure. Never claim it can't make mistakes.

check.q: A mobile detailer runs his whole business from Instagram DMs and has no website. Do you lead with Greet?
options: No. Greet lives on a website. Ask about missed messages and look at the Answer collection, which includes a free Station-built site.
Yes, Greet works without a website.
Yes, and tell him to build a site himself first.
check.why: Pitch the fit. With no website, Greet has nothing to answer on.

check.q: The owner says, "I'll text you my website login so you can put the chat on." You:
options: Take the login and add it yourself to save time.
Forward the login to Station by email.
Thank him and say no. Station adds it after signup, with an invite or one line of code.
check.why: You never handle a client's logins or passwords. Station does all setup.

lessons.title: Slate: they book themselves, then they show up
lessons.goal: Pitch Slate to an appointment business, and know when not to sell it at all.
film: 9:00 AM, Tuesday. An empty barber chair, a cape folded on it. A wall clock ticks to 9:20. A phone screen: "Voicemail."
Tuesday, nine o'clock. The chair's empty. He calls. Voicemail. "Totally forgot, man."
Text on paper: "A paid hour, empty." The hour block on a calendar greys out.
That hour is gone. You can't sell it again.
The Slate painting, then the real station.solutions/slate/ page in a browser frame, on its "same Tuesday morning" story.
Station's Slate fixes both ends of that. Customers book themselves into the owner's real availability, so there's no back-and-forth.
The "With Slate" side plays: "Reminder: 9 AM tomorrow. Reply C to confirm." He replies C. He walks in.
Then texts and emails remind them, at booking, the night before and two hours out. They can reply to confirm. Miss anyway, and a rebook text goes out on its own.
Price lines count in: "$59 a month · 1,000 reminders", "Busy $97 a month · 2,500". A small blue tag: "Free inside Frontdesk."
It's $59 a month for 1,000 reminders a month, or Busy at $97 a month. And it's free inside Frontdesk.
A five-minute timer on a short form: "Services and how long they take", "Hours you'll take". Two status lines: "Email reminders: day one." "Texts: about 2 business days, carrier registration."
It's live today after a five-minute hours form. Email reminders run on day one. Text reminders wait about two business days on carrier registration for a business that's new to it. Station files it.
Split card. "For": barbers, salons, clinics, gyms, detailers. "Not for": a calendar app already open on a salon owner's phone, and a Frontdesk tag.
It's for any business that runs on appointments. Not for an owner who's happy with the booking app she already pays for, and not as an extra for anyone buying Frontdesk. It's already inside.
The Slate cheat sheet in Partner World; the opener highlights blue.
Open with: How do customers book with you right now? Do they call, or is there a lot of back-and-forth?
Red rule through: "Texts start today." "Cuts no-shows by half."
Never promise text reminders today, and never put a number on the no-shows it saves.
Do-this-now: "Ask the opener to the next owner who mentions no-shows."
Next owner who mentions a no-show, ask how they book today.
lessons.read_md:
**What it does.** Station's Slate lets customers book themselves into the owner's real availability, with no double-booking.
Reminders go out by text and email (at booking, the night before and two hours out), customers can reply to confirm, and a
missed appointment gets an automatic rebook text.

**Who it's for:** appointment businesses: barbers, salons, clinics, gyms, detailers, and trades with booked visits.
**Not for:** an owner happy with a booking app they already pay for (don't pitch booking to someone who has it), and anyone
buying Frontdesk, because Slate is free inside it.

**Price:** $59 a month for 1,000 reminders a month, or Busy $97 a month (2,500). Free inside Frontdesk. 14-day
free trial.

**Live in:** today, after a five-minute hours form. Email reminders run on day one; text reminders wait about 2 business days on
carrier registration for a business new to it. Station files it with the legal business name, EIN and address.
**Station needs:** services with real durations, working hours, and their calendar.

**Open with:** "How do customers book with you right now? Do they call, or is there a lot of back-and-forth?"
**One-line pitch:** "Slate lets customers pick a time from your real schedule, then sends reminders so they show up. It's $59 a month."

**Never promise:** text reminders today, a number of no-shows saved, or that it works with a particular booking app (Station can
confirm that).

check.q: An owner buying Frontdesk asks you to add Slate too. You:
options: Tell him to buy Slate first and Frontdesk next month.
Add Slate so he gets online booking.
Tell him Slate comes free inside Frontdesk, so there's nothing to add.
check.why: Frontdesk includes Slate and a number. Selling both charges him twice for the same thing.

check.q: A new client says, "So the text reminders start tomorrow morning?" You say:
options: "Yes, everything's live tomorrow."
"Texts start the minute you pay."
"Email reminders run from day one. Texts start after carrier registration, about 2 business days, and the carriers control that."
check.why: Never promise same-day texting. Carrier registration comes first.

check.q: A salon owner already pays for a booking app she likes. What do you do?
options: Tell her Slate is better and she should switch.
Promise Slate works with her app.
Leave booking alone and ask about clients who haven't been back in a while.
check.why: Don't pitch booking to someone who has it. How Station sits beside her app is a question for Station.

lessons.title: Lineback: missed the call, not the customer
lessons.goal: Pitch Lineback to an owner who misses calls on the job, without promising when the texts start.
film: 4:47 PM, Friday. A plumber flat on his back under a kitchen sink, wrench in hand. On the floor beside him his phone rings and rings.
Friday, four forty-seven. He's under a sink. The phone rings.
4:48 PM: "Voicemail." 5:10 PM: a text on paper, "She booked the next plumber on the list."
Voicemail. Nobody leaves one anymore. Twenty minutes later, she's booked the next plumber on the list.
The Lineback painting, then the real station.solutions/lineback/ page in a browser frame, on "the same Friday afternoon" story.
Station's Lineback is for exactly that call.
The "With Lineback" side plays: 4:48 PM a text goes out, "Sorry we missed you, what's going on?" 4:52 PM she replies. 5:30 PM he answers from the van.
Every call the owner misses gets a text back within seconds, in the business's name, asking what they need. The reply lands in their inbox, and they answer when they're free.
Price lines count in: "$197 a month · 1,500 texts", "Busy $297 a month · 5,000". A tag: "Business number included."
It's $197 a month for 1,500 texts a month, or Busy at $297 a month. A business number is included.
A two-day calendar strip, both days shaded: "Carrier registration." Three fields fill in: "Legal business name", "EIN", "Address". A dotted arrow: "Your number forwards."

It's live in about two business days, because US carriers require registration for business texting. Station files it. The owner gives their legal business name, EIN and address, exactly as the IRS has them. They keep their own number; it forwards.
Split card. "For": plumber, roofer, HVAC, a taqueria at lunch rush. "Not for": a front desk where someone answers every call.
It's for anyone who misses calls while they work: trades on jobs, a restaurant in the lunch rush. If someone already picks up every call, they don't need it.
Lineback cheat sheet; opener highlights blue.
Open with: About how many calls do you miss in a normal week, when you're on a job or driving?
Red rule through: "Live today." "It pays for itself." "You're losing [amount] a month." "We'll port your number."
Never promise it's texting today. Never say it pays for itself, never tell an owner what they're losing, and never say Station will port their number.
Do-this-now: "Say the opener. Then ask what one job is worth to them."
Say the opener, then let them do the math on one job.
lessons.read_md:

check.q: It's Monday morning. The owner says, "Can it be texting my missed calls by this afternoon?" You say:
options: "It takes about 2 business days for carrier registration, and the carriers control that. Station files it; you just give your legal business name, EIN and address."
"I'll ask Station to skip the registration for you."
"Yes, it'll be live this afternoon."

check.q: "Do I have to change my phone number?" You say:
options: "Yes, Station ports your number over."
"Yes, you'll stop using your old number."
"No. You keep your number, and it forwards. Station doesn't port your line."

check.q: The owner asks, "So how much am I losing on missed calls?" You:
options: Say Lineback pays for itself in the first month.
Ask what an average job is worth and how many calls go to voicemail, and let them do the math.
Tell them they're losing about five jobs a week.

lessons.title: Frontdesk: every call answered, even the 2 AM one
lessons.goal: Pitch Frontdesk honestly as an automated receptionist, and know the questions you hand to Station.
film: 2:04 AM. A kitchen floor, water spreading from under the sink. A woman in a robe holds her phone to her ear; it rings, and rings.
Two oh four in the morning. A burst pipe. She calls the first plumber that says 24/7.
2:05 AM. She hangs up and dials the next number. Text on paper: "Their phone answered."
It rings six times. She hangs up and calls the next number on the list. Their phone answered.
The Frontdesk page's own painting (day-night.webp), then the real station.solutions/frontdesk/ page in a browser frame, on "the same ninety seconds" story.
Station's Frontdesk is an AI receptionist. It picks up every call, day or night.
The "With Frontdesk" side plays: "Answered on the second ring." "Is the water off? What's the address?" "Booked for 7 AM."

It answers the common questions, books the job into the calendar, takes messages, and always offers to transfer the caller to a person. Every call is transcribed into the inbox. If it ever fails, calls ring the owner's phone.
Price lines count in: "$397 a month · 750 min", "Busy $597 a month · 1,200", "High Volume $897 a month · 2,500". Two tags: "Slate included." "Number included."
It's $397 a month for 750 minutes a month. Busy is $597 a month, and High Volume is $897 a month. Slate and a number come with it.
A clock: "Live the same day." Under it: "Business facts. What it may and may not say. Call forwarding. Calendar. One test call with Station."
It's live the same day. Voice has no carrier wait. Station needs the business facts, what it may and may not say, call forwarding, the calendar, and one test call.
Split card. "For": a shop where the owner is always with a customer, emergency trades, multi-truck shops. "Not for": a one-man shop that misses two calls a week.
It's for businesses where the phone rings while everyone's busy. A one-man shop that misses a couple of calls a week may only need Lineback.
Frontdesk cheat sheet; opener highlights blue.
Open with: Who answers the phone when you're busy with a customer?
Red rule through: "Callers can't tell it's a robot." "It never makes mistakes." "It's HIPAA compliant." "It'll quote your prices."

Never say callers can't tell it's a robot, or that it never makes mistakes. Never answer a HIPAA or compliance question. And it never quotes custom prices or promises timelines; those go to a message or a transfer.
Do-this-now: "Practice the robot answer out loud." The answer types on screen.
Practice this out loud: It's an automated assistant. It answers from your business facts and always offers a transfer to a person.
