lessons.title: Dial: a business number, not your cell
lessons.goal: Pitch Dial to an owner whose cell is the company line, and know who doesn't need it.
film: Saturday, 9 PM. A family dinner table. A dad's phone buzzes face-up next to his plate: "Hey, can you quote a drain cleaning?"
Saturday night, family dinner. A customer texts his personal cell. Again.
Sunday: the same thread scrolls. Family photos, then a drain-cleaning quote, then more photos. Monday: a new hire asks, "Which number do I text customers from?"
Family photos and a drain quote in the same thread. Then he hires someone, and there's no number for them to use.
The Dial painting, then the real station.solutions/dial/ page in a browser frame, on "the same weekend" story.
Station's Dial gives the business its own number.
The "With Dial" side plays: "Day 1: pick a local number, or forward your old one." "Day 2: texts go out from the app or your desk." "Day 30: you hire. The number is the company's."
A local business number with two-way texting, from the owner's phone or desk. Every thread is saved and searchable, and shared if they add staff.
Price line counts in: "$47 a month · 1,000 texts".
It's $47 a month for 1,000 texts a month. The cheapest way into Station.
A two-day strip, shaded: "Carrier registration." Fields fill: "Legal business name", "EIN", "Address".
It's live in about two business days, for carrier registration. Station files it with the legal business name, EIN and address. No EIN? Tell Station before anything else.
Split card. "For": solo owners and small crews using a personal cell. "Not for": Lineback and Frontdesk tags, each with "number included".
It's for owners whose personal cell is the business line. Not for anyone buying Lineback or Frontdesk: both come with a number. It's in the Answer collection too.
Dial cheat sheet; opener highlights blue.
Open with: Is the number on your truck and your website your personal cell phone?
Red rule through: "Texting today." "We'll port your number."
Never promise texting today, and never say Station ports their number. They keep it and forward it.
Do-this-now: "Check: is the number on their website a cell?"
Before your next call, look at the number on their website and their truck. That's your opener.
lessons.read_md:
**What it does.** Station's Dial gives the business a local number with two-way texting, from the owner's phone (in the app) or
desk. Threads are saved, searchable and shared with staff. They can pick a new local number or forward their existing line to it.

**Who it's for:** solo owners and small crews whose personal cell is the business line, especially anyone about to hire.
**Not for:** anyone buying Lineback or Frontdesk (both include a number). Dial is also part of the Answer collection.

**Price:** $47 a month for 1,000 texts a month. 14-day free trial.

**Live in:** about 2 business days, for carrier registration. **Station needs:** legal business name, EIN and address, and where
calls forward. If the business has no EIN, tell Station.

**Open with:** "Is the number on your truck and your website your personal cell phone?"
**One-line pitch:** "Dial gives your business its own local number, with texting, that works from your phone. It's $47 a month."

**Never promise:** same-day texting. Never say "port": they keep their number and forward it.

check.q: An owner buying Lineback asks you to add Dial so he has a business number. You:
options: Add Dial; Lineback has no number.
Tell him Lineback already includes a business number, so he doesn't need Dial.
Add Dial and Frontdesk to be safe.
check.why: Lineback and Frontdesk both come with a number. Don't sell Dial on top.

check.q: "Do I have to give up my cell number?" You say:
options: "No. You can keep it and forward it to the business number. Station doesn't port your line."
"Yes, you'll need to cancel it."
"Yes, Station ports it over and you get a new personal number."
check.why: Say "forward", never "port".

check.q: The owner runs his business under his own name and doesn't have an EIN. You:
options: Sign him up and hope it goes through.
Tell him to make one up for now.
Tell Station, because carrier registration needs the legal business name, EIN and address.
check.why: A business with no EIN, or any carrier registration problem, goes to Station.

lessons.title: Tap: paid before the van leaves the drive
lessons.goal: Pitch Tap to an owner who waits to get paid, and get the money and card-fee answers exactly right.
film: Friday, a driveway. A tradesman packs his tools. The homeowner waves from the door: "I'll mail you a check!"
Friday. The job's done. "I'll mail you a check."
+3 weeks: a calendar flips; he types an awkward text, "Hi, just checking on…" +5 weeks: text on paper, "A collections agency with a wrench."
Three weeks later, no check. He texts, awkwardly. Five weeks later, he's a collections agency with a wrench.
The Tap painting, then the real station.solutions/tap/ page in a browser frame, on "the same finished job" story.
Station's Tap gets the owner paid on the spot.
The "With Tap" side plays: "4:02 PM: the estimate they accepted becomes the invoice." "4:05 PM: their card taps your phone." "The receipt texts itself."
Tap-to-pay on the owner's own phone, no new hardware. Or a text-to-pay link. Unlimited estimates and invoices, and receipts go out automatically. With Repute, a paid invoice can send the review ask.
Price line counts in: "$47 a month + your processor's card rates". Under it: "Station takes 0% of your revenue."
It's $47 a month, plus the card processor's standard rates, which the site puts at about 2.6 to 2.9 percent, paid to the processor. Station takes zero percent of their revenue.
Money icon travels from a customer's card straight into the owner's bank, past the Station mark, which doesn't touch it. Text: "Their own Stripe or Square account."
The money goes straight to the owner's bank, through their own free Stripe or Square account. Station never holds a dollar.
A clock: "Live in 1 to 2 days." Under it: "Station needs: their own processor account, set up by them, about 10 minutes."
It's live in one to two days. The owner sets up their own processor account, about ten minutes. You never set it up and never touch their bank details.
Split card. "For": trades, detailers, cleaners, mobile services, anyone who invoices and waits. Tap cheat sheet below; opener highlights blue.
It's for anyone who finishes a job and waits to get paid. Open with: How do customers pay you right now: invoice, cash, check or card?
Red rule through: "No card fees." "Station holds your money." "Give me your bank details."
Never say there are no card fees, never say Station holds their money, and never ask for their bank details.
Do-this-now: "Say the price line exactly: '$47 a month plus the normal card fees.'"
Say the price the same way every time: $47 a month, plus the normal card fees.
lessons.read_md:
**What it does.** Station's Tap lets the owner take payment on the spot: tap-to-pay on their own phone (no new hardware) or a
text-to-pay link. It includes unlimited estimates and invoices and automatic receipts, and it works in the mobile app. With
Repute, a paid invoice can trigger the review ask.

**Who it's for:** anyone who finishes a job and waits to be paid: trades, detailers, cleaners, mobile services.
**Not for:** an owner who won't set up their own processor account. Tap runs on their account, never Station's.

**Price:** $47 a month, plus their processor's standard card rates (the site puts them at about 2.6 to 2.9%), paid to the processor.
Station takes zero percent of their revenue. 14-day free trial.

**Live in:** 1 to 2 days. **Station needs:** their own free Stripe or Square account, set up by them (about 10 minutes). The money
goes straight to their bank.

**Open with:** "How do customers pay you right now: invoice, cash, check or card?"
**One-line pitch:** "Tap lets you take payment on the spot, by tapping a card on your phone or by texting a payment link. The money
goes straight to your own bank. It's $47 a month plus the normal card fees."

**Never promise:** no card fees, faster payment by a set date, or that Station holds or moves their money. Never set up their
account or handle bank details.

check.q: "Where does the money actually go?" You say:
options: "Station collects it and pays you at the end of the month."
"Into your Station account, minus Station's cut."
"Straight from your customer to your bank, through your own Stripe or Square account. Station never holds it and takes none of your revenue."
check.why: Tap runs on the owner's own processor account. Station takes zero percent.

check.q: The owner says, "Can you set up the Stripe account for me? I'll read you my bank details." You:
options: Pass his bank details to Station by Message Station.
Write down the details and set it up for him.
Say no thanks. He sets up his own account in about ten minutes, and Station connects Tap to it.
check.why: You never handle bank details, passwords or ID.

check.q: "So it's $47 a month and nothing else?" You say:
options: "$47 a month, plus the normal card fees from your processor. Station adds nothing on top."
"Yes, no card fees at all."
"Plus Station's own percentage on every sale."
check.why: Card rates are the processor's and paid to them. Station takes zero percent.

lessons.title: Marquee: be the name they remember
lessons.goal: Pitch Marquee self-serve or Managed, and handle "social doesn't bring me work."
film: Monday. A landscaper scrolls his own business Facebook page on his phone: last post, 2024. He opens "Create post", stares, closes it.
Monday. He means to post something. What, though?
Wednesday: a competitor's before-and-after of a backyard gets shared again and again; share counts tick up. Month 6: two parents talking at school pickup, "Use them, they're great."
Wednesday, the competitor's before-and-after gets shared all over town. Six months later, theirs is the name people say at school pickup.
The Marquee painting, then the real station.solutions/marquee/ page in a browser frame, on "the same six months" story.
Station's Marquee keeps the owner's name in front of people.

Nine platform names line up on a hairline: Facebook, Instagram, Google profile, LinkedIn, TikTok, Pinterest, YouTube, Threads, Bluesky. A tenth slot, "X", greys out. A brand board card flips in: "Week one."
A brand board in week one, so everything matches. Posting to nine platforms from one place, not X. And a self-serve ad manager for Meta and Google.
Two price columns: "Self-serve $197 a month" and "Managed $597 a month + ad spend: 12 posts a month, ads built and run, monthly numbers."
Self-serve is $197 a month, and the owner can still post their own jobs. Managed is $597 a month plus ad spend: Station makes twelve posts a month, runs the ads and sends the numbers.
A card icon labelled "Their card" with a cap dial set by a hand. Text: "Ad spend: theirs, on their card, capped by them."
Ad spend is always the owner's, on their own card, with a cap they set. The page has the rest of the ad fine print; point them there.
A clock: "Live in 5 to 7 days." Under it: "Station needs: social accounts connected by the owner on a guided setup, logo, job photos. Managed: their ad account."
It's live in five to seven days. The owner connects their own accounts on a guided setup, and sends logo files and job photos. Managed needs their ad account too.
Split card. "For": landscapers, remodelers, salons, restaurants with pages that stopped. "Not for": "I want social to bring me jobs next week." Marquee cheat sheet below; opener highlights blue.
It's for any business whose pages have gone quiet. Not for someone expecting social to bring jobs next week. Open with: When did you last post anything on your business's social media?
Red rule through: "More followers." "Jobs from social." "Posts to X." "Send me your passwords."
Never promise followers, jobs or ad results. It doesn't post to X. And never take their social passwords.
Do-this-now: "Practice: 'People check it after your reviews.'"
When they say social doesn't bring them work, agree, then say: people check it after your reviews.
lessons.read_md:
**What it does.** Station's Marquee builds a brand board in week one, posts to nine platforms from one place (Facebook, Instagram,
Google profile, LinkedIn, TikTok, Pinterest, YouTube, Threads and Bluesky; not X), and includes a self-serve ad manager for Meta
and Google.

**Two tiers:**
- **Self-serve, $197 a month:** the owner runs it, with templates and the brand board.
- **Managed, $597 a month plus ad spend:** Station makes 12 posts a month, builds and runs the ads, and sends monthly numbers.
  Ad spend goes on the client's own card with a cap they set. Managed ads above a set monthly spend add a percentage of spend;
  the Marquee page has the exact terms.

**Who it's for:** businesses whose pages stopped posting, especially visual work: landscaping, remodeling, salons, restaurants.
**Not for:** an owner who expects social to bring jobs directly and fast.

**Live in:** 5 to 7 days. **Station needs:** social accounts, connected by the owner on a guided setup (never their passwords to
you), logo files and job photos; Managed also needs their ad account.

**Open with:** "When did you last post anything on your business's social media?"
**One-line pitch:** "Marquee keeps your social media posting regularly, on Facebook, Instagram, your Google profile and more. It's
$197 a month, and you can still post your own jobs whenever you like. For $597 a month plus ad spend, Station makes the
posts and runs your ads for you."

**If they say "Social doesn't bring me work":** "Often not directly. But people check it after your reviews, and a page that
stopped posting two years ago makes them wonder if you're still open."

**Never promise:** followers, jobs, leads or ad results. Never say it posts to X.

check.q: "Can it post to X for me?" You say:
options: "Yes, X is included."
"Yes, on Managed."
"No. It posts to nine platforms, like Facebook, Instagram and your Google profile, but X isn't one of them."
check.why: X isn't one of Marquee's nine platforms.

check.q: On Managed, "Who pays for the ads?" You say:
options: "You pay me and I pass it to Station."
"Station covers the ads inside the Managed price."
"You do, on your own card, with a cap you set. That's on top of the Managed price."
check.why: Ad spend is always the client's, on their card, capped by them. You never take payments.

check.q: To get going, the owner offers you his Facebook and Instagram passwords. You:
options: Take them and pass them to Station.
Log in and set up the first posts yourself.
Say no thanks. He connects his own accounts on Station's guided setup.
check.why: You never handle a client's passwords or set anything up.

lessons.title: The custom website: see it before you pay
lessons.goal: Send an owner to a free custom-website demo, and never put a number on a site or its care.
film: 9:12 PM. A homeowner on a laptop searches a remodeler's name. She lands on a Facebook page, last updated in 2023.
Nine twelve at night. She looks him up. She finds a Facebook page last updated in 2023.
9:13 PM: she clicks a competitor's site. Clean, a "Book now" button. 9:16 PM: "Booked." Text on paper: "She never knew you existed."
One minute later, she's on his competitor's site. Clean, with a book-now button. Three minutes after that, she's booked them.
The Storefront painting, then the real station.solutions/storefront/ page in a browser frame.
Station designs custom websites, from scratch, around the business. Not a template.
Three steps draw down a hairline: "A few minutes of questions at station.solutions/custom/." "A free demo, by hand, in 2 to 3 business days." "Nothing charged until they say yes."

The owner answers a few minutes of questions on station.solutions/custom/, from your link. Station builds a free demo by hand and emails it within two to three business days. Nothing is charged until they've seen it and said yes.
The demo lands in an inbox as a live link. Two notes: "Revisions until it's right." "Your domain and your site stay yours." Booking and lead forms wire into a Station inbox icon.
Booking and lead forms go straight to their Station inbox. Station revises it until it's right, and the domain and the site stay theirs.
A price tag spins in and reads only: "Priced to the project." A second tag: "Hosting & care: quoted by Station."

There's no published price. It's priced to the project. After it's built, the owner runs it themselves, or Station hosts and looks after it for a monthly fee Station quotes. You never quote either one.

Split card. "For": an owner who cares how the business looks and has outgrown a do-it-yourself site. "Not for": an owner buying a collection who only needs a simple site, with a tag "Free Station-built site included."
It's for owners who want to look like the most established firm in town. If they're buying a collection or plan and only need a simple site, one comes free with it.
The Custom website cheat sheet in Partner World; "Your link" and Copy highlight blue. Then the opener.

Send your link from the Custom website cheat sheet, so the demo is credited to you. Open with: Is your website bringing in the kind of customers you want, or is it something you've been meaning to fix?
Red rule through: "Usually a few thousand." "Hosting is about…" "It'll be live by the 1st." "I'll build you a mock-up."
Never give a price, a range, a hosting number or a launch date. And you never build anything yourself.
Do-this-now: "Copy your custom website link from Products."
Copy your custom website link from Products now, so it's ready the first time someone asks.
lessons.read_md:
**What it does.** Station designs a custom website from scratch around the business, not a template, with booking and lead forms
wired to their Station inbox. Station revises it until it's right. The domain and site stay the client's.

**How it works:** send your link from the Custom website cheat sheet (station.solutions/custom/?ref=yourcode) and mark the call
Interested. The owner answers a few minutes of questions. Station builds a free demo by hand and emails it within 2 to 3 business
days. Nothing is charged until they've seen it and said yes. Mark it Won only when Station tells you they've said yes. Websites
never have a free trial.

**Price:** priced to the project, with no published price. After it's built, the client runs it themselves, or Station hosts and
looks after it for a monthly **hosting & care** fee that Station quotes for each client. You earn 40% of the setup fee,
once; hosting & care earns nothing.

**Who it's for:** owners who care how the business comes across and have outgrown a do-it-yourself site.
**Not for:** an owner on Core or Pro who just needs a simple site: a free Station-built website of up to 5 pages comes with those
plans (Max includes a custom-designed one). Owners on a collection get 50% off a custom website, which Station quotes.

**Station needs:** the form answers, their domain (or Station registers one), logo, photos and services.

**Open with:** "Is your website bringing in the kind of customers you want, or is it something you've been meaning to fix?"
**One-line pitch:** "Station builds custom websites from scratch around your brand. You answer a few minutes of questions, and
Station builds a free demo of your own site, usually within 2 to 3 business days. Nothing's charged unless you like it and say yes."

**Never:** quote a price or a range for the build or for hosting & care, promise a launch date, build or mock up anything yourself,
or send a demo to someone who didn't ask for it. Don't call any site in the portfolio a client or reference unless Station says so.

check.q: "Ballpark, what does a site like that cost?" You say:
options: "It's priced to the project, so there's no set price I can quote. Station builds a free demo of your own site first, and nothing's charged unless you say yes."
"About the same as a few months of Frontdesk."
"Usually somewhere in the low thousands."
check.why: Never quote or estimate a custom website price.

check.q: "And what would hosting it cost every month?" You:
options: Say it's free forever.
Quote what your last client pays.
Say Station quotes hosting & care for each business, and pass on what they need with Message Station.
check.why: Hosting & care has no list price. Station quotes it, every time.

check.q: An owner signing up for the Answer collection says, "I also need a website." You:
options: Tell him the collection comes with 50% off a custom website, send him the custom website link, and let Station quote it.
Quote him half of what your last client paid.
Tell him a free website comes with the collection.
check.why: Collections get 50% off a custom website, quoted by Station. Only Core and Pro include a free Station-built site.

lessons.title: The free mobile app

Job done. He replies to a customer and takes the payment, from the driveway, on his own phone.
Paper. Headline: "The mobile app." Under it a tag, blue: "Free with every Station account."
That's the Station mobile app. It's free with every Station account, and it's never sold on its own.

Real lines from station.solutions slide in, one by one, inside browser frames: Dial page, "Texts go out from the app or your desk." Tap page, "Works in the mobile app." Repute page, "Or mark it in the app."

An onboarding call card: "Station sends download details."
Station gives the owner the download details during onboarding.

Do-this-now: "Use it near the close: 'And the mobile app is free with your account.'"

lessons.read_md:
The Station mobile app is **free with every Station account** and isn't sold separately, so never quote a price for it.

It lets the owner run their account from their phone. The product pages mention texting from it (Dial), taking payments in it
(Tap), and marking a job done so Repute sends the review request. Station gives download details during onboarding.

check.q: "How much extra is the app?" You say:
options: "Nothing. It's free with your Station account, and it isn't sold separately."
"It's a small monthly add-on."
"It's free for the first year."

"Yes, your own branded app in the app stores."
"The app is for you to run your account. If you want more than that, Station can confirm what's possible."

check.q: A new client asks where to download the app. You say:

modules.title: Collections & plans
modules.outcome: Say what's in each collection and plan, the trial and website rules for each, and pick the smallest one that fits in three questions.

lessons.title: Lead with the smallest fix
lessons.goal: Explain why you always start with the smallest thing that fixes what's hurting most.
film: A phone call card: "Jaylen, mobile detailer". A big price slides onto it: "Max · $2,797 a month". The call card greys out: "Call ended".
Here's the fastest way to lose a small owner. Say a big number first.
Rewind sweep. Paper. A ladder draws up from a hairline, three rungs labelled bottom to top: "One product." "A collection." "A plan."
Station sells at three sizes. One product. A collection, a few products built to work as one. Or a plan that covers the whole front office.
The bottom rung that matches the detailer's problem lights blue: "Start here."
You start on the lowest rung that fixes what's hurting most. Every time.
Reason one types in: "They keep listening." A small price, "$47 a month", sits under it.
Why? One: an owner who hears a small number keeps listening. Single products start at $47 a month. Collections start at $297 a month.
Reason two: "They can undo it." Two tags clip on: "14 days free" and "No contract".
Two: people say yes to what they can undo. Single products and collections start with a 14-day free trial, and there's no contract.
Reason three: "It works, so they add more." A client card gains products months apart: Lineback, then "+ Repute", then "+ Pursuit".
Three: a client who sees one thing working adds more later. Every product they add is in your book.
The three reasons fold into one line: "Pitch the fit, not the biggest number."
So pitch the fit, not the biggest number. A plan is the right answer only when the owner tells you most of the front office is the problem.
Do-this-now: "Before every call, read the best fit on the card. Lead with that."
Before every call, read the best fit on the card in Calls, and lead with that.
lessons.read_md:
Station sells at three sizes:
1. **One product**, from $47 a month.
2. **A collection**: a few products built to work as one, from $297 a month.
3. **A plan** (Core, Pro or Max): the whole front office, from $1,297 a month.

**Always lead with the smallest one that fixes what's hurting most.** Three reasons:
- **They keep listening.** A small owner who hears a plan price first usually stops listening.
- **They can undo it.** Single products and collections start with a 14-day free trial, and there's no contract.
- **It works, so they add more.** A client who sees one product working adds more later, and each one is in your book.

Offer a plan when the owner says most of the front office is the problem, not before.

check.q: A roofer says his reviews are thin. His Google listing is fine and he answers his own calls. What do you lead with?
options: Every product, so he can pick.
Station's Repute, the single product for reviews.
Core, because it covers reviews and much more.
check.why: Lead with the smallest thing that fixes the one gap he named. He can add more once it's working.

check.q: Why lead with the smallest fix?
options: Small owners keep listening, it's easy to try and undo, and one product working leads to more.
It pays you the most.
Plans aren't allowed on a first call.
check.why: The small, reversible first step is the one people say yes to. You earn on every product they add later.

lessons.title: The three collections
lessons.goal: Say what's in Answer, Get Found and Follow Up, who each is for, and what comes with them.
film: The real station.solutions/products/ page scrolls to "Pick what hurts." in a browser frame. Three collection cards sit side by side.
A collection is a few products built to work as one, priced under buying them separately. There are three, and each one matches a kind of pain.
The Answer card lifts forward; its tag "Most start here" pulses once. Price: "$297 a month".
The Answer collection, $297 a month. For the shop that misses calls. Most clients start here.
Five product paintings fan out from the Answer card, labelled: Lineback, Greet, Slate, Dial, Tap.
Inside: Lineback texts back missed calls. Greet chats with website visitors. Slate takes bookings and sends reminders. Dial gives them a business number that texts. Tap takes card payments.
A sixth painting, Frontdesk, hovers beside the fan with a "+" and the label "Add-on".
And Answer can add Frontdesk, the receptionist that answers every call, as an add-on. The add-on price is on the Answer page. Quote it from there.
Get Found lifts forward: "$497 a month". Three paintings fan out: Echo, Repute, Marquee.

The Get Found collection, $497 a month. For the shop people can't find. Echo manages their Google profile, Repute asks for reviews and drafts replies, and Marquee posts to their social pages, self-serve.
Follow Up lifts forward: "$427 a month". Three paintings fan out: Pursuit, Revive, Dispatch.

The Follow Up collection, $427 a month. For leads that went quiet and customers who drifted. Pursuit follows up every new lead, Revive wins back old customers, and Dispatch sends email campaigns, self-serve.
Under all three cards, three tags drop in, one per beat: "No setup fee." "14 days free." "50% off a custom website."
All three have no setup fee and start with a 14-day free trial. And each one comes with 50% off a custom website. The custom website is still quoted by Station, so you never say a number.
A Radar painting tries to join a collection fan and is set aside, labelled "Add-on, business-to-business only".
Radar is never in a collection. It's a separate product for business-to-business trades.
Do-this-now: "Open Products. Filter by Collections. Read all three cheat sheets."
Open Products in Partner World, filter by Collections, and read all three cheat sheets.
lessons.read_md:
Each collection costs less than buying its products one by one (each collection card on station.solutions shows what they'd be worth
separately). All three have **no setup fee**, start with a **14-day free trial**, and come with **50% off a custom website**
(Station still quotes the custom website, so never say a number).

| Collection | Price | What's in it | For the owner who says |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Answer** | $297 a month | Lineback (missed-call text-back), Greet (website chat), Slate (booking and reminders), Dial (business number with texting), Tap (card payments) | "I miss calls and messages." |
| **Get Found** | $497 a month | Echo (Google profile, managed), Repute (review requests and replies), Marquee (social posting, self-serve) | "I need reviews and Google." |
| **Follow Up** | $427 a month | Pursuit (lead follow-up), Revive (win-back campaigns), Dispatch (email campaigns, self-serve) | "Leads and old customers go cold." |

lessons.goal: Say what Core, Pro and Max each include, and who each one is for.

Three owner cards line up under the plans: "Most of the front office is the problem" → Core. "Busy, and wants marketing done" → Pro. "Top volume, wants it all handled" → Max.

lessons.read_md:
Every plan covers **every product except Radar**, has **no setup fee**, and costs less than buying the same products one by one.

| Plan | Price | What's in it |
|---|---|---|
| **Core** | $1,297 a month | All twelve products except Radar at their Standard size, including Frontdesk at 750 minutes, plus a **free Station-built website**. |
| **Pro** | $2,197 a month | Everything at its busy size (for example Greet 750 chats, Lineback 5,000 texts, Frontdesk 1,200 minutes, Slate 2,500 reminders, Pursuit 6,000 texts and 40,000 emails). Station writes and posts 12 social posts a month and writes and sends 4 email campaigns a month. Plus a **free Station-built website**. |
| **Max** | $2,797 a month | Everything at its top size (for example Greet 1,750 chats, Frontdesk 2,500 minutes), social and email done for them, priority support and a quarterly review call, plus a **custom-designed website**. |

**Plans have no free trial.** They're billed at checkout, with a **30-day money-back guarantee on the first paid month**.

Max was called Custom before October 4, 2026. "Custom" now only means a quoted custom website.

**Who each is for:** Core when most of the front office is the problem; Pro when the business is busy and wants its social and email
run for it; Max when they want the top size, done for them, with a custom site. If the owner hesitates at the price, a collection or
a single product with a free trial may be the better start.

lessons.title: Trials, money-back and the website
lessons.goal: State the trial, refund and website rules exactly, so you never promise one that doesn't exist.
film: Two doors on paper. Left door: "Single products and collections". Right door: "Core, Pro, Max".
There are two sets of rules, and mixing them up is the most common mistake partners make.
Left door opens: a calendar with 14 days shaded blue: "Free trial".
Single products, at every tier, and the three collections start with a 14-day free trial. That's the only trial you may advertise.
A hand writes "30 days?" on the calendar; the note slides off to a Message Station bubble.
If someone asks for longer, only Station can agree it, case by case, and never more than 30 days. Pass the question on.
Right door opens: a receipt prints "Billed at checkout". A stamp lands: "30-day money-back on the first paid month".
Core, Pro and Max have no trial. They're billed at checkout and carry a 30-day money-back guarantee on the first paid month.
A red strike through "Money back any time."
Never say "money back any time". Refunds are only for billing errors, or that money-back guarantee on a plan's first paid month.
A month-to-month strip: "No contract. Cancel by email. Service runs to the end of the paid period."
Everything is month to month. A client cancels by emailing main@station.solutions from the account owner's email, and service stays on to the end of the period they've paid for.

Now the website rule. Three tags snap under the plan cards: Core "Free Station-built website", Pro "Free Station-built website", Max "Custom-designed website". Under the collections: "50% off a custom website".

Now websites, as the live site states them. Core and Pro include a free Station-built website. Max includes a custom-designed website. The collections come with 50% off a custom website, which Station quotes.
A free-website timeline draws: "First paid month clears" → "Draft in 5 business days" → "Two rounds of changes".

The free website is up to five pages. Station builds it after the first paid month clears, never during a trial. The draft arrives within five business days, with two rounds of changes. Hosting and small text changes are included while they're subscribed.
A door marked "If they cancel" opens to three choices: "Site comes down at the end of the paid period", "Quoted hosting & care", "$1,250 to keep it".

If they cancel, they keep their domain, words and photos. The site comes off Station's hosting at the end of the paid period, unless they take a quoted hosting and care plan, or pay $1,250 once to keep the built site.
Do-this-now: "Say it: '14 days free on products and collections. Plans: 30-day money-back.'"
Say the rule out loud once: 14 days free on products and collections. Plans are billed at checkout with a 30-day money-back.
lessons.read_md:
**Single products (every tier) and the three collections:** a **14-day free trial**. It's the only trial you may advertise.
Only Station can agree a longer trial, case by case, and never more than 30 days. Nothing is earned during a trial.

**Core, Pro and Max:** **no trial**. Billed at checkout, with a **30-day money-back guarantee on the first paid month**.

**Websites never trial.**

**Refunds** are only for billing errors, or the 30-day money-back on a plan's first paid month. Never say "money back any time".

**Cancelling:** month to month, no contract. The client emails main@station.solutions from the account owner's email. Service stays on
to the end of the paid period; months already delivered aren't refunded. They keep their data and get a full export.

**The website rule, as station.solutions states it:**
- **Core and Pro** include a **free Station-built website**.
- **Max** includes a **custom-designed website**.
- **Collections** come with **50% off a custom website**. Station quotes the custom website; never say a number.

**The free Station-built website:** up to 5 pages. Station builds it **after the first paid month clears**, never during a trial. The draft
arrives within 5 business days, and the client gets two rounds of changes. Hosting and small text changes are included while they're
subscribed. If they cancel, they keep their domain, words and photos; the site comes off Station hosting at the end of the paid period,
unless they take a quoted hosting & care plan or pay a one-time **$1,250** to keep the built site.

check.q: An owner on the fence about Answer asks, "Can I get my money back if I don't like it?" You say:

There's a 14-day free trial and no contract, so he can try it and cancel any time.
check.why: Collections don't need a refund promise: they have a free trial. Refunds are only for billing errors or a plan's money-back.

You'll build a quick one for them yourself.

lessons.title: Yearly billing, extra locations and upgrading one product
lessons.goal: Answer the three "what if" questions about plans and collections without inventing a price.
film: The Monthly / Yearly switch on the real products page flips to "Yearly · 2 months free". The prices roll.
Three questions come up once owners like what they see. First: can I pay yearly?
Twelve month-blocks line up; two of them fade to "Free". Text: "Yearly = 10 × monthly".
Collections and plans can be billed yearly at ten times the monthly price. That's two months free.
A Message Station bubble slides in: "Owner wants yearly on Get Found."
Before you offer it, check with Station. Send the request with Message Station.
Small green text: "Prepaid commission: paid monthly, across the prepaid months."
If they prepay, your commission still arrives in equal monthly instalments, not one lump.
Second question. Three map pins drop; the second and third light up: "+ $397 a month each".
Second: what about my other locations? An extra location pack is $397 a month. It covers a Google profile, reviews and a missed-call text-back line for one more location.
Third question. A Frontdesk meter fills to 80%; a notice pings: "You've used 80% of your minutes."
Third: what if they outgrow one product? Allowances reset on the first of every month. The client is told at 80%, and the first month they go over isn't charged.
The meter overflows; a small line: "After that: twice the per-unit rate. Service never pauses." Then a dial clicks Frontdesk up from "Standard $397 a month" to "Busy $597 a month".
After that, extra use is billed at twice the per-unit rate. Service never pauses. If it keeps happening, they upgrade just that one product, for the difference. Not a bigger plan.
Do-this-now: "Open Frontdesk's cheat sheet. Find its Busy size."
Open Frontdesk's cheat sheet in Products and find its Busy size. That's the upgrade you'll suggest most.
lessons.read_md:
**Yearly billing:** collections and plans can be billed yearly at **10 times the monthly price**, which is two months free. **Check with
Station before offering a yearly plan** (Message Station). If a client prepays, your commission is paid in equal monthly instalments
across the prepaid months.

**Extra locations:** an **extra location pack** is **$397 a month**: a Google profile, reviews and a missed-call text-back line for
one more location. On single products, Repute's extra location is $177 a month each and Echo's is $197 a month each.

**Outgrowing one product:**
- Usage allowances (chats, texts, call minutes, emails) reset on the 1st of each month. The client is told at 80%.
- The first month over isn't charged. After that, extra usage is billed at twice the plan's per-unit rate on the next invoice. Top-ups
  bought ahead are cheaper. Service is never paused.
- If it keeps happening, the client **upgrades just that product, for the difference**. For example, Frontdesk Standard is
  $397 a month for 750 minutes; Busy is $597 a month for 1,200.

**Adding a product** (an upsell): the client adds it from **My Services** in their Station account, which previews the charge first, or
from the product page. Tell Station about it with **Message Station**.

check.q: A client on Frontdesk Standard goes over her minutes two months running. What do you suggest?
options: Moving her to Max.
Nothing, her calls will stop when she runs out.
Upgrading just Frontdesk to its Busy size, for the difference.
check.why: Upgrade the one product she's outgrown. Service never pauses, and extra use after the first month costs twice the rate.

check.q: An owner asks if he can pay for Get Found yearly. You say:

You'll knock another month off if he pays today.
Yearly is ten times the monthly price, two months free, and you'll confirm it with Station before he signs up.
check.why: Yearly billing exists, but you check with Station before offering it. You never add a discount of your own.

check.q: A client prepays a year of Follow Up. How is your commission paid?
options: Nothing, prepaid plans don't earn commission.
All at once, when the payment clears.
In equal monthly instalments across the prepaid months.
check.why: Prepaid payments are spread across the months they cover.

lessons.title: Pick the right one in 3 questions
lessons.goal: Use three questions to land on the right single product, collection or plan.
film: Three empty question slots on paper, numbered 1, 2, 3. A product shelf waits faded behind them.
Fourteen products, three collections, three plans. You can find the right one with three questions.
Slot 1 fills: "What's costing you the most work right now?" Four answers fan out: "Missed calls", "Reviews and Google", "Leads going cold", "Finding business customers".

One: "What's costing you the most work right now?" Their answer picks the area. Missed calls and messages. Reviews and Google. Leads and old customers going cold. Or, for a business-to-business trade, finding new business customers.
"Finding business customers" slides straight to the Radar card: "$297 a month".
If it's finding business customers, that's Radar, on its own. You're done.
Slot 2 fills: "Is it that one thing, or a few things like it?" "One thing" points to a single painting; "A few" points to a collection card.
Two: "Is it that one thing, or a few things like it?" One thing, say only reviews, is the single product: Repute. A few in the same area is that area's collection.
The three collection cards flash in order with their areas: Answer "calls and messages", Get Found "reviews and Google", Follow Up "leads and old customers".
Calls and messages: Answer. Reviews and Google: Get Found. Leads and old customers: Follow Up.
Slot 3 fills: "Or is it most of the front office?" Only now does the plan row fade up: Core, Pro, Max.
Three, and only if they're nodding at everything: "Or is it most of the front office?" That's a plan.
Two quick follow-ups pick the size: "Busy? Want social and email run for you?" → Pro. "Top volume, custom site, done for you?" → Max. Otherwise Core glows.
Core by default. Pro if they're busy and want their social and email run for them. Max for the top volume, done for them, with a custom site. More than one location? Add a location pack.
The three questions stack into one card: "What costs you most? One thing or a few? Most of the front office?"
That's the whole decision. What costs you most? One thing or a few? Or most of the front office?
Do-this-now: "Write the three questions on a sticky note by your phone."
Write the three questions on a sticky note and put it by your phone.
lessons.read_md:
**1. "What's costing you the most work right now?"** Their answer picks the area:
- Missed calls and messages → the Answer area.
- Reviews and Google → the Get Found area.
- Leads and old customers going cold → the Follow Up area.
- Finding business customers (business-to-business trades only) → **Radar**, on its own. Never in a collection or plan.

**2. "Is it that one thing, or a few things like it?"**
- One thing → the **single product** (only reviews: Repute; only missed calls: Lineback; only the phone answered: Frontdesk).
- A few in the same area → that area's **collection**: Answer $297 a month, Get Found $497 a month or Follow Up $427 a month.

**3. "Or is it most of the front office?"** Ask only if they're agreeing to everything. If yes → a **plan**:
- **Core** $1,297 a month by default.
- **Pro** $2,197 a month if they're busy and want their social and email run for them.
- **Max** $2,797 a month for the top size, done for them, with a custom-designed website.
- More locations → add an **extra location pack** at $397 a month each.

If you're unsure between two sizes, pick the smaller one. They can add or upgrade later, and you earn on every step.

check.q: A salon owner says her past clients never hear from her and new inquiries go quiet. Booking is fine. Which fits?
options: The Follow Up collection.
Core.
The Answer collection.
check.why: Two gaps in the same area, leads and old customers going cold. That's Follow Up. She already has booking.

check.q: A plumber says only one thing: he wants every call answered, day and night, and booked into his calendar. Which do you lead with?
options: Max.
Station's Frontdesk, on its own.
Get Found.
check.why: One gap, one product. Frontdesk answers every call. Lead with it and let him add more later.

check.q: A busy two-location clinic says calls, reviews, follow-up and social are all a mess, and they want the marketing done for them. Which fits?
options: Pro, plus one extra location pack.
Answer.
Radar.
check.why: Most of the front office, busy, marketing run for them: Pro. The second location is a location pack.

modules.title: The software your client gets

lessons.title: Their Station account
lessons.goal: Describe what a client sees in their Station account, and show it without logging into anyone's account.

[NEEDS: demo client account screenshot of the inbox, conversations listed newest first] in a device frame.

[NEEDS: demo client account screenshot of one conversation thread, with a Lineback text and the customer's reply] The cursor scrolls the thread.

[NEEDS: demo client account screenshot of a Frontdesk call transcript]

Bookings land in their calendar. Customers book themselves into real availability, and reminders go out on their own.

And they only see what they bought. As station.solutions puts it: one app, with the tabs you bought and nothing else.
A red rule strikes through a login screen with a partner's cursor on it: "Never log into a client's account."

lessons.read_md:
After checkout, every client gets **their own Station account**, with login details by email. Their products switch on with
pre-written wording they can edit. In it they:
- **Read every message** in one inbox: replies to missed-call texts (Lineback), leads from the website chat (Greet), and other
  messages their products handle.
- **Open any conversation** to read it in full, and change what their products say.
- **Read call transcripts** if they have Frontdesk, which transcribes every call.
- **See their bookings**: customers book themselves into real availability (Slate, and Frontdesk books into the calendar too), and
  reminders go out by themselves.
- **See only what they bought.** station.solutions says it's one app, with the tabs they bought and nothing else.

**You never log into a client's account,** and never ask for or handle their passwords, bank details, card numbers or ID.

**To show an owner what they'd get,** use station.solutions: the products page walks through one example day at an example business,
with each product's screen in the Station app, and every product page shows what it does and how long it takes to go live.

Ask for their password by email.

lessons.read_md:
**Your Words:** every message a product sends is pre-written, and the owner can edit any of it in their Station account under

options: They should dispute it with their bank.
It's probably overage, so it'll be refunded.
Billing is handled by Station directly, you've passed it on, and they'll reply by email.
check.why: Never guess at a charge or promise a refund. Billing questions go to Station, fast.

lessons.title: The first week: onboarding, carriers and the app
lessons.goal: Walk a new client through what happens after they pay, and what they should have ready.
film: A checkout completes on station.solutions in a browser frame. A blue path starts drawing from it.
They've paid. Here's their first week, so you can tell them exactly what happens next.
Stop 1: a thank-you email with a receipt attached. Stop 2: a second email, "Your Station account is ready", with login details blurred.
First, a thank-you email from Station with their receipt. Then their Station account is set up, and the login details arrive by email.
Stop 3: the real station.solutions/onboarding/ page: "Pick a time for your onboarding call."
Next, they book their onboarding call at station.solutions/onboarding. Station walks them through the account and connects their phone and calendar.
A checklist builds beside the page: "Hours." "Services and prices." "Google Business Profile link." "Social handles." "Brand colour."
They should have five things ready: their hours, their services and prices, their Google Business Profile link, their social handles, and a brand colour.
Stop 4: a form with three fields lighting in turn: "Legal business name", "EIN", "Address". A clock reads "About 2 business days".

If anything they bought sends texts, Station files carrier registration. It uses their legal business name, EIN and address exactly as the IRS has them. It takes about two business days, and the carriers control the timing.
A phone rings and is answered straight away; a text bubble beside it waits with a small clock.
Calls work right away. Texting starts when registration clears. So never promise same-day texting. And if the business has no EIN, tell Station.
[NEEDS: demo client account screenshot of the free Station mobile app home screen on a phone]
Every Station account comes with the free mobile app. It lets the owner run their account from their phone. Station gives download details during onboarding.
Small grey text: "Free. Not sold separately. Never quote a price."
It's free and not sold separately, so never quote a price for it.
The path ends at a hand-off card: "Your part: make sure they book the call. Tell Station what you learned."
Your part in all this: make sure they book the onboarding call and know what to bring. And tell Station what you learned on your calls.
Do-this-now: "Copy the 'What happens after I pay?' reply from the guide."
Find the "What happens after I pay?" reply in the partner guide, and keep it handy for your next close.
lessons.read_md:
**What happens after a client pays:**
1. **Checkout** on station.solutions, or through a link Station sends. You never take payments.
2. **Receipt:** Station emails a thank-you with the receipt attached.
3. **Account:** their own Station account, with login details by email. Products switch on with pre-written wording they can edit.
4. **Onboarding call:** they book it at **station.solutions/onboarding/**. Station walks them through the account and connects their phone
   and calendar. They should have ready: **hours, services and prices, Google Business Profile link, social handles and a brand colour.**
5. **Carrier registration** for anything that texts (Lineback, Dial, and the text parts of Slate, Pursuit and Repute). Station files it
   with the legal business name, EIN and address exactly as the IRS has them. About 2 business days; the carriers control the timing.
   Calls work right away. If the business has no EIN, tell Station.
6. **Product setup:** Station sets up each product.

**The mobile app** is free with every Station account and isn't sold separately, so never quote a price. It lets the owner run their
account from their phone; the product pages mention texting from it (Dial) and taking payments (Tap). Station gives download details
during onboarding. Don't describe it as an app with the client's name on their customers' phones unless Station confirms that.

**Your part:** tell Station what you learned (hours, services, concerns, who decides, anything they think you promised), make sure they
book onboarding and know what to have ready, and check in after the first few weeks. Never promise a go-live date.

check.q: A new Lineback client asks, "Will the texts work today?" You say:
options: Within the hour, once you switch it on.
Station files carrier registration first, which takes about 2 business days and is controlled by the carriers.
Yes, it's live today.
check.why: Never promise same-day texting. Calls work right away; texts wait on carrier registration.

check.q: What should a new client have ready for the onboarding call?
options: Their bank details and card number.
Their passwords, so Station can log in.
Hours, services and prices, Google Business Profile link, social handles and a brand colour.
check.why: Those five let Station set them up. Passwords and bank details are never asked for.

check.q: An owner asks how much the mobile app costs. You say:
options: It's free with every Station account and isn't sold separately.
Station quotes it after onboarding.
It's an add-on on top of the products.
check.why: The app is free. Never quote a price for it.

lessons.title: What each product needs from the client
lessons.goal: Tell a client exactly what they'll need to give Station for each product, so nothing surprises them.
film: A grey strike through "You won't have to do anything."
Station does the setup. But "you won't have to do anything" isn't true, so never say it. Each product needs a little from the owner.
Paintings flip past with one need under each: Greet "Chat code on the site, or site access", Slate "Services, durations, hours, calendar".
Greet needs the chat code on their site, or site access, and nothing at all if Station built the site. Slate needs their services with real durations, their hours and their calendar.
Lineback and Dial: "Legal name, EIN, address, where calls forward." Frontdesk: "Business facts, what it may say, forwarding, calendar, a test call."
Lineback and Dial need the legal name, EIN, address, and where calls forward. Frontdesk needs their business facts, what it may and may not say, call forwarding, their calendar, and one test call.
Pursuit: "Nothing. They can review the messages."
Pursuit needs nothing. They can review the messages if they want to.
Repute and Echo: a Google invite email icon, with a red strike through a padlock labelled "password".
Repute and Echo need access to their Google profile through Google's own invite. Never a password. Echo also needs photos.
Dispatch and Revive: a customer list icon travels straight to Station, past your side of the screen, labelled "Their own list. Never bought."
Dispatch and Revive need their own customer list, never a bought one. And it goes to Station, not to you.
Radar: "Who they want as customers." Tap: "Their own processor account, set up by them." Marquee: "Social accounts connected by them, logo and job photos."

Radar needs who they want as customers. Tap needs their own payment processor account, set up by them, so the money goes straight to their bank. Marquee needs their social accounts connected by them, their logo and job photos. Managed Marquee also needs their ad account.
A custom website card: "Form answers, domain, logo, photos, services."
And a custom website needs the form answers, their domain, or Station registers one, their logo, photos and services.
Do-this-now: "Before you close, tell them what their product needs."
Before you close, tell the owner what their product will need. A client who knows what's coming gets set up faster.
lessons.read_md:
Station sets everything up. Each product still needs something from the client:

| Product | What the client provides |
|---|---|
| **Custom website** | Form answers, domain (or Station registers one), logo, photos, services |
| **Greet** | The chat code on their site, or site access (nothing if Station built it), and their common questions |
| **Slate** | Services with real durations, working hours, their calendar |
| **Lineback and Dial** | Legal name, EIN, address, and where calls forward |
| **Frontdesk** | Business facts, what it may and may not say, call forwarding, calendar, a test call |
| **Pursuit** | Nothing; they can review the messages |
| **Repute and Echo** | Google profile access through Google's invite (never a password); Echo also needs photos |
| **Dispatch and Revive** | Their own customer list, never a bought list |
| **Radar** | Who they want as customers |
| **Tap** | Their own payment processor account, set up by them |
| **Marquee** | Social accounts connected by them, logo and job photos; Managed needs their ad account |

**Never** collect a customer list yourself (the client gives it to Station), and never ask for or handle a password.

check.q: A new Repute client asks, "Do you need my Google password?" You say:
options: Yes, email it to you and you'll pass it on.
No. Station sends a Google invite for access, never a password.
Yes, but only Station will see it.
check.why: Google access is always through Google's invite. Passwords are never asked for or handled.

check.q: A Revive client offers to send you their customer spreadsheet. You:
options: Take it and forward it to Station.
Say it goes straight to Station, and never take it yourself.
Buy a bigger list for them to add to it.
check.why: The client gives their own list to Station. Never collect it, and never use a bought list.

check.q: What does Pursuit need from the client?
options: Their Google password.
A test call.
Nothing. They can review the messages if they like.
check.why: Pursuit's messages are already written. The client can read and edit them, but nothing is required.

lessons.title: Where changes, support and billing go
lessons.goal: Send every client request to the right place, the same business day, without fixing anything yourself.
film: Four client bubbles drop onto paper at once: "Change my text." "The booking page is wrong." "Why this charge?" "Can you update my website?"
Clients will bring you all sorts of things. Every one has a place to go, and none of them is you fixing it.
"Change my text." slides to a card: "Settings, then Your Words."
Wording: they change it themselves, in Settings, then Your Words.
"The booking page is wrong." slides to: [NEEDS: demo client account screenshot of the Help page] with "Replies in 24 to 72 hours" under it.
Other changes and problems: the Help page in their Station account, or main@station.solutions. The in-account help says replies come within 24 to 72 hours.
"Why this charge?" slides to: "main@station.solutions · one business day".
Billing: main@station.solutions. Station aims to answer within one business day.
"Can you update my website?" splits two ways: "Station-built, they run it now → station.solutions/site-help/" and "Cancel hosting → station.solutions/cancel-hosting/".
A Station-built site they now run themselves: station.solutions/site-help. Cancelling website hosting: station.solutions/cancel-hosting.
Your Partner World Help tab: the cursor types into Message Station: "Hanley Plumbing says the booking page shows the wrong hours." and presses Send to Station.
And every time, you tell Station too, the same business day, with Message Station. Tell the client Station will handle it and that you've passed it on.
The Clients tab: "Book Station support" opens a time picker.
If they'd rather talk, book Station support from the Clients tab, and tell the client when it is.
A red strip lists hand-off-now moments: "Wants to cancel." "Complaint." "Refund or chargeback." "Mentions a lawyer."
And some things go to Station straight away: a client who wants to cancel, complains, or mentions a refund, a chargeback, a lawyer or a regulator.
Do-this-now: "Open Help in Partner World. Find Message Station."
Open Help in Partner World and find Message Station. It's where most of your hand-offs will go.
lessons.read_md:
| The client wants | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| To change a message's wording | **Settings, then Your Words** in their Station account |
| Any other change, or something's broken | The **Help page** in their Station account, or **main@station.solutions** (in-account help says replies within 24 to 72 hours) |
| A billing answer | **main@station.solutions** (Station aims to reply within one business day) |
| Changes to a Station-built site they now run | **station.solutions/site-help/** |
| To cancel website hosting | **station.solutions/cancel-hosting/** (the site stays live to the end of the paid period) |
| To add a product | **My Services** in their account (previews the charge), or the product page |
| To cancel Station | Email **main@station.solutions** from the account owner's email |
| To talk to someone | **Book Station support** from your Clients tab |

**Every time:** tell the client Station will handle it, and pass it to Station **the same business day** with **Message Station**.

**Straight away:** a client who wants to cancel, downgrade or pause; complains; asks for a refund or credit; mentions a chargeback, a
lawyer or a regulator.

**Never** log into a client's account, make the change yourself, guess at a charge, or promise a fix date or price.

check.q: A client says, "The booking page shows the wrong hours." You:
options: Tell them Station will handle it, point them to the Help page in their account, and pass it to Station the same business day with Message Station.
Tell them it'll be fixed by tomorrow.
Ask for their login and fix the hours.
check.why: Support is Station's. Your job is to get it there fast and never promise a date.

check.q: A client tells you, "I want to cancel, and I might talk to my lawyer." What do you do?
options: Tell Station straight away, and tell them they can cancel by emailing main@station.solutions from the account owner's email.
Wait to see if they calm down before telling Station.
Offer them a free month to stay.
check.why: Cancellations and legal mentions go to Station immediately. You never offer credits or discounts.

modules.title: Partner World
modules.outcome: Run a whole calling session in Partner World: sign in, find the next call, log every outcome the right way, and know where everything else lives.

lessons.title: Getting in
lessons.goal: Sign in, pass the 1-minute check, and know the eight tabs.
film: A phone in a device frame shows the real Partner World sign-in page. The cursor blinks in the email box.
This is Partner World. Every call you make for Station starts here, on your phone or your computer.
The cursor taps "First time here? Activate your invite". Three fields light up in turn: partner code, email, password.

The very first time, press "First time here? Activate your invite". Type the partner code from your invite email, the email Station has for you, and a password of at least ten characters. You only do this once.
Back on the sign-in form. A box ticks itself: "This is a shared computer".
After that, you just Sign in. On a computer other people use, tick "This is a shared computer", so you aren't left signed in.
One line types in: "Forgot your password?" An envelope flies from it to "main@station.solutions".
There's no reset button. If you forget your password, email main@station.solutions. Once Station has reset it, use "First time here?" again to set a new one.
The 1-minute check: six dots across the top. One question shows; a wrong pick shakes gently and clears; the right one fills a dot blue.
On a new device, a one-minute check asks six questions on the rules that matter most. A wrong pick just means you try again.
Home appears. The tab bar slides up, each label lighting on the beat: Home, Products, Calls, Leads, Calendar, Clients, Money, Help.
Then you're in. Eight tabs: Home, Products, Calls, Leads, Calendar, Clients, Money and Help. Partner Leads see a ninth, Team.
Zoom on the top bar. The cursor presses "AA" and every line of text grows a size. Then "Earned so far" pulses once, green.
At the top, AA makes all the text bigger. Earned so far opens your money.
Do-this-now card: "Open partners.station.solutions/?demo and tap every tab once."
Now open the demo: partners dot station dot solutions, slash, question mark, demo. It's sample data, so nothing you press goes anywhere. Tap every tab once.
lessons.read_md:
Partner World is at **partners.station.solutions**. It's where you do all your Station work.

- **First time:** press **First time here? Activate your invite**. Enter your partner code (it's in your invite email), the email Station
  has on file, and a password of at least 10 characters. You can only do this once.
- **Every time after:** **Sign in** with your email and password. On a computer other people use, tick **This is a shared computer**.
- **Forgot your password?** There's no reset button. Email main@station.solutions. Once Station has reset it, use **First time here?** to set a new one.
- **The 1-minute check:** on a new device, or after you sign out, six questions on the rules that matter most. A wrong pick just means
  you try again.

Once you're in, you'll see eight tabs: **Home, Products, Calls, Leads, Calendar, Clients, Money** and **Help**. Partner Leads also see
**Team**. At the top, **AA** makes the text bigger, and **Earned so far** opens Money.

**Practise in the demo:** partners.station.solutions/?demo is Partner World with sample businesses. Nothing you press there is sent to
Station or to anyone, so it's the safe place to try every button in this module.

check.q: You've forgotten your Partner World password. What do you do?
options: Email main@station.solutions, then use "First time here?" to set a new one once Station has reset it.
Request a new account with the same email.
Press the reset link under the sign-in box.
check.why: There's no reset button. Station resets it, and you set the new one through "First time here?".

check.q: You sign in on a computer at the public library. What else do you do?
options: Use the demo instead.
Tick "This is a shared computer", so you aren't left signed in.
Nothing, Partner World signs you out by itself.
check.why: Your login opens real businesses and your money. On a shared computer, never stay signed in.

lessons.title: Home: your next call
lessons.goal: Read Home and start a calling session from it.
film: The demo's Home, full screen: "Hi Sam." Under it, "Your next call: Bayou City Plumbing Co."
Open Partner World and Home tells you one thing before anything else: who to call next.
A soft highlight runs along "Pitch Lineback" and the opening question in quotes beneath it.
Your next call shows the business, what to pitch, and the exact line to open with.
The cursor rests on "Start calling". A small clock in the corner rolls past 8 pm, and the button morphs to "See my list".
Start calling takes you straight into Calls. Outside calling hours it reads See my list, because nobody can be called right now.
The label above the business morphs: "Your next call" to "Call-back due now", then to "Call-back overdue".
When a call-back is up, it takes the top spot: Call-back due now, or Call-back overdue if you're running late.
The "Earned so far" box; under the number, "2 setup steps before Station can pay you".
Earned so far shows your money, and how many setup steps are left before Station can pay you.
"Your referral link" box. The cursor presses "Copy"; a blue tick lands.
Your referral link, with Copy. Send it every time. It's what credits a sale to you.
"What's new" scrolls past: a call booked, a first payment cleared, Station adding a client to your book.
What's new lists what happened on your account, newest first: a booking, a payment that cleared, Station's answer about a client.
The three cards at the bottom light in turn: all the products, "Found a business yourself?", "Who buys? Ten real buyers".
And at the bottom: every product, a way to add a business you found yourself, and the ten kinds of buyer you'll meet.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, find your next call and read its opener out loud."
In the demo, find your next call and read its opening line out loud, the way you'd say it to the owner.
lessons.read_md:
**Home** is where every session starts.

- **Your next call:** the business to call next, what to pitch and the line to open with, plus **Start calling**. Outside calling hours
  the button reads **See my list**. When a call-back is up, the box says **Call-back due now** or **Call-back overdue**, and the line beside
  the button counts call-backs due, businesses to call today, and the ones you tried today that come back tomorrow.
- **No businesses yet?** Home says so and offers **Ask for my first businesses**. When every business Station sent you has a result, it
  offers **Ask for my next batch** (Module 8).
- **Your Partner Lead:** if Station has given you one, their name, your training level and their latest notes to you.
- **Earned so far:** your money, and how many setup steps are left before Station can pay you. It opens Money.
- **Today:** the calls you've logged, your conversations, and the businesses that were interested or won. Before your first call, it
  points you to the Answer collection to learn first.
- **Your referral link** with **Copy**, and three numbers: visits through your link, people tied to your code, and paying clients.
- **What's new:** what happened on your account, newest first. A client's purchase and a booking also reach you by email.
- At the bottom: all the products, **Found a business yourself?** and **Who buys? Ten real buyers**.

check.q: Home says "Call-back overdue" above a roofer's name. What do you do first?
options: Leave it until tomorrow, the time has passed anyway.
Start on the new businesses and come back to the roofer later.
Call the roofer now, as long as it's inside their calling hours.
check.why: A call-back is a promise you made to an owner. It goes to the top so you keep it.

check.q: The big button on Home reads "See my list" instead of "Start calling". Why?
options: You've finished every business Station sent you.
Your account is on hold.
It's outside calling hours, so nobody on your list can be called right now.
check.why: Calls run 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone. Outside that, Partner World lets you look but not dial.

lessons.title: Products and cheat sheets
lessons.goal: Find any product's cheat sheet and use it to prepare a pitch.
film: The demo's Products tab: a wall of product tiles, each with its painting and "You earn" line.
Products is the whole shelf: every product, collection and plan, and what you earn per paying client.
The filter chips light one by one: "Everything", "Easiest", "Top pay", "Collections", "Plans". The wall reshuffles under each.
Filter it: Everything, Easiest, Top pay, Collections or Plans. New partners, start with Easiest.
The cursor opens the Answer collection. Its cheat sheet unfolds in sections: who it's for, who buys it, what to open with.
Every product opens a cheat sheet. Who it's for, who buys it, and what to open with.
The next sections slide in: what to say if they ask the price, the close, the push-back you'll hear most.
What to say when they ask the price, how to close, and the push-back you'll hear most, with the answer.
"Your link" with a "Copy" button. The cursor copies it.
Your link for that product, with Copy. That's the link you send when they're interested.
"Everything else" opens: the full script, "Copy the whole script", answers to push-back, price details.
Under Everything else: the full script, which you can copy whole, every push-back answer, and the price details.
The cursor presses "Start calling for" the product at the bottom. Calls opens, and every card now reads "Pitch" that product. A second later, "Use each business's best fit" switches them back.
Start calling for a product pitches it to every business in Calls for the rest of the day. Use each business's best fit switches back.
One plain line: "If a price here differs from station.solutions, quote the site and tell Station."
And if a price here ever differs from station.solutions, quote the site, and tell Station.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, tap Easiest, open the Answer collection and read its opener and its close."
In the demo, tap Easiest, open the Answer collection, and read its opener and its close.
lessons.read_md:
**Products** lists every product, collection and plan Station sells, with what you earn per paying client each month (arithmetic, not a
forecast or a promise). Filters: **Everything**, **Easiest**, **Top pay**, **Collections** and **Plans**.

Each product opens a **cheat sheet**:
- who it's for and who buys it
- what to open with, and what to say if they ask the price
- the close, and the push-back you'll hear most
- **Your link** with **Copy**

Under **Everything else**: the full script (**Copy the whole script**), answers to push-back, what to do when they say yes, why they buy
it, price details and more about the product.

**Start calling for [product]** at the bottom of a cheat sheet pitches that product to every business in Calls for the rest of the day.
**Use each business's best fit** in Calls switches back.

If a price in Partner World ever differs from station.solutions, **quote the site** and tell Station.

check.q: At 10 am you press "Start calling for Repute". What happens?
options: Every business in Calls is pitched Repute for the rest of the day, until you switch back to each business's best fit.
Station sends Repute's details to every business on your list.
Only the next business changes to Repute.
check.why: It changes what you pitch, not what's sent. Nothing goes to a business unless you call or write to them.

check.q: The price on a cheat sheet doesn't match station.solutions. What do you quote?
options: The price on station.solutions, and you tell Station about the difference.
Whichever is lower, so the owner is happy.
The cheat sheet's price, since Partner World is the partner tool.
check.why: station.solutions is the one source for every price.

lessons.title: Calls: reading the card
lessons.goal: Read every part of a business's card before you dial.
film: The demo's Calls tab. At the top: "0 called", "18 new left". One business fills the screen.
This is Calls, your list. One business per screen, so you only ever think about one owner at a time.
The pills along the top of the card light in turn: "Yours till" a date, "New", the "Sale" tag.
Up top: Yours till, and a date. New, if you haven't called them. And the Sale tag, which is what you'd earn a month if they buy what you're pitching.
The name, trade, city and star rating type in. Below them: "OK to call now", with their local time.
The business, their trade, city and rating, and their local time, with whether it's OK to call right now.
"Pitch Lineback" with "Change" beside it. The cursor presses Change; a list of products drops open, then closes.
What to pitch, with Change if you'd rather lead with something else. The best-fit button takes you back.
The opening question in quotes, then "Why them" highlighted.
Your opening line, and Why them: the reason Station picked this business. Read it. It's often your best first question.
A calendar strip under "Yours till". A call is logged; the date jumps 14 days forward. Then a card with no calls fades and slides back into a shared pool.
Every business Station sends is yours for 14 days. Every call you log gives you another 14 from that call. Go 14 days without one, and it goes back to Station's shared list for another partner.
A hand-added card with the pill "Your lead".
A business you added yourself says Your lead. It stays until you remove it.
The list reorders itself on the beat: call-backs due, then Interested, then Station's new ones and try-agains, then your own, then finished. "Due now" appears at the top with one name in it.
Calls puts them in order for you: call-backs that are due, then Interested, then Station's new businesses and ones to try again, then your own. Due now at the top lists every call-back that's up.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, read Why them on the first three cards."
In the demo, read Why them on the first three cards. Then press Change on one and look at the other products.
lessons.read_md:
**Calls** is your list: the businesses Station sends you and the ones you add yourself, one per screen. You, Station and your Partner Lead
(if you have one) can see it. Other partners can't.

**Each card shows:**
- the business, trade, city and rating, their local time and whether it's OK to call
- what to pitch, with **Change** (and **Pitch [product] instead (best fit)** to go back)
- your opening line and **Why them**, plus your lines: who you are, the opener, what it does, the price answer and the close
- the **Sale** tag: what you'd earn a month if they buy it

**Yours till:** every business Station sends is yours for **14 days**, and every call you log on it gives you another
14 days from that call. If 14 days go by without a call logged, it goes back to Station's shared list so
another partner can call it. Businesses you added are tagged **Your lead** and stay until you remove them.

**Order:** call-backs that are due, then Interested, then Station's new businesses and ones to try again, then your own, then finished
ones. Businesses you tried today go to the back. **Due now** at the top lists every call-back from 15 minutes before its time, and marks
it **Overdue** two hours after. Tap a name to jump to its card.

check.q: A business Station sent you shows "Yours till" in three days. You log a call on it today. Now what?
options: It's yours for good once you've called it.
Nothing changes, it still goes back in three days.
It's yours for another 14 days, counted from today's call.
check.why: Every call you log restarts the 14 days. Businesses nobody calls go back to the shared list.

check.q: A business you added yourself shows "Your lead". How long does it stay on your list?
options: 14 days, like Station's businesses.
Until Station reviews it.
Until you remove it.
check.why: Only Station's businesses have a "Yours till" date.

check.q: Where do you look for the reason Station picked a business?
options: The Sale tag.
Why them, on its card.
What's new on Home.
check.why: Why them is Station's reason. It's often the best thing to ask about first.

lessons.title: Making the call
lessons.goal: Dial from Partner World and log the first result the right way.
film: Close on the demo card's "Call" button. A thumb presses it; the label on a phone reads "Call now".
When you're ready, press Call now. On a computer, it just says Call.
The "Ready to call" sheet slides up: the big call button, the tip line, and your lines underneath.
Ready to call opens first. Your lines, and a reminder: put it on speaker somewhere private, then come back to the app.
One line of the tip enlarges: "Never record a call." A record icon gets a hairline strike.
And never record a call. Not for practice, not for notes. Never.
The phone dials. Cut back: the app reopens and the sheet "On the call with" the business is already up, its outcome buttons waiting. Beside it, "I've hung up".
When you come back to the app, the outcomes are already open, waiting. Or press I've hung up.
Four buttons on the first row light one by one: "No answer", "Voicemail", "Bad lead", "Talked to them".
First, what happened. No answer. Voicemail. Bad lead. Or Talked to them.
The cursor presses "Voicemail". The card flips to "✓ Tried today" and slides to the back of the list.
No answer and Voicemail bring a business back tomorrow. The card shows Tried today until then. Nobody gets called twice in one day.
The cursor presses "Voicemail?" on a card. A short message to leave appears.
Voicemail, with a question mark, on the card gives you a short line to leave. Leaving one is fine.
"Bad lead" with its three reasons: "Wrong number", "Closed", "Not a fit".
Bad lead means the lead itself is wrong: a wrong number, a closed business, or not a fit.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, don't dial. Press How did it go? on the first card, choose Voicemail, and watch it move."
In the demo, don't dial. Press How did it go? on the first card, choose Voicemail, and watch it move to the back.
lessons.read_md:
1. Press **Call now** (on a computer, **Call**). **Ready to call** opens: your lines and a reminder to use speaker somewhere private,
   then the phone. **Never record a call.** On a phone, after a few calls you can choose to skip the Ready card.
2. When you come back to the app, the outcomes open by themselves. You can also press **I've hung up**.
3. Pick what happened: **No answer**, **Voicemail**, **Bad lead** (wrong number, closed, or not a fit) or **Talked to them** (next lesson).

**No answer** and **Voicemail** bring the business back tomorrow, and the card shows **✓ Tried today** until then. Nobody gets called twice
