in one day. **Voicemail?** on the card has a short line to leave.

The note box is optional, and holds business facts only (for example, "ask for Maria after 2"). **What do these buttons mean?** explains
each one.

**Why the call button is grey:** it's outside calling hours where the business is (9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone), you've already tried them
today, there's no phone number, or Partner World doesn't know their state (the button reads **Add their state to call**).

check.q: You dial a business and get the owner's voicemail. What do you do?
options: Leave the short line from Voicemail?, log Voicemail, and they come back tomorrow.
Log Not interested, since they didn't pick up.
Hang up and call again in ten minutes.
check.why: Nobody gets called twice in one day, and a voicemail isn't a no.

check.q: The number on the card reaches a dentist, but the card says it's a plumber. Which result?
options: Do not call.
Bad lead.
Not interested.
check.why: Bad lead means the lead itself is wrong: a wrong number, a closed business, or not a fit.

check.q: Can you record a call to listen back to it later?
options: No. Never record a call.
Yes, if you delete it within a week.
Yes, as long as it's only for you.
check.why: Recording calls is never allowed. Your notes and your logged results are the record.

lessons.title: Talked to them: every outcome
lessons.goal: Pick the right result after a conversation, and always leave a next step.
film: The cursor presses "Talked to them". A second row opens: "Interested", "Call back", "Not interested", "Do not call", and a wide "Won: they're buying".
You talked to them. Now, how did it go? Five answers.
"Interested" highlights; its small line reads "Wants to see more". A third row opens: "Set a call-back time" and "Book a call".
Interested means they want to see more. And Interested always needs a next step: Set a call-back time, or Book a call on your own booking calendar.
"Call back" opens day buttons: "Tomorrow", "In 2 days", "Next week", and a day picker. Then a row of times, each showing your time and theirs.
Call back asks for the day, then the time. Times are in your own time, and if they're in another time zone, each one shows theirs too. Only times inside their calling hours can be picked.
A "Later today" button appears, then greys out as the clock passes 5 pm their time.
Later today sets it for three hours from now, and only shows when that's still inside their hours.
"Due now" at the top of Calls fills with a name 15 minutes before its time; two hours after, the line turns "Overdue".
From 15 minutes before the time, they're under Due now. Two hours after, they're marked Overdue.
"Not interested" ("They said no") and "Do not call" ("They asked you to stop") sit side by side. A rule draws under each.
Not interested: you reached them and they said no. Do not call: they asked not to be called again. Those are different, and Module 8 shows why it matters.
The cursor presses "Won: they're buying". The card asks for their email and shows "Write them an email" and "Copy link".
Won: they're buying. The card asks for their email and gives you Write them an email and Copy link. Send the link every time. Signing up through it is what credits the sale to you.
Money's "Wins Station is checking" list gains a row. Under the card: "Marked Won by mistake? Change it".
A Won on a business Station sent you goes to Station to check, and shows on Money under Wins Station is checking. Marked Won by mistake? Change it, until Station confirms.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo: Talked to them, Interested, Set a call-back time, Tomorrow, pick a time."
In the demo, on the second card: Talked to them, Interested, Set a call-back time, Tomorrow, and pick a time. Then find it in Calls.
lessons.read_md:
After **Talked to them**, pick one:

| Result | Means | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **Interested** | They want to see more. | Always needs a next step: **Set a call-back time** or **Book a call**. |
| **Call back** | They asked you to call another time. | Pick the day (Tomorrow, In 2 days, Next week, or the day they said), then the time. |
| **Not interested** | You reached them and they said no. | The card closes. |
| **Do not call** | They asked not to be called again. | The card closes, for good. |
| **Won: they're buying** | They said yes. | Get their email, send your link, Station checks the win. |

**Call-back times** are in your own time. If they're in another time zone, each time shows theirs too, and only times inside their
calling hours can be picked. **Later today** sets three hours from now, and only appears when that's still inside their hours.

**Interested and Won cards** ask for their email and give you **Write them an email** and **Copy link**, your referral link for what you
pitched. Send the link every time.

**Won** on a business Station sent you goes to Station to check. Money lists it under **Wins Station is checking** until Station confirms it
and matches it to their signup. **Marked Won by mistake? Change it** works until Station confirms; after that, email main@station.solutions.

check.q: You press Interested. What does Partner World ask for next?
options: Their card details for the trial.
Nothing, the card is finished.
A next step: a call-back time, or a call booked on your booking calendar.
check.why: An Interested owner with no next step is a lead you'll lose. Partner World won't let you leave one.

check.q: Halfway through your opener, the owner says "Take me off your list." What do you do?
options: Mark Not interested and try again next month.
Say sorry, end the call, and mark Do not call.
Ask one more question first, then mark Call back.
check.why: "Take me off your list" is absolute. Do not call means nobody calls them again.

check.q: You mark Won on a business Station sent you. When does the client show up in Money as paying?
options: After 14 days.
After Station confirms the win, matches it to their signup, and they pay.
The moment you press Won.
check.why: Station's records decide every win. That's why you send your link every time.

lessons.title: Undo, keys and a dropped connection
lessons.goal: Fix a wrong tap, work fast on a computer, and keep your results safe offline.
film: The cursor presses "Not interested" on the wrong card. A bar slides up at the bottom: the result, "or press U", and "Undo".
Pressed the wrong button? It happens. Right after a save, a bar shows at the bottom with Undo.
The cursor presses "Undo". The card snaps back to how it was. The bar slides away.
Press Undo and it's as if it never happened. On a computer, U does the same.
A small arrow carries the result off toward a Station mark only once the Undo bar has gone.
A result goes to Station once its Undo has gone. Until then, it's still yours to take back.
A closed card shows "Change this". A Do not call card beside it shows a lock.
Closed a card the wrong way? Most closed results have Change this. Do not call and Bad lead are locked once Station has them. If you got one wrong, email Station.
A keyboard fills the bottom of the screen. Keys light as the voice names them: J, K, C, L, 1, 2, 3, 4, U.
On a computer, keys move you through the list. J next, K back, C call, L how did it go, 1 to 4 for the first results, U undo.
A wide screen: the card on the left, your lines on the right.
And on a wide screen, your lines sit right beside the card.
A wifi icon drops. A line appears at the top: "2 saves haven't reached Station yet", with "Try now". Wifi returns; the count runs to zero.
If your connection drops, keep going. Your results wait in that browser and send by themselves as soon as Station answers. The line at the top says how many are still waiting.
The cursor hovers "Sign out". A warning appears: signing out deletes them from this browser.
Don't sign out while saves are waiting. Signing out deletes them from that browser, and Partner World warns you first.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo on a computer: L, then 1 for No answer, then U."
In the demo, on a computer, press L on a card, then 1 for No answer, then U to undo it.
lessons.read_md:
- **Undo:** press **Undo** at the bottom of the screen right after a save (on a computer, **U** also works). A result goes to Station once
  its Undo has gone.
- **Change this:** most closed results can be changed later. **Do not call** and **Bad lead** on a business Station sent you are locked
  once Station has them. If you marked one by mistake, email main@station.solutions.
- **Keys on a computer:** **J** next, **K** back, **C** call, **L** how did it go, **1** to **4** for the first results, **U** undo. A wide
  screen shows your lines beside the card.
- **If your connection drops:** your results wait in that browser and send by themselves as soon as Station answers. A line at the top
  says how many haven't reached Station yet. Keep that browser open, and **don't sign out**: signing out deletes waiting saves from that
  browser (Partner World warns you first).

check.q: A second ago you pressed Not interested on the wrong business. What do you do?
options: Press Undo at the bottom of the screen, or U on a computer.
Log another result on top of it.
Email Station and ask them to delete it.
check.why: Undo is there for exactly this, until the bar goes away.

check.q: The top of Calls says "3 saves haven't reached Station yet." What do you do?
options: Sign out and back in to push them through.
Log the same three calls again.
Keep that browser open. They send by themselves as soon as Station answers.
check.why: Signing out deletes waiting saves from that browser, and logging twice gives Station a wrong record.

lessons.title: Leads and Calendar
lessons.goal: Find any business on your list, book a call, and request a website.
film: The demo's Leads tab: a long list with a search box and chips: "All", "New", "Tried", "Call back", "Interested", "Booked", "Won", "Closed".
Calls shows one business at a time. Leads shows your whole list at once.
The cursor types "Roofing" in the search box; the list shrinks to one row.
Search by name, trade, city or phone. Or show just one kind: New, Call back, Interested, Booked, Won or Closed.
The cursor opens Red River Roofing. Its phone, website and last note show, with "Call", "Book a call", "Request a website", "Add a note".
Tap a business for its phone, email, website and your last note. Then call it, book a call, request a website, or add a note.
The cursor presses "Request a website". The button turns to "Website: asked ✓".
Request a website: Station builds it, shows the owner a free demo, and quotes it. You never build one. If they buy, you earn 40% of the setup fee, once.
"Book a call" opens open times for the next 7 days. The cursor picks one and presses "Book it". The card shows "Call booked" and the time.
Book a call shows open times on your own booking calendar for the next seven days. Pick one, press Book it, and Station emails you the details.
A phone in your hand at the booked time; you dial.
At that time, you call them, from your own phone.
The Calendar tab: "Coming up", grouped by day, with calls to businesses, a call with Station, and a Station support call for a client.
Calendar shows every call you've booked, in your own time: with businesses, with Station, and Station support calls for your clients.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, search Leads for Roofing, open it, and press Request a website. Then open Calendar."
In the demo, search Leads for Roofing, open it and press Request a website. It's a preview, so nothing is sent. Then open Calendar.
lessons.read_md:
**Leads** is your whole list in one place: every business Station sent you and every one you added. Search by name, trade, city or phone,
or show only one kind (New, Tried, Call back, Interested, Booked, Won or Closed). Tap a business to see its phone, email, website and
your last note, then **Call** it, **Book a call**, **Request a website** or **Add a note**. **Add a business you found** is at the top.

**Request a website** works for any business on your list, as long as Station has a phone number, an email or their current website.
Station builds it, shows them a free demo and quotes it; you earn 40% of the setup fee once they pay. It shows
**Website: asked ✓** once it's sent. (On an Interested card in Calls, the same thing is **They want a website**.)

**Book a call** appears once you've talked and they're Interested or want a call back. It shows open times on your own booking calendar
for the next 7 days, in your time. Press **Book it**: Station emails you the details, and the card shows **Call booked**. You call them from
your own phone then. Until Station has set up your booking calendar, the button says so: set a call-back time instead.

**Calendar** shows every call you've booked, in your own time. **Coming up** is the next 14 days. **Book a call** there lets you pick a
business from your list, or book a call with Station.

check.q: An owner says, "Honestly, my website is embarrassing." What do you do?
options: Offer to put a quick mock-up together yourself this weekend.
Give them a rough price for a new site.
Request a website for them; Station builds a free demo and quotes it.
check.why: You never build a website or quote one. You request it, Station builds and quotes it.

check.q: You booked a call with a roofer for Thursday at 10. Who calls whom?
options: You call them, from your own phone, at that time.
They call Station's number.
Station calls them for you.
check.why: The booking is your call. Station emails you the details, and Station has no phone number.

lessons.title: Clients and Money
lessons.goal: Look after a client in your book, and find your money and your setup steps.
film: The demo's Clients tab: "Your clients", one example row with a latest message: "Can we add the review requests too?"
Once a business you brought in is paying Station, it shows up in Clients. This is where you talk to them.
The cursor opens a client: the conversation thread, a reply box, and "Send email".
Open a client to read the whole conversation. Send email replies by email, from Station, with your name on it. There's no texting.
The client asks: "My booking page shows the wrong hours." An arrow carries it to "Message Station".
If a client brings you a problem, any problem, tell them Station will handle it, and pass it to Station the same business day with Message Station.
The cursor presses "Add a client". A short form: the business name, the email they pay Station with, what they bought. A pill appears: "Waiting for Station".
Closed a business yourself? Press Add a client: the business name, the email they pay Station with, and what they bought. It waits for Station to accept it.
"Add a note" on a client, then "Interested in" a product, saved beside their name.
Add a note on any client, and save what they're Interested in, so you remember to raise it.
Cut to Money: "Earned so far", "On hold", "Paid to date" count up in green.
Money is your money, from Station's payment records. What's earned, what's on hold, and what you've been paid.
The two setup steps: "Upload my tax form" and "Set up payouts with Stripe".
And the two setup steps before Station can pay you: your tax form, and your payouts. Module 1 covered every line.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, open Clients, then Money. Find the two setup steps."
In the demo, open Clients and look at the example. Then open Money and find the two setup steps.
lessons.read_md:
**Clients** holds your conversations with the clients in your book. A client shows up once a business you brought in is paying Station, or
once Station has accepted one you added.

- **Add a client:** closed a business yourself? Give the business name, the email they pay Station with, what they bought, and a note if
  you like. It shows **Waiting for Station** until Station accepts or declines it. The answer lands in **What's new** and in your email.
  Up to five requests a day. A business already in another partner's book can't be added.
- **Add a note** (business facts only). Saving **Interested in** a product keeps it beside the client.
- **Book a Station support call** for a client: Station handles the call, and you tell the client when it is.
- **Send email** replies by email from Station, with your name in the subject. There's no texting.
- **The rule:** talk with your clients here, including about adding Station products at published prices. A question or a problem
  (technical, their account, billing or a change) goes to Station the **same business day** with **Message Station**. Don't fix it yourself.
- **Hosting & care** is always quoted by Station.

**Money** is from Station's payment records, which decide what you're paid: **Earned so far**, **On hold**, **Paid to date**, the
**two setup steps** (your tax form, and **Set up payouts with Stripe**), **Your clients** with **Where it stands**, **Wins Station is
checking**, and **Payouts sent**. Module 1 explains each one.

check.q: You closed a salon you found yourself, and they've paid. They aren't in Clients. What do you do?
options: Ask the owner for their account login so you can check.
Nothing, it appears by itself in a day or two.
Press Add a client with the email they pay Station with. It shows Waiting for Station until Station accepts it.
check.why: Station has to match your own wins to a payment. Add a client is how you ask.

check.q: A client emails you through Clients: "Can you change the hours on my booking page?" You:
options: Ask for their login and change the hours.
Tell them Station will handle it, and pass it on with Message Station the same business day.
Tell them to look in the help pages.
check.why: All support is Station's. Your job is to make sure it reaches Station fast.

lessons.title: Help and Message Station
lessons.goal: Get an answer from Station fast, the right way.
film: The Help tab. At the top, "Message Station": a thread, a text box, and "Send to Station".
Stuck? Help. And at the very top of Help is Message Station.
A message types itself: "Owner at Red River Roofing asked about a longer trial." The cursor presses "Send to Station". A reply appears in the same thread.
It goes to the Station team, which is people. Type your message, press Send to Station, and their reply shows up in the same thread.
Labels stack beside the box: "Your account", "Your leads", "Your pay", "A client's problem, same business day".
Use it for anything about your account, your leads, your pay or a client, and to pass on a client's problem the same business day.
A tax form and a bank card try to slide into the box and bounce off.
Never send a tax form or bank details through it.
"Ask Station": a question about a product's trial gets an answer underneath.
Ask Station answers questions about the products, the prices and the rules, from the partner guide and the catalogue. If it can't answer, your question goes to the Station team.
"Talk with Station": a few open times; one is picked.
Talk with Station books a call with the Station team. Say in a few words what it's about.
"The partner guide" with a search box. The word "trial" is typed; results appear. Then "Show me the tour again" and "Retake the check".
The whole partner guide is here, with search. So are the tour, what every button means, and the six-question check.
A line: "Station has no phone number." Under it, "main@station.solutions".
One more thing. Station has no phone number. The only contacts are Message Station and main@station.solutions.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, open Help, search the partner guide for trial, and press Show me the tour again."
In the demo, open Help, search the partner guide for "trial", and press Show me the tour again.
lessons.read_md:
**Message Station** is at the top of Help. It goes to the Station team, which is people.
- Type your message and press **Send to Station**. It reaches the team by email, and replies show in the same thread on Help.
- Use it for anything about your account, your leads, your pay or a client, and to pass on a client's question or problem the same
  business day. If something can't wait, email main@station.solutions.
- **Never** send tax forms or bank details here.

Also on Help:
- **Ask Station** answers questions about the products, the prices and the rules, from the partner guide and the product catalogue.
  Forty questions a day. If it can't answer, your question goes to the Station team.
- **Talk with Station** books a call with Station on Station's own calendar. You can have three booked ahead.
- **The partner guide**, with a search box.
- **The rules, in one breath**, **How a call works** (with **Show me the tour again** and **What the buttons mean**), your 30-second pitch,
  **See who buys** and **Retake the check**.
- **Your account**, with **Sign out**. If some saves haven't reached Station yet, Sign out warns you first.

Station has **no phone number**. Never give one out for Station.

(In the demo, Help shows Station's email address where Message Station would be. Once you're signed in, Message Station is there.)

check.q: A client asks you why they were charged twice. Where does it go?
options: Nowhere, you explain the invoice yourself.
Ask Station, so the answer comes back faster.
To Station, the same business day, with Message Station.
check.why: Billing questions are Station's. Message Station reaches people; Ask Station answers questions about products and rules.

check.q: A prospect asks for Station's phone number. You say:
options: Say you'll find it and call them back.
Station works by email: main@station.solutions.
Give them your own number as Station's.
check.why: Station has no phone number. Never give one out for Station.

lessons.title: Team, for Partner Leads
lessons.goal: Know what a Partner Lead sees on Team, and what they can and can't do there.
film: The tab bar with a ninth tab sliding in at the end: "Team".
If Station makes you a Partner Lead, you get one more tab: Team. Station picks the partners on your team.
Team's top row counts up: calls today, calls this week, conversations this week, wins.
The top shows your team's calls today and this week, conversations this week, and wins.
A list of partners, each with a training level and numbers. Flags pop beside three of them: "Quiet", "Asked for more", "Won waiting for Station".
Each partner shows their training level, their numbers, and flags: Quiet, Asked for more, and Won waiting for Station.
One partner opens: their list, greyed to show it's read-only. A level picker: "Not started", "Ready", "Working", "Closer", "Coach".
Open a partner to see their list, read-only, and record their training level: Not started, Ready, Working, Closer or Coach.
A coaching note types in and sends. Cut to that partner's Home: "Your Partner Lead" card shows it.
Send coaching notes. They see your two latest notes on their Home.
A money icon tries to appear on Team and is struck through.
There's no money on the Team tab.
Do-this-now card: "Not a Partner Lead? Nothing to press. If you are: open Team and read every flag."
The demo doesn't have a team. If Station makes you a Partner Lead, open Team and read every flag first.
lessons.read_md:
If Station has made you a **Partner Lead**, you also see a **Team** tab. Station assigns the partners on your team.

- The top shows your team's calls today and this week, conversations this week, and wins.
- Each partner shows their training level, their numbers, and flags such as **Quiet**, **Asked for more** and **Won waiting for Station**.
- Open a partner to see their list (**read-only**), record their training level (**Not started, Ready, Working, Closer** or **Coach**) and
  the steps they've done, and send coaching notes. They see your two latest notes on their Home.
- There's **no money** on the Team tab.

If you have a Partner Lead, their card is on your Home: their name, your training level, what comes next, and their latest notes to you.

check.q: A partner on your team has a business you think you could close. Can you log a call on their list?
options: Yes, if you tell Station afterwards.
No. Their list is read-only to you. Coach them with a note instead.
Yes, Partner Leads can work any list on their team.
check.why: You see their list so you can coach. The calls stay theirs.

check.q: Where do you see what your team earns?
options: On each partner's row in Team.
In the team's top numbers.
You don't. There's no money on the Team tab.
check.why: Team is for coaching: activity, levels and notes.

modules.title: Station Lens & the free audit
modules.outcome: Use Station Lens on a business's website to find one true gap, turn it into an honest question, and send an owner to the free audit, without ever claiming more than was checked.

lessons.title: What Station Lens is
lessons.goal: Get Station Lens, sign in, and run it on a business's website.
film: A real local business's website in a browser frame. The cursor drifts up to the toolbar and clicks the Station mark.
You're on a business's website, deciding whether to call. One click, and Station Lens tells you what Station's audit sees.
The real Lens popup: "Sign in with your Partner World account", and under it "Same email and password as partners.station.solutions. No new account."
Lens is Station's Chrome extension for partners. You sign in with your Partner World email and password. There's no new account.
The popup's "Checking their website…" state, with "Twelve checks, the same ones as Station's free audit."
It runs the same twelve checks as Station's free audit, usually in under a minute.
The popup closes; a second later it reopens with the answer waiting.
You can close it while it works. The answer is waiting when you click again.
The result: a ring with a number out of the checks it could make, a verdict line, and three chips: gaps, solid, couldn't check.
You get a tally: how many checks came back solid, how many are gaps, and how many it couldn't check.
"Biggest problems", numbered 1 to 3, each with a headline, why it matters, and "What fixes it:".
Then the three biggest problems, in the audit's own words, each with what fixes it.
The line "Website only: Lens doesn't look up their Google listing, so those checks read 'couldn't check'." draws a hairline under itself.
One thing to know. Lens checks the website only. It doesn't look up their Google listing, so those checks always read couldn't check.
A laptop with Chrome lights up; a phone beside it stays grey. A card: "Station sends you the install link."
Lens works in Chrome on a computer, not on a phone. It isn't in the Chrome Web Store yet, so Station sends you the install link.
Do-this-now card: "Ask Station for your Lens install link with Message Station."
Ask Station for your install link with Message Station. Once it's in, pin Lens to your toolbar.
lessons.read_md:
**Station Lens** is Station's Chrome extension for partners. On any business's website, click **Station Lens** and you get:

1. **Station's audit tally** for the site: how many checks came back solid, how many are gaps, and how many it **couldn't check**.
2. **The three biggest problems**, in the audit's own words: what it found, why it matters, and what fixes it.
3. **Send them a preview**, which asks Station for a preview website and never sends anything to the business (lesson 7.4).

**Sign-in:** your Partner World email and password. Lens has no accounts of its own.

**It's the same twelve checks as Station's free audit**, usually in under a minute. You can close the popup while it works.

**Website only:** Lens doesn't look up the business's Google listing, so the Google checks always read "couldn't check" in Lens. The free
audit (lesson 7.5) does check the listing.

**Getting it:** Lens works in Chrome on a computer. It isn't in the Chrome Web Store yet, so **Station sends you the install link** and the
steps. Ask with **Message Station**.

check.q: How do you sign in to Station Lens?
options: With a new Lens account you create the first time.
You don't sign in, anyone can use it.
With your Partner World email and password.
check.why: Lens uses your Partner World account. There's nothing new to set up.

check.q: In Lens, every Google listing check reads "couldn't check". Why?
options: The business doesn't have a Google listing.
Their Google listing failed the check.
Lens checks the website only. It doesn't look up the Google listing.
check.why: Couldn't check means it wasn't looked at. It says nothing about their listing.

lessons.title: Reading "couldn't check"
lessons.goal: Read a Lens result honestly, and never present "couldn't check" as a fault.
film: Three words on paper, side by side: "Solid." "Gap." "Couldn't check." The third one is grey.
Every check in Lens lands in one of three places. Solid. Gap. And couldn't check.
"Solid" gets a tick: a real booking button sits under it, outlined.
Solid means the audit saw it working, something a visitor can actually use.
"Gap" gets a mark: an empty space where a booking button would be.
A gap means the audit could see that it's missing.
"Couldn't check" opens: a website with a chat button that loads three seconds late, after the check has already left.
Couldn't check means just that. The page didn't show it clearly, a button loaded late, or it wasn't looked at. It is never a fail.
Lens's folded list: "Couldn't check (3) — not a fail". The cursor opens it.
Lens folds them away under a heading that says so: couldn't check, not a fail.
A speech bubble to an owner, "Your site failed our chat check", gets a hairline strike.
So you never tell an owner that something they might have is missing. Not from a couldn't check.
Two other Lens states slide in: "Their website didn't load for us" and "No problems in what we could check".
Two more you'll see. Their website didn't load for us: sites have off moments, so don't call it down. Try a re-check in a few minutes.
The second state's line highlights: "Lead with what Station adds, not with a problem."
And no problems in what we could check: don't go looking for one. Lead with what Station adds.
Do-this-now card: "Before every Lens-based call, open the couldn't-check list and read it."
Before every call you make off a Lens result, open the couldn't-check list and read it. Then you know what you can't say.
lessons.read_md:
Every check in Lens lands in one of three places:

- **Solid:** the audit saw it working, something a visitor can actually use.
- **Gap:** the audit could see it's missing. Only these become problems.
- **Couldn't check:** the audit couldn't tell. A button loaded late, the page didn't show it clearly, or (for the Google checks) Lens
  didn't look. **It is never a fail.** Lens folds these under **Couldn't check: not a fail**.

**Never tell an owner that something is missing because Lens couldn't check it.** They may have it. If it's worth raising, ask a neutral
question ("How do customers reach you after hours?"), and let them tell you.

**Other results you'll see:**
- **Their website didn't load for us:** sites have off moments. Don't tell anyone it's down. Try **Re-check** in a few minutes.
- **Nothing here could be checked from outside:** there's no score. That isn't a fail either.
- **No problems in what we could check:** don't invent one. Lead with what Station adds, not with a problem.

check.q: Lens lists "Instant answers on your site" under Couldn't check. On the call, you:
options: Don't present it as a problem. If it matters, ask how visitors get a quick question answered now.
Tell them their site has no chat.
Tell them their website failed Station's chat check.
check.why: Couldn't check means the audit couldn't tell. They may have it, and saying otherwise costs you the call and Station's name.

check.q: Lens says "Their website didn't load for us." What do you tell the owner?
options: That their website is down and losing them customers.
Nothing about it. Re-check in a few minutes before you call.
That Station found a serious problem with their site.
check.why: Sites have off moments. One failed load isn't proof of anything.

check.q: Lens says "No problems in what we could check." What now?
options: Pick the closest couldn't-check item and call it a gap.
Skip the business, there's nothing to sell.
Lead with what Station adds, not with a problem.
check.why: A good site still misses calls and still needs reviews. Start with what they'd gain.

lessons.title: One gap, one honest question
lessons.goal: Turn one Lens gap into an opening question the owner can answer.
film: Lens's problem 1, headline: "No way to book online".
Here's the whole trick. Take one gap, and turn it into one honest question.
The cursor opens the business's website on a phone in a device frame and scrolls it: no booking button anywhere.
First, look for yourself. Open their site, on your phone if it's a phone problem. Only say what you've seen.
The headline morphs into a question, typed in quotes: "I was on your website and couldn't find a way to book online. How do customers book with you right now?"
Then ask about it. I was on your website and couldn't find a way to book online. How do customers book with you right now?
The question slides to the left; an owner's answer appears on the right: "They call. Or text my cell."
Now the owner is telling you how it works, in their words. That's the conversation you wanted.
Three lines try to slide in and get struck through: "You're losing customers every day." "Your site failed our audit." "Our audit proves you need this."
What you never say: that they're losing a certain amount, that their site failed, or that an audit proves anything.
The gap links by a hairline to one product tile: Slate, with its painting.
One gap points to one product. Booking points to Slate. Missed calls, to Lineback or Frontdesk. Few reviews, to Repute. Check the cheat sheet for the right one.
One rule card: "One gap. One question. One product."
One gap. One question. One product. Leave the rest of the list for later.
Do-this-now card: "Take problem 1 from any Lens result and say your one question out loud."
Take problem one from any Lens result, check it on their site yourself, and say your one question out loud.
lessons.read_md:
A Lens result is not a script. It's a reason to ask one good question.

1. **Pick one gap**, usually problem 1.
2. **Look for yourself.** Open their website (on your phone, if it's about phones). Only say what you've actually seen.
3. **Ask about it, don't accuse.** "I was on your website and couldn't find a way to book online. How do customers book with you right
   now?" Then listen.
4. **Match it to one product**, using the cheat sheet. One gap, one question, one product.

**Never say:**
- that they're losing a specific amount, or any statistic you didn't see
- that their site "failed" anything
- that an audit "proves" they need Station
- anything from the couldn't-check list as if it were a problem

check.q: Lens's problem 1 for a landscaper is "No way to book online." Which opener is best?
options: "You're losing thousands a month without online booking."
"Your website failed Station's booking audit."
"I was looking at your website and couldn't find a way to book online. How do customers book with you now?"
check.why: Ask about what you saw. Never quote a loss, and never call it a fail.

check.q: Before you bring up a gap on the call, you:
options: Look at it on their website yourself, so you only say what you've seen.
Read all three problems to them in order.
Run Lens a second time to be sure.
check.why: You're the one saying it. Make sure it's true where the owner can check it.

lessons.title: Send them a preview
lessons.goal: Ask Station for a preview website from Lens, knowing nothing goes to the business.
film: The bottom of a Lens result: "Send them a preview", and under it "Nothing goes to the business."
At the bottom of every Lens result: Send them a preview. And right under it: nothing goes to the business.
The cursor presses it. A form slides in: Business name, City, State, Their phone, Their email (optional), Note for Station (optional).
Press it, and Lens asks for the business name, city and state, their phone, and a note for Station if you like.
The phone field shakes empty: "Add their 10-digit phone number. It keeps two partners off the same business."
The phone number is required. It's how Station keeps two partners off the same business.
The email field highlights; a small tag beside it: "Only if they gave it to you."
Leave their email empty unless the owner gave it to you.
The cursor presses "Ask Station for the preview". The popup reads "Asked. Station has it."
Press Ask Station for the preview. Asked. Station has it.
A card flips into Partner World's Calls with the pill "Your lead".
The business goes onto your list in Partner World as your own lead, so the usual rules apply. Never one another partner gave you, never one that asked not to be called.
A path draws: Station builds, a founder approves, then a link arrives for you.
Station builds the preview, a founder approves it, and then you get the link to show them.
The link reaches an owner only after a speech bubble: "Sure, send it over."
Show it only to an owner who asked to see it, or agreed to. And if they buy a website, you earn 40% of the setup fee, once.
Do-this-now card: "Press Send them a preview only for a business you'll actually call."
Use Send them a preview only for a business you're really going to call. Every one lands on your list.
lessons.read_md:
**Send them a preview** asks Station to build a preview website for the business. **It never sends anything to the business.**

1. Press **Send them a preview**. Lens fills in what it can from their site: business name, city, state and phone.
2. Check the details. **Their phone** is required (it keeps two partners off the same business), and the state is two letters, like TX.
   **Leave their email empty unless the owner gave it to you.** Add a **Note for Station** if it helps ("Owner is Dana, wants online
   booking first").
3. Press **Ask Station for the preview**. Lens says **Asked. Station has it.** (or **Station already has this one**).

**What happens next:** the business goes onto your Partner World list as **Your lead**, so the rules for your own leads apply: never one
another partner gave you, and never one that asked not to be called. Station builds the preview, a founder approves it, and then you get
the link to show them.

**Show it only to someone who asked to see it or agreed to receive it.** If they buy a custom website, you earn 40% of the
setup fee, once. Never quote a website price: Station quotes it.

check.q: You press "Ask Station for the preview." What does the business receive?
options: A text with a link to the preview.
An email from Station with their new website.
Nothing. Station builds it, a founder approves it, then you get the link.
check.why: Lens never sends anything to a business. Whether they see it is up to the conversation you have.

check.q: The preview is approved. When can you send the link to the owner?
options: Right away, it's free.
Never, only Station can send it.
Once they've asked to see it or agreed to receive it.
check.why: Send a demo only to someone who asked for it or agreed to it.

check.q: Lens won't take the preview request without a phone number. Why?
options: So Lens can call them for you.
The phone number keeps two partners off the same business.
So Station can text the owner the preview.
check.why: Nobody texts or calls the owner from Lens. The phone is how Station spots a business someone else already has.

lessons.title: The free audit at station.solutions/audit/
lessons.goal: Explain Station's free audit and send an owner to it the right way.
film: The real station.solutions/audit/ page in a browser frame: "What is your front office leaking?" and "Free · no card · 60 seconds".
This is Station's free audit. It's for the owner, not for you.
The page's five areas tick in: website, Google listing, getting in touch, keeping customers, being seen.
Twelve checks, the same ones Station runs for paying clients: their website, their Google listing and reviews, how customers get in touch, follow-up, and whether anything is marketing them right now.
The form fills in by itself: Your name, Business, Email, Phone (optional), City (optional), Website. The cursor presses "Send my audit".
The owner fills in their name, business, email and website, and presses Send my audit. No card, no call.
An inbox: the report arrives. A line: "check Promotions if you don't see it."
The report lands in their inbox in about a minute. Tell them to check Promotions if it doesn't show.
The FAQ line highlights: "We only call something a gap when we can see it is missing, never because we failed to find it."
And the same rule as Lens: anything it can't measure says couldn't check. It only calls something a gap when it can see it's missing.
The address bar: "station.solutions/audit/" gets "?ref=" and a partner code added on the end.
Send it with your code on the end: station dot solutions slash audit, question mark ref equals your code. Any station.solutions page works that way.
Lens and the audit side by side. Lens: "For you. Website only." Audit: "For the owner. Website and Google."
So: Lens is for you, before a call, website only. The free audit is for the owner, and it also checks their Google listing and reviews.
Do-this-now card: "Open station.solutions/audit/ and read the twelve checks."
Open station.solutions slash audit and read the twelve checks, so you can describe them in one breath.
lessons.read_md:
**station.solutions/audit/** is Station's free audit for owners: **free, no card, no call**, and the report is theirs either way. Fixing
anything with Station is optional.

- **Twelve checks**, the same ones Station runs for paying clients: their website, their Google listing and reviews, how customers get in
  touch (booking, chat, after-hours, texting), keeping customers (follow-up, email list, paying online), and being seen.
- **The owner fills it in:** name, business, email, website (phone and city are optional). No website? They type "none" and it checks
  everything else. The report arrives by email in about a minute (tell them to check Promotions).
- **Couldn't check** works the same as in Lens: it's marked as such, never guessed.

**How to send it:** add your code to the end, **station.solutions/audit/?ref=yourcode**, so the lead is tied to you. Let the owner fill it
in themselves; never type an owner's email in for them. Your first email to a business can't carry a link, so offer it on the call or
after they've written back.

**Lens or the audit?** Lens is for you, before a call, and checks the website only. The free audit is for the owner, and also checks their
Google listing and reviews.

check.q: An owner says, "I don't even have a website." Can they still get the free audit?
options: Yes, but only if you run it for them.
Yes. They type "none" in the website box, and it checks everything else.
No, it only checks websites.
check.why: The audit also looks at their Google listing, reviews and how customers reach them.

check.q: How do you share the free audit so the lead is tied to you?
options: Send station.solutions/audit/ with ?ref= and your code on the end, and let the owner fill it in.
Fill it in for them with their email while you're on the call.
Send the plain link and tell Station afterwards.
check.why: Your code on the link is what ties it to you, and the owner's details are theirs to enter.

check.q: What's the difference between Station Lens and the free audit?
options: Lens is for you and checks the website only; the free audit is for the owner and also checks their Google listing.
They're different checks with different rules.
Lens sends the owner a report; the free audit doesn't.
check.why: Same twelve checks and the same honesty rules. Different reader, and Lens skips Google.

modules.title: Prospecting
modules.outcome: Fill your day the allowed way, with Station's batches and businesses you found yourself, call them in the right order inside the rules, and open every call with one true thing.

lessons.title: Where your businesses come from
lessons.goal: Name the only two places your businesses come from, and what you never do.
film: Two doors drawn in hairline on paper. Left: "Station sends them." Right: "You found them yourself."
Every business you'll ever call comes through one of two doors. There isn't a third.
The left door opens. A batch of cards drops into the real Calls tab, each with a "Yours till" pill.
Door one: Station sends you businesses in batches. Each one is yours for 14 days, and every call you log adds another 14.
The right door opens. One card walks through on its own, with the pill "Your lead". Behind it, quick sketches: a work van at a gas pump, a salon sign, a flyer on a corkboard.
Door two: a business you came across yourself. The van at the gas pump. The salon next to your dentist. The flyer at the hardware store.
Four labels slide toward the doors and get struck through: "Search tools." "Scrapers." "Bought lists." "Another partner's list."
What you never do: search for, scrape, pull or buy leads. Finding businesses in bulk is Station's job. Never yours.
A map with partner dots spread out, each in its own patch.
Station decides how many businesses each partner gets, and from which area. That's how two partners never end up calling the same owner.
One line, set large: "Two doors. That's it."
Two doors. Station's batches, and the ones you found yourself.
Do-this-now card: "Think of three businesses you passed this week. Those are door two."
Think of three businesses you passed this week. Those are door two. Next lesson: how to add them.
lessons.read_md:
Your businesses come from **only two places**:

1. **Station sends them**, in batches. Each one is yours for **14 days**, and every call you log on it gives you another
   14 days from that call.
2. **You found them yourself**: a business you came across in your own life, added with **Found a business yourself?** (lesson 8.2).

**Partners never search for, scrape, pull or buy leads.** Finding businesses in bulk is Station's job. Station decides how many businesses
each partner gets and from which area, which is what keeps two partners off the same owner.

There's **no quota**, and Station doesn't promise any number of leads.

check.q: A friend offers you a spreadsheet of 500 local contractors. What do you do?
options: Send the file to Station with Message Station.
Say no thanks. Partners never use bought or pulled lists.
Add them one by one as your own leads.
check.why: Your own leads are businesses you came across yourself. A list from anyone else is neither door.

check.q: On Sunday night you search a map app for every roofer in town and plan to add forty. Is that allowed?
options: No. Searching for leads is Station's job.
Yes, if you only call them inside calling hours.
Yes, as long as you add them by hand.
check.why: Partners don't search for or pull leads. Station deals them, so nobody collides.

lessons.title: Adding your own
lessons.goal: Add a business you found yourself, with the right details and nothing you shouldn't have.
film: A phone photo of a plumbing van's side panel: the business name and a phone number.
You're at a red light and the van in front says "Gulf Coast Drains", with a number. That's a lead you found.
Three places light up in the real app: "Found a business yourself?" on Home, "Add a business you found" on Leads, "+ Add a business you found yourself" at the end of Calls.
Add it from Home, from Leads, or from the end of Calls.
The real form box at the top: "Only businesses you found yourself. Never one another partner gave you, and never one that asked not to be called."
The form says it before anything else. Only businesses you found yourself. Never one another partner gave you. Never one that asked not to be called.
The form fills field by field: Business name, Their phone number, City, State.
You need their name, their business phone, and their state, so Partner World knows their time zone. City helps too.
The optional fields fill: What kind of business, Why they might need Station ("Missed my call twice"), What to pitch them.
If you have them: what kind of business, why they might need Station, and what to pitch. Leave the pitch blank and the app suggests the Answer collection.
"Their email (optional)" with its hint underneath: "Only if they gave it to you."
Their email, only if they gave it to you. Not one you dug up.
The cursor presses "Add to my list". The card appears in Calls with the pill "Your lead". A small Station mark checks it.
Press Add to my list. Station checks every business you add, and tells you if it can't be yours.
The card shows "Edit" and "Remove".
Your own cards have Edit and Remove. To get a removed one back, email Station.
Do-this-now card: "Write down one business you passed this week: name, phone, state, and why they might need Station."
Write down one business you passed this week: its name, its phone, its state, and why it might need Station. That's your first own lead.
lessons.read_md:
**Where:** **Found a business yourself?** on Home, **Add a business you found** on Leads, or **+ Add a business you found yourself** at the
end of Calls.

**The form asks for:**
- **Business name**, **their phone number** (the business line you'll call) and **state** (so Partner World knows their time zone)
- **City**, if you have it
- if you have them: what kind of business, why they might need Station, and what to pitch them (blank = the Answer collection)
- **their email, only if they gave it to you**, and their website

**Only businesses you found yourself.** Never one another partner gave you, and never one that asked not to be called. The calling rules
are the same as for Station's businesses.

**Station checks every business you add** and tells you if it can't be yours (for example, another partner already has it). It won't say
who. Your own cards have **Edit** and **Remove**; to get a removed one back, email main@station.solutions. Your own businesses stay on your list
until you remove them, and they never hold up **Ask for my next batch**.

check.q: Which of these can you add as your own lead?
options: A list of salons another partner shared with you.
A landscaper whose truck you saw parked at your neighbor's house.
A bakery that told you last month not to call again.
check.why: Only businesses you came across yourself, never another partner's, and never one that asked not to be called.

check.q: What goes in "Their email"?
options: Only an email the owner gave you.
A guess like info@ their website.
Any email you can find on their website or social pages.
check.why: The form says it: only if they gave it to you.

check.q: Station tells you a business you added can't be yours. What do you do?
options: Call it anyway, you found it first.
Accept it and move on. Station won't say why, and it doesn't need to.
Add it again with a slightly different name.
check.why: Usually someone else already has it, or it's asked not to be contacted. Either way, it's not yours to call.

lessons.title: Ask for my next batch
lessons.goal: Know when and how to ask Station for more businesses.
film: A brand-new Home with no businesses yet, and the button "Ask for my first businesses".
Brand new, with nothing on your list? Home says so, with one button: Ask for my first businesses.
Calls fills with a batch. One by one, each card gets a result stamped on it.
Station sends a batch. You work it. Every business gets a result logged.
The last of Station's cards gets its result. At the end of Calls, "Ask for my next batch" turns on.
When every business Station sent you has a result, Ask for my next batch turns on, at the end of Calls and on Home.
Three of your own "Your lead" cards sit to one side, untouched. The button stays on.
Businesses you added yourself never hold this up.
The cursor presses it. A line: "Asked. Station reviews every request, then your new businesses show up here."
Press it, and Station reviews the request. Station decides how many it sends and from which area. The new ones show up in Calls.
A small line at the top: saves waiting to reach Station. The ask waits until they've gone.
If some of your results haven't reached Station yet, the ask waits until they have.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, scroll to the end of Calls and read what it says about your next batch."
In the demo, scroll to the end of Calls and read what it says about your next batch.
lessons.read_md:
- **Before your first batch:** Home and Calls offer **Ask for my first businesses**.
- **After that:** when **every business Station sent you has a result**, press **Ask for my next batch** at the end of Calls or on Home.
- **Your own businesses never hold it up.**
- **Station reviews every request** and decides how many it sends at a time and from which area. The new businesses show up in Calls.
- If some results haven't reached Station yet (a dropped connection), the request waits until they have.

There's no quota, and Station doesn't promise a number of leads.

check.q: Three of Station's businesses on your list have no result yet, and ten of your own are untouched. Can you ask for your next batch?
options: Yes, as long as you've called at least half.
No, you have to finish your own ten first.
Not yet. Log a result on Station's three first. Your own never hold it up.
check.why: Only Station's businesses need a result before you ask.

check.q: How many businesses will your next batch have?
options: Station decides each time, and doesn't promise a number.
Always the same as your first batch.
As many as you ask for.
check.why: Station reviews every request and picks the count and the area.

lessons.title: Your daily rhythm
lessons.goal: Run a calling session in the right order, every day.
film: A morning kitchen table: coffee, a phone, the real Partner World Home on it.
Here's what a good calling day looks like.
Home's top box reads "Call-back due now". A blue "1" stamps on it.
First, call-backs. They're people who asked you to call. Home puts them at the top, and Calls lists them under Due now.
A "2" stamps on Interested cards.
Then the businesses who were Interested.
A "3" stamps on Station's new businesses and the ones to try again; a "4" on your own; finished ones fade to the bottom.
Then Station's new businesses and ones to try again. Then your own. Calls already sorts them this way, so trust the order.
A clock beside each card shows their local time. One card turns grey at 8 pm their time; Sunday's whole column is grey.
Every card shows their local time. Calls run 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone. No Sundays.
A card stamped "✓ Tried today" slides to the back.
Didn't reach someone? They're back tomorrow. Nobody gets called twice in one day.
Between two calls, a 2-minute timer and a Google listing. Then the result logged, before the next dial.
Before each call, two minutes on their Google listing. After each call, log the result before you dial the next one.
End of day: Calendar's "Coming up" and tomorrow's call-backs.
At the end of the day, look at tomorrow: your call-backs and your booked calls.
Do-this-now card: "In the demo, press Start calling on Home and work three cards in order."
In the demo, press Start calling on Home and work three cards in order, logging each one.
lessons.read_md:
**A good calling day, in order:**
1. **Call-backs that are due.** They asked you to call. Home shows **Call-back due now**; Calls lists them under **Due now**.
2. **Interested** businesses.
3. **Station's new businesses** and ones to **try again**.
4. **Your own** businesses.

Calls already sorts your list this way. Businesses you tried today go to the back.

**Inside the hours:** 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone. Every card shows their local time.

**Once a day:** No answer and Voicemail bring a business back tomorrow. Nobody gets called twice in one day.

**Each call:** two minutes on their Google listing first (lesson 8.7), then the call, then **log the result before the next dial**.
Station's records decide who gets credit, and a call you didn't log doesn't keep the business yours.

**End of day:** check tomorrow's call-backs and your Calendar.

check.q: It's 10 am. One call-back is due now, and fifteen new businesses are waiting. Who do you call first?
options: The newest business on the list.
Your own businesses, since they don't expire.
The call-back.
check.why: A call-back is someone who asked you to call. It always comes first.

check.q: You called a bakery at 9:30 and got no answer. Can you try again at 2 pm?
options: Yes, twice a day is fine.
Yes, if you leave a voicemail the second time.
No. They're back on your list tomorrow.
check.why: Nobody gets called twice in one day.

lessons.title: Calling hours and do-not-call
lessons.goal: Know exactly when you may call, how you dial, and what to do when someone says stop.
film: A big clock face, ticks between 9 and 8 shaded blue; the word "Sunday" sits outside it in grey.
The calling rules fit on one clock.
One line: "9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone."
Calls run 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone.
Two clocks side by side: "You, Houston: 10:30 am" and "Them, Los Angeles: 8:30 am". The second is grey.
Their time, not yours. If you're in Houston at half past ten, a shop in Los Angeles is at half past eight. Too early.
A grey call button reading "Add their state to call".
Partner World switches the call button off outside their hours. Without their state, it can't know their time, so it asks for it.
A finger dials one number. Beside it, three things struck through: an autodialer, a recorded message, a list of numbers.
Dial every call yourself, one at a time. No autodialers, no recordings, no robocalls.
A speech bubble: "Take me off your list." The voice line plays as the cursor presses "Do not call".
When someone says take me off your list: say sorry, end the call, and mark Do not call, the same day.
The card locks. A small line: "Station never contacts them either."
After that, nobody calls them again. Not you, not Station, not even if you come across them again yourself.
Two struck-through bubbles: a text message and an email with a link.
And never text a business. Email one only after you've talked and they're happy to hear from you, from the card, with no link in your first email.
Do-this-now card: "Say it out loud: 'I'm sorry to bother you. I'll take you off my list.'"
Practise the line now, so it's ready: I'm sorry to bother you. I'll take you off my list.
lessons.read_md:
**When:** 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone. Partner World shows their local time on every card and switches the call button off outside those hours.
Without their state it can't know their time, and the button reads **Add their state to call**.

**How:** dial every call yourself, one at a time. **No autodialers, no recordings, no robocalls.** Respect do-not-call requests and
do-not-call lists. If you're unsure whether a call is allowed, check with Station first.

**When someone says stop:** "Take me off your list" is absolute. Say sorry, end the call, and mark **Do not call** the same day. Nobody calls
them again: not you, not Station, and not you later if you come across them yourself.

**Texts and email:**
- **Never text a business.** Station doesn't have a texting number for partners.
- **Email** a business only after you've talked and they're happy to hear from you, with **Write them an email** on their card, so it goes
  from your Station sending address with the right footer. Your first email can't carry a link: ask a question, and send the link once
  they answer.

check.q: You're in Houston. It's 10:30 am your time. Can you call a salon in Los Angeles?
options: Yes, if you only leave a voicemail.
No. It's 8:30 am there, before calling hours.
Yes, it's after 9 am for you.
check.why: Calling hours are in the business's own time zone.

check.q: A tool promises to dial 300 businesses an hour and play your pitch. Can you use it?
options: Yes, for your own leads only.
Yes, if you only use it inside calling hours.
No. Every call is dialed by hand, with no recordings.
check.why: Autodialers and recorded messages break the calling rules and your agreement.

check.q: An owner you talked to says "Sure, email me something." What do you send first?
options: An email with every product page linked.
A text with your referral link.
A short email from Write them an email, with a question and no link.
check.why: Never text a business, and your first email can't carry a link. Send it once they answer.

lessons.title: Bad lead, Not interested, Do not call
lessons.goal: Close a card with the right one of the three, every time.
film: Three closed cards side by side, each with a different stamp: "Bad lead", "Not interested", "Do not call".
Three ways to close a card. They look alike. They mean very different things.
"Bad lead" lifts: a disconnected tone, a "Closed" sign on a door, a dentist where a plumber should be.
Bad lead: the lead itself is wrong. A wrong number, a closed business, or not a fit.
"Not interested" lifts: a speech bubble, "We're all set, thanks."
Not interested: you reached them, and they said no.
"Do not call" lifts: "Don't call here again."
Do not call: they asked not to be called again.
A reflex bubble: "Not interested." A calm reply: "No problem. Is it timing, or you've already got it covered?"
A quick "not interested" is often a reflex. One calm question is fair. If they say it again, stop.
Under each stamp, what Station does next: Bad lead, "skipped"; Not interested, "skipped for 180 days"; Do not call, "never again".
It matters what you pick. On a business Station sent you, Station's own outreach skips it afterwards: for good after Bad lead or Do not call, and for 180 days after Not interested.
Do-this-now card: "Open What do these buttons mean? on any card and read all three."
On any card in the demo, open What do these buttons mean? and read all three.
lessons.read_md:
| Pick | When | After |
|---|---|---|
| **Bad lead** | The lead itself is wrong: wrong number, closed, or not a fit. | Closes the card. |
| **Not interested** | You reached them and they said no. | Closes the card. Station's own outreach skips it for 180 days. |
| **Do not call** | They asked not to be called again. | Closes the card. Nobody contacts them again. |

All three close the card. On a business Station sent you, Station's own outreach skips it afterwards: after **Do not call** or **Bad lead**,
and for **180 days** after **Not interested**. Station locks **Do not call** and **Bad lead** once it has them; if you picked one by
mistake, email main@station.solutions.

**A reflex "not interested" is not "do not call."** One calm question is fair ("Is it timing, or you've already got it covered?"). If they
say it again, stop, and log Not interested. "Take me off your list" is always **Do not call**.

check.q: The number reaches a business that closed last year. Which do you pick?
options: Not interested.
Do not call.
Bad lead.
check.why: Bad lead is for a lead that's wrong in itself: wrong number, closed, or not a fit.

check.q: The owner says "Not interested." You ask one calm question, and they say "Really, no thanks." Now?
options: Thank them, end the call, and log Not interested.
Ask two more questions to find the real objection.
Log Do not call to be safe.
check.why: One question is fair, then stop. They didn't ask not to be called, so it's Not interested.

check.q: "Please don't call this number again." Which do you pick?
options: Not interested.
Call back, in a few months.
Do not call.
check.why: They asked not to be called again. That's absolute.

lessons.title: Two minutes on their Google listing
lessons.goal: Find one true, specific thing about a business before you dial.
film: A 2:00 timer appears in the corner and starts counting down.
Before every call, two minutes. Not twenty. Two.
A business's Google listing in a browser frame. The cursor looks at the hours: "Closed Saturday".
Open their Google listing. Look at the hours.
The cursor moves to the rating and review count, then to the newest reviews. One review reads: "Called three times, nobody picked up."
The rating, how many reviews, and the newest few. Owners hear about missed calls in their reviews first.
The cursor checks photos and the website link.
Photos, and whether there's a website link that works.
One true detail lifts out of the page and becomes a question in quotes: "Your Google listing shows you're closed on Saturdays. Is that right?"
Then pick one true, specific thing, and ask about it. Your Google listing shows you're closed on Saturdays. Is that right?
Two bubbles get struck through: "You're losing half your customers." "Studies show most callers never call back."
Never quote a dollar loss, a statistic, or anything you didn't actually see.
The card's "Why them" sits beside the listing detail.
The card's Why them is Station's reason. Your two minutes give you something you saw with your own eyes.
Do-this-now card: "Pick a business near you. Two minutes on its listing. Write down one true thing."
Pick any business near you. Spend two minutes on its listing, and write down one true thing you'd ask about.
lessons.read_md:
Two minutes on their **Google listing** earns the owner's attention and makes the problem real. Look at:
- their **hours** (do they look right?)
- their **rating and review count**, and the **newest reviews** (any about missed calls or slow replies?)
- **photos**, and whether the **website link** works

Then **say one true, specific thing you saw, and ask about it**. Don't accuse.
- "Your Google listing shows you're closed on Saturdays. Is that right?"
- "I saw a couple of your reviews mention trouble getting through on the phone. Is that something you've noticed?"

**Never** quote a dollar loss, a statistic, or anything you didn't actually see. This is two minutes on one business already on your list,
not a search for new ones.

check.q: Before calling a pool company, you see three recent reviews saying nobody answered the phone. Your opener:
options: "I noticed a few of your recent reviews mention trouble getting through on the phone. Is that something you've seen?"
"Your reviews prove you need Station's Frontdesk."
"You're losing about a third of your callers to competitors."
check.why: Say what you saw, and ask. Never a number you can't back up, never "prove".

check.q: How long do you spend on a business's listing before you call?
options: None, the card has everything.
About two minutes: enough for one true, specific thing.
As long as it takes to read every review.
check.why: Two minutes makes the call specific without eating your day.

lessons.title: What you never do
lessons.goal: Know the moves that get a partner removed, so you never make one.
film: A plain list on paper, each line struck through with a red hairline as the voice reads it.
Short lesson. Things you never do, whatever anyone tells you works.
"Autodialers. Recordings. Robocalls." Struck.
No autodialers, no recorded messages, no robocalls.
"Mass texts. Mass emails." Struck.
No mass texts and no mass emails. Not to businesses, not to anyone.
"Buying, renting or scraping lists." Struck.
No buying, renting, scraping or pulling lists.
"Copying leads into your own spreadsheet or CRM." Struck.
No copying leads or clients into your own spreadsheet, phone contacts or CRM.
"Calling outside hours. Calling a do-not-call." Struck.
No calls outside their hours, and never a business that asked not to be called.
"Posting about Station without saying you earn a commission." Struck.
And if you ever recommend Station in a post, a review or a video, say you earn a commission.
A door closing: "Removed. Unpaid commission forfeited."
Any of these can get a partner removed, and unpaid commission forfeited.
Do-this-now card: "Not sure if something's allowed? Message Station first."
Not sure if something's allowed? Ask Station first. Asking is always better than guessing.
lessons.read_md:
**Never:**
- use **autodialers**, recorded messages or robocalls (dial every call by hand)
- send **mass texts or mass emails**, or any unsolicited bulk message
- **buy, rent, scrape or pull** lists of businesses
- **copy** leads or client details into your own spreadsheet, phone contacts, CRM or mailing list (Partner World has no export, on purpose)
- call **outside calling hours**, or call a business that asked not to be called
- call a business another partner gave you
- recommend Station publicly without saying **you earn a commission** ("I earn a commission if you sign up through my link.")
- bid on Station's name in paid search ads

Station can suspend or remove a partner, and forfeit unpaid commission, for spam, misrepresentation, fake or self-referrals, misuse of lead
or client data, or conduct that damages Station's name. **If you're unsure, ask Station first** with Message Station.

check.q: You'd like to keep a backup of your leads in a spreadsheet at home. Can you?
options: Yes, if the spreadsheet has a password.
Yes, for your own leads only.
No. Lead and client details never leave Partner World.
check.why: Copying leads into a personal spreadsheet or CRM breaks your agreement, and Partner World has no export for that reason.

check.q: You post a video about Station on your social account. What must it say?
options: Nothing, it's your own account.
That you earn a commission if people sign up through your link.
That you work for Station.
check.why: The law requires the disclosure, and you're an independent partner, not an employee.

modules.title: The call
modules.outcome: Run a whole call from hello to a dated next step, in the right order and the right words, then log it, and write a first email that gets a reply.

lessons.title: The shape of a call
lessons.goal: Name the five parts of every call and say what each one is for.
film: A phone on a desk, a Partner World Calls card lit beside it. A thumb hovers over "Call now".
Every call you make for Station has the same shape. Learn the shape once and you'll never wonder what to say next.
A single hairline draws across paper. Five ticks drop onto it, labelled one by one: "Intro." "Open." "Ask." "Pitch." "Close."
Five parts. Intro, open, ask, pitch, close. In that order, every time.
"Intro" lifts and grows. Under it: "Who you are. Independent partner. Is now OK?"
The intro is who you are. Your name, that you're an independent partner with Station, and whether now's a good time.
"Open" lifts. Under it, one question in quotes: "When the phone rings and you can't get to it, what happens to that caller?"
The open is one question about what it costs them. Not about the product. About their day.
"Ask" lifts. A second question stacks under the first, and a speech bubble from the owner starts filling with dots.
The ask is the follow-up question. This is where they talk and you listen.
"Pitch" lifts. One product painting slides in, Lineback, with a single line: "Texts back every call you miss."
The pitch is one product, in one or two sentences, in their words. Not fourteen products. One.
"Close" lifts. A blue envelope icon and a calendar square with a date in it: "Thursday, 10 am."
The close is a small next step. Send the page so the price is in writing, get their email, and name the day you'll check back.
Cut to the real Calls card. The cursor runs down its lines: "Say who you are", "Open with", "Then ask", "What it does", "If they ask the price", "Close". Each lights blue as it's touched.
You don't have to remember the words. Every card in Calls has your lines for that business, in exactly this order.
The five ticks shrink into a small strip that docks at the top of the card.
The card gives you the words. This module gives you the feel.
Do-this-now: "Open any card in Calls and read its lines out loud, top to bottom."
Open any card in Calls right now and read its lines out loud, top to bottom.
lessons.read_md:
Every call has five parts, always in this order:

1. **Intro.** Who you are, that you're an independent partner with Station, and whether now's a good time.
2. **Open.** One question about what the gap costs them. Not about the product.
3. **Ask.** A follow-up question. They talk, you listen.
4. **Pitch.** One product, in one or two sentences, in their words, and the price if they ask.
5. **Close.** A small next step: send the page so the price is in writing, get the best email, and name the day you'll check back.

Every card in **Calls** shows your lines in this order: **Say who you are**, **Open with**, **Then ask**, **What it does**,
**If they ask the price** and **Close**. The words change with the product you're pitching. The shape never does.

check.q: You've said who you are and they've said they have a minute. What comes next?
options: The price, so they know straight away.
One question about what the gap costs them, like what happens to calls they can't get to.
A quick run through what each Station product does.
check.why: The open is a question about their day. The product only makes sense once they've said the problem out loud.

check.q: What is the close on a first call?
options: Ask them to buy before you hang up.
Send the page so the price is in writing, get their email, and name the day you'll check back.
Tell them you'll set it up for them this week.
check.why: The first-call close is small and reversible. Nobody is asked to decide on the phone, and you never set anything up.

lessons.title: The first ten seconds
lessons.goal: Open a call honestly: your name, that you're independent, and permission to keep going.
film: A clock face with a red second hand sweeping from 0 to 10. A phone rings once and picks up: "Yeah, Dave's Heating."
The owner picked up. You've got about ten seconds before they decide if you're worth listening to.
A speech bubble, yours, types in: "Hi, is this the owner? My name is Sam, and I'm an independent partner with Station. I'll be quick."
Say it plainly. "Hi, is this the owner? My name is Sam, and I'm an independent partner with Station. I'll be quick."
The words "independent partner" underline themselves in blue.
Independent partner. Every call, first sentence. You don't work for Station, and you never let them think you do.
A second bubble: "Did I catch you at a bad time?" A small pause icon sits after it.
Then ask permission, and stop talking. "Did I catch you at a bad time?"
Owner's bubble: "I'm on a job." Your bubble: "No problem. When's better, later today or tomorrow morning?"
If it's a bad time, believe them. Ask when's better, and go. A call you end politely is a call you can make again.
Three lines try to slide in and get struck out in red: "I'm calling from Station." "You're expecting my call." "This is a quick survey."
Never say you're calling from Station, never say they're expecting you, never pretend it's a survey. Cold calls already feel like scams. Don't give them a reason.
The Calls card's local-time chip glows: "Their time 7:42 pm. OK to call." Then it flips to "Calls open 9 am" and the button greys.
You only call inside calling hours: 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone. Partner World switches the button off outside them.
A microphone icon with a red line through it.
And you never record a call. Not even for practice with a real business.
Do-this-now: "Say your intro out loud with your own name, then the permission question. Five times."
Say your intro out loud five times, with your own name, then the permission question. It should feel like saying hello.
lessons.read_md:
**Your first ten seconds:**

> Hi, is this the owner? My name is [your name], and I'm an independent partner with Station. I'll be quick. Did I catch you at a bad time?

Then stop and let them answer.

- **Say "independent partner" in your first sentence.** You're not a Station employee and never suggest you are.
- **If it's a bad time, believe them.** "No problem. When's better, later today or tomorrow morning?" Log it as **Call back**
  with that time.
- **Never say** you're calling from Station, that they're expecting your call, or that it's a survey.
- **Calling hours:** 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone. The call button is off outside them.
- **Never record a call.**

You'll tell them you earn a commission too, just before you ask for anything (lesson 9.6).

check.q: Which intro is right?
options: "Hi, I'm doing a quick survey of local businesses about missed calls."
"My name is Sam, and I'm an independent partner with Station. I'll be quick. Did I catch you at a bad time?"
"Hi, it's Sam from Station's sales team. You were expecting my call?"
check.why: Say who you are, that you're independent, and ask permission. Anything else misleads the owner and breaks the agreement.

check.q: The owner says, "I'm on a roof right now." What do you do?
options: Say it'll only take two minutes and keep going.
Ask when's better, log a Call back for that time, and hang up.
Pitch fast before they hang up.
check.why: Believe them. A polite short call keeps the door open; pushing through closes it.

lessons.title: Gatekeepers and voicemail
lessons.goal: Get past the person who answers and leave a voicemail that keeps the door open.
film: Phone picks up: "Lakeside Dental, this is Jen." A name tag "Jen, front desk" pins itself to the bubble.
Most calls don't reach the owner first. They reach Jen.
Your bubble: "It's Sam, an independent partner with Station. Is the owner around, or when's a good time to catch them?"
Be brief and honest. "It's Sam, an independent partner with Station. Is the owner around, or when's a good time to catch them?"
Jen's bubble: "She's in after two on Wednesdays." A note writes itself on the card: "Ask for Dr. Patel, Wed after 2."
Get a name and a time. Write it on the card as a note. Business facts only.
Three lines struck through in red: "Pitching Jen." "Saying Dr. Patel is expecting you." "Asking Jen to decide."
Don't pitch the person who answers. Don't say the owner's expecting you. And don't ask Jen to make the call for her boss.
The Calls card: "How did it go?" The cursor presses "Talked to them", then "Call back", picks Wednesday, 2:15 pm.
Log it as a call back on the day and time Jen gave you. Partner World reminds you.
Hard cut: a voicemail beep. A waveform starts drawing.
Now, voicemail. Most dials end here.
The voicemail line types in: "Hi, this is Sam, an independent partner with Station, calling for the owner of Lakeside Dental. I'll try you again another day. Thanks!"

Say who you are, who you're calling for, and that you'll try again. "Hi, this is Sam, an independent partner with Station, calling for the owner of Lakeside Dental. I'll try you again another day. Thanks!"
A price tag tries to drop into the waveform and bounces off. Text: "No price. No pitch."
No price on voicemail, and no pitch. Fifteen seconds, then hang up.
The card: cursor presses "Voicemail". It shows "Tried today" and slides to the back of the list.
Press Voicemail. They come back on your list tomorrow. Nobody gets called twice in one day.
Do-this-now: "Find 'Voicemail?' on any card and read the line out loud."
Find "Voicemail?" on any card in Calls and read the line out loud, so it sounds like you the first time you need it.
lessons.read_md:
**When someone else answers:**

> It's [your name], an independent partner with Station. Is the owner around, or when's a good time to catch them?

Get a name and a time. Add it as a note (business facts only, like "Ask for Dr. Patel, Wed after 2") and log **Call back** for that day.
