Don't pitch the person who answers, don't say the owner's expecting your call, and don't ask them to decide for the owner.

**When you get voicemail** (the line is under **Voicemail?** on every card):

> Hi, this is [your name], an independent partner with Station, calling for the owner of [business]. I'll try you again another day. Thanks!

No price and no pitch on voicemail. Press **Voicemail**: the card shows **Tried today** and comes back tomorrow.

check.q: The receptionist asks, "What's it about?" What do you say?
options: Pitch the receptionist so she can pass it on.
"Missed calls. I'm an independent partner with Station. When's a good time to catch the owner?"
"She's expecting my call."
check.why: Be brief and honest, get a time, and save the pitch for the person who decides.

check.q: What goes in a voicemail?
options: Your link, read out slowly.
The price and a reason to call you back today.
Your name, that you're an independent partner with Station, who you're calling for, and that you'll try again.
check.why: Voicemail keeps the door open. No price and no pitch, and press Voicemail so they come back tomorrow.

lessons.title: Let them do the math
lessons.goal: Help an owner weigh the price against one job of their own, without promising a return.
film: A torn invoice on paper: "Furnace repair." The amount is blank.
Here's the most useful question you'll ask, and you never have to do the sum yourself.
Your bubble: "What does an average job run you?" Owner's bubble fills in: "Four, five hundred."
Ask what an average job is worth to them. Their number, not yours.
Your bubble: "About how many calls go to voicemail in a week?" Owner: "Five, six, maybe." A row of six phone icons, greyed.
Then ask how many calls go to voicemail in a week. Again, their number.
The Answer painting slides in with a price tag: "Answer · $297 a month".
Now put the price beside it. "Station's Answer collection is $297 a month."
Your bubble, last line: "Does that math work for you?" A long pause bar fills slowly. Nothing else moves.
And ask. "Does that math work for you?" Then stop talking. Let them do the sum in their own head.
Three lines struck out in red: "It'll pay for itself." "You're losing thousands a month." "My other clients got ten jobs."
Never say it'll pay for itself. Never tell them how much they're losing. Never quote another client's numbers. You don't know, and neither does anyone else.
The owner's bubble: "If it saved one job a month, sure." The phone icons stay grey; the word "his math" stamps under it.
When they say it works, that's their math, about their business. That's worth far more than any number you could promise.
Do-this-now: "Write the two questions on a card by your phone."
Write those two questions on a card and keep it by your phone.
lessons.read_md:
You never need to promise a return. Ask two questions and let the owner compare it to the price:

> What does an average job run you? About how many calls go to voicemail in a week? Station's Answer collection is $297 a month. Does that math work for you?

Then stop talking.

**Never say:** "it'll pay for itself," that they're losing a specific amount, or anything about other clients' numbers. Every number
on the call should be theirs or a published price.

check.q: The owner says jobs run about four hundred and he misses five calls a week. What do you say next?
options: "My last client got eight extra jobs in the first month."
"So you're losing two thousand a week. This pays for itself in a day."
"Station's Answer collection is $297 a month. Does that math work for you?"
check.why: Give the price and let him decide. Working out his "loss" or quoting other clients is a promise you can't keep.

check.q: Whose numbers belong in this part of the call?
options: Your estimate of what they're losing.
An industry average you read online.
The owner's own numbers, and Station's published price.
check.why: Their numbers about their business are honest and persuasive. Anything else is a guess dressed up as a fact.

lessons.title: Speed and tone
lessons.goal: Sound like a calm neighbor, not a script: slow, short, and quiet after every question.
film: A waveform racing, jagged, too fast to read. A caption above it: "Hi-this-is-Sam-with-Station-and-we-help-local-businesses-like-yours-"
You can hear a sales call in the first breath. Fast, flat, and reading.
The waveform relaxes into slow, even swells. Caption: "Hi, is this the owner?" (pause)
Slow down. Slower than feels natural. On the phone, slow sounds sure of itself.
A stopwatch: the pitch line types out and the watch stops under 45 seconds.
Keep your pitch short. One or two sentences, well under a minute. If you're still talking after forty-five seconds, you've lost them.
Your question in a bubble, then a long empty space after it. A small label: "Quiet. They're thinking."
After every question, stop. Silence feels long to you. To them it's thinking time. Don't fill it.
Two questions stacked in one bubble; the second one gets struck out.
One question at a time. Two at once and they'll answer the easier one.
Mr. Chen's shop counter. The price appears once, large and slow: "$497 a month". Beneath: "No contract."
With anyone who's careful with English, drop the idioms. Say the price once, slowly, and say "no contract".
A jargon pile tumbles in: "automation", "workflow", "leverage". It's swept off; in its place: "texts back when you miss a call".
Use their words. "Texts back when you miss a call" lands. "Automation" doesn't.
Do-this-now: "Record yourself saying your intro on your own phone, and listen back."
Record yourself saying your intro and pitch, just to yourself, and listen back. You'll hear exactly where to slow down.
lessons.read_md:
- **Slow down.** Slower than feels natural. Short spoken sentences.
- **Keep the pitch short:** one or two sentences, well under a minute.
- **One question at a time,** then stop and let the quiet work. Don't stack two questions.
- **Use their words,** and say a product name like a name ("Station's Answer collection"). No jargon like "automation" or "workflow".
- **With owners who are careful with English:** no idioms, no fast talk. Say the price once, slowly, and say "no contract".

Practice by recording yourself on your own, never a real call.

check.q: You ask the owner a question and there's a long pause. What do you do?
options: Fill it with more about the product.
Ask a second question to keep things moving.
Wait. Let them think and answer.
check.why: The pause is thinking time. Filling it takes their answer away.

check.q: An owner whose first language isn't English is listening carefully. What helps most?
options: Plain words, no idioms, the price said once and slowly, and "no contract".
Explaining every product so they have the full picture.
Talking a bit faster so the call is shorter for them.
check.why: Clear and slow builds trust. Speed and long lists feel like a trap.

lessons.title: A whole call, line by line
lessons.goal: Run one complete call, from intro to a dated next step, with the commission said out loud.
film: Title on paper: "One call. Start to finish." Under it, the five ticks: Intro, Open, Ask, Pitch, Close. A small "Dave, HVAC, 4 techs" card slides in.
Here's one real-shaped call, all the way through. Dave runs a heating and plumbing company with four techs. Watch the ticks light up as we go.
"Intro" lights blue. Your bubble types.
You: Hi, is this the owner? My name is Sam, and I'm an independent partner with Station. I'll be quick. Did I catch you at a bad time?
Owner's bubble, grey.
Owner: I've got a minute. What's it about?
"Open" lights. Your bubble.
You: When you're under a house and the phone rings, what happens to that caller?
Owner's bubble. A voicemail icon pulses beside it.
Owner: Voicemail. Half of them don't leave a message.
"Ask" lights. Your bubble.
You: When you miss one, do those callers usually wait for you, or try someone else?
Owner's bubble.
Owner: Probably call the next guy. I had a lady tell me last week she called us first.
Your bubble; a small label "his numbers" appears.
You: What does an average job run you? And about how many calls go to voicemail in a week?
Owner's bubble; two numbers write themselves on a notepad: "four or five hundred", "five or six a week".
Owner: Four, five hundred. Five or six a week, I'd guess.
"Pitch" lights. The Answer painting slides in behind your bubble.

You: Station's Answer collection texts back anyone you miss, so the conversation stays with you, and customers can book themselves. It's $297 a month, with no setup fee and a 14-day free trial. Does that math work for you?
A long pause bar. Then the owner's bubble.
Owner: If it saved me one job a month, sure. Does it sound like a robot?
Your bubble. The word "Text" underlines itself.
You: It's a text, from your business, asking what they need. They reply, and you answer when you're out from under the house. You keep your own number.
A small calm line appears, set apart: "Say it before you ask." Your bubble.
You: And just so you know, I earn a commission if you sign up.
"Close" lights. Your bubble.
You: Want me to send you the page with the price, so it's in writing? It starts with a 14-day free trial and there's no contract. What's the best email?
Owner's bubble. An email address writes itself onto the card, blurred.
Owner: Dave at the company name dot com. My wife does the books, though.
Your bubble. A second person icon joins Dave's on the card.
You: Then I'll send it so you can both look. I'll check back Thursday morning. Does ten work?
Owner: "Ten's fine." The calendar square stamps blue: "Thu 10:00 am".
Owner: Ten's fine.
All five ticks lit. Cut to Calls: "How did it go?" The cursor presses "Talked to them", "Interested", "Set a call-back time", Thursday, 10 am. A note: "Wife does books. 5-6 voicemails a week."
That's the whole call. Under three minutes. Now log it: Talked to them, Interested, call-back Thursday at ten, and a note.
Do-this-now: "Read this call out loud with a friend playing Dave."
Read this call out loud with a friend playing Dave. Then swap. This is the call you'll record for your certification.
lessons.read_md:
**Dave, heating and plumbing, four techs. A whole call:**

> **You:** Hi, is this the owner? My name is Sam, and I'm an independent partner with Station. I'll be quick. Did I catch you at a bad time?
>
> **Dave:** I've got a minute. What's it about?
>
> **You:** When you're under a house and the phone rings, what happens to that caller?
>
> **Dave:** Voicemail. Half of them don't leave a message.
>
> **You:** When you miss one, do those callers usually wait for you, or try someone else?
>
> **Dave:** Probably call the next guy.
>
> **You:** What does an average job run you? And about how many calls go to voicemail in a week?
>
> **Dave:** Four, five hundred. Five or six a week.
>
> **You:** Station's Answer collection texts back anyone you miss, so the conversation stays with you, and customers can book themselves. It's $297 a month, with no setup fee and a 14-day free trial. Does that math work for you?
>
> **Dave:** If it saved me one job a month, sure. Does it sound like a robot?
>
> **You:** It's a text, from your business, asking what they need. They reply, and you answer when you're free. You keep your own number.
>
> **You:** And just so you know, I earn a commission if you sign up.
>
> **You:** Want me to send you the page with the price, so it's in writing? It starts with a 14-day free trial and there's no contract. What's the best email?
>
> **Dave:** [gives email] My wife does the books, though.
>
> **You:** Then I'll send it so you can both look. I'll check back Thursday morning. Does ten work?

**Notice:** one product, his numbers, the commission said before the ask, nothing promised, and a day and time to call back.
Then log it: **Talked to them → Interested → Set a call-back time**, plus a note.

check.q: When do you tell the owner you earn a commission?
options: Only if they ask.
Never. It puts people off.
Just before you ask for anything, like their email.
check.why: Being straight about the commission is part of being honest about who you are. Say it before the ask, every call.

check.q: Dave says his wife does the books. What's the right move?
options: Ask for her cell number and call her yourself today.
Push for a yes before he talks to her.
Send the page so they can both look, and set a call-back time.
check.why: Include whoever decides. Pushing someone who needs a second person loses the sale.

check.q: Dave asks if it sounds like a robot. What's true for the Answer collection's text-back?
options: It's a text from his business asking what they need, and he replies when he's free.
Callers can't tell it isn't him.
It never makes mistakes.
check.why: Describe what it actually does. Never claim callers can't tell, or that it's perfect.

lessons.title: End with a date, then log it
lessons.goal: End every call with a dated next step and log the result before you dial again.
film: A call ends: "Sounds good, send it over." The line goes dead. Empty calendar.
"Sounds good, send it over." Most calls end there, and most of them go nowhere. Here's why.
The word "Sure" floats away like a balloon.
A "sure" with no day attached is a goodbye.
Your bubble: "I'll check back Thursday morning. Does ten work?" The calendar square fills: "Thu 10:00". It turns blue.
So every call ends with a date. "I'll check back Thursday morning. Does ten work?" One small step, with a day on it.
The Calls card opens "How did it go?" Four buttons: No answer, Voicemail, Bad lead, Talked to them.
Then, before you dial anyone else, log it. Press how it went.
After "Talked to them", five more buttons fan out: Interested, Call back, Not interested, Do not call, Won: they're buying.
If you talked to them, pick what happened.
Cursor taps "Interested"; two choices appear: "Set a call-back time" and "Book a call".
Interested always needs a next step: a call-back time, or a call booked on your calendar. Partner World won't let you skip it.
The call-back picker: "Tomorrow", "In 2 days", "Next week", a time list. Times outside their calling hours are greyed.
Pick the day and time they agreed to. Partner World shows it in your time and theirs, and only offers times inside their calling hours.
The "Due now" list at the top of Calls. A card ticks over to "Overdue" two hours past its time.
When the time comes, it's in Due now. Two hours late, it's marked Overdue. Keep your word on the time.
"Yours till Nov 4" on a card. A call is logged; the date jumps forward 14 days.
Every call you log on a business Station sent you keeps it yours for another 14 days. Go 14 days without logging one, and it goes back for another partner.
A note box: "Ask for Maria after 2." Under it, struck out: "Seemed grumpy."
Add a note if it helps: business facts only.
Do-this-now: "Open 'What do these buttons mean?' in Calls and read it once."
Open "What do these buttons mean?" in Calls and read it once. Then you'll never guess.
lessons.read_md:
**End every call with a dated next step:**

> I'll check back Thursday morning. Does ten work?

A "sure, send it over" with no day on it usually goes nowhere.

**Log it before you dial again.** On the card, **How did it go?**:
- **No answer** or **Voicemail**: they come back tomorrow.
- **Bad lead**: wrong number, closed, or not a fit.
- **Talked to them**, then **Interested**, **Call back**, **Not interested**, **Do not call** or **Won: they're buying**.

**Interested always needs a next step:** a call-back time, or **Book a call** (lesson 10.7). **Call back** asks for the day and time; only
times inside their calling hours can be picked. Due call-backs show under **Due now**, and turn **Overdue** two hours after.

A business Station sends you is **yours for 14 days**, and each call you log gives you another 14 days. Notes are
business facts only. Pressed the wrong button? **Undo** at the bottom, right after you save.

check.q: The owner says, "Sure, send me something." What do you say before you hang up?
options: "Call me when you've had a look."
"I'll check back Thursday morning. Does ten work?"
"Great, talk soon."
check.why: Every call ends with a day and time. A next step with no date usually goes nowhere.

check.q: You mark a business Interested. What does Partner World need next?
options: A call-back time or a booked call.
Nothing, Interested is enough.
Their card number.
check.why: An Interested lead always needs a next step, and you never take payment details.

check.q: Which is a good note on a card?
options: "Wife does the books. Ask for Dave before 8 am."
"Rude guy, probably broke."
His home address and his kids' names.
check.why: Notes are business facts only. Station and your Partner Lead can read them.

lessons.title: Emails and messages
lessons.goal: Write a first email that gets a reply: plain text, one-to-one, short, and with no link.
film: An inbox. A glossy email with a logo banner, bold headings and three buttons slides into a tab labelled "Promotions".
This is the email most salespeople send. Logo, buttons, bold. It looks like an ad, so it gets treated like one.
It crumples. A plain email types in instead, no formatting, like a note from a neighbor.
Yours looks like a person wrote it. Because a person did.
Subject line types in lowercase: "dave, the page we talked about".
A personal subject, the way you'd write to someone you just spoke to.

Body types out, short: "Hi Dave, thanks for your time on the phone today. Before I send the page for Station's Answer collection, is this the best address for you and your wife both? I'll check back Thursday at 10 like we said. Sam, independent partner with Station"
Short. Thank them, one question, the day you'll check back, and who you are. Under a hundred words.
A link icon tries to drop into the email and bounces off. Text: "First email: no link."
No link in your first email. Ask a question first. When they reply, the page goes in your next email, with your link on it.
A reply lands: "Yes, send it." Your second email: one line, one link, blue.
One link, one line, once they've answered.
Partner World card: "Write them an email". Below: "Sent today: 3 of your limit."
Send it with Write them an email on their card, from your Station sending address. Replies come back to Station and show under the button.
A stack of identical emails fanning out to fifty addresses gets struck out in red. Then a single text bubble and a social DM icon, each with a question mark.
One person at a time. Never a mass email, never copied to a list. Texts only go to someone who agreed to hear from you, one at a time, and stop the moment they say stop.
Do-this-now: "Write your Dave email in plain text. Count the words. Under 100, no link."
Write the Dave email yourself, in plain text. Count the words. Under a hundred, and no link.
lessons.read_md:
**Every email to a business is one-to-one and plain text:** no logo, no bold, no bullets, no images, no buttons.

- **Subject:** personal, the way you'd write to someone you just spoke to, like "dave, the page we talked about".
- **Body:** under about 100 words. Thank them, ask one question, say when you'll check back, and sign it as an independent partner with Station.
- **No link in the first email.** Ask a question first; send the link once they've answered. After that, one link per email.
- **Send it with Write them an email** on their card, from your Station sending address. Station adds your name, its postal
  address and an unsubscribe line, and replies come back to Station. Until partner email is switched on for you, you may email from
  your own address, as long as you say you're a Station partner and follow these rules.
- **Only email people who agreed** to hear from you. Never a mass email. Never paste one email to a list.
- **Texts:** only to someone who agreed to hear from you, one at a time. Honor STOP, and any request to stop, immediately.
- **Social media messages:** Station can confirm whether you may start a conversation by direct message. Until it does, only reply
  to a business that messaged you first, one-to-one, with no link in your first reply.
- **Never say** in an email what you wouldn't say on the call: no promises, no urgency, no prices that aren't on the page.

check.q: Which first email is right?
options: A designed email with Station's logo, bold headings and a "See pricing" button.
Plain text, a personal subject, a thank-you, one question and the day you'll check back. No link.
Plain text with links to five product pages so they can choose.
check.why: Plain, short and link-free reads like a person. The link goes in your next email, once they've replied.

check.q: You've found twenty roofers' emails on their websites. Can you send them all the same email?
options: No. Email only people who agreed to hear from you, one person at a time.
Yes, as long as there's an unsubscribe line.
Yes, if you put them in BCC.
check.why: Mass and unsolicited email is spam, and spam gets a partner removed.

modules.title: Discovery & demo
modules.outcome: Find the one gap that matters to this owner, match it to one product, include whoever decides, and use their Google listing, their free audit, a website preview or a booked call to move them forward.

lessons.title: The questions
lessons.goal: Ask two or three qualifying questions, one at a time, and listen for the gap.
film: An owner's bubble, already long: "...and then the guy says he called us twice..." Your side stays empty.
The best discovery call is one where the owner does most of the talking.
A deck of seven cards fans out on paper, each with one question.
Station gives you seven questions. You'll use two or three on any call.
Cards flip one at a time: "What kind of work do you do, and where?" "When the phone rings and you can't answer, what happens to that caller?"
What kind of work do you do, and where? When the phone rings and you can't answer, what happens to that caller?
Next cards: "How do customers book you today?" "When someone asks about a job and goes quiet, how many times do you follow up?"
How do customers book you today? When someone asks about a job and goes quiet, how many times do you follow up?
Last cards: "How many Google reviews do you have, compared with the competitor you lose work to?" "Do you have past customers you never email?" "Who else makes the decision with you?"
How many Google reviews do you have, compared with the competitor you lose work to? Do you have past customers you never email? And who else makes the decision with you?
Three cards slide forward, four slide away. A label: "Pick 2 or 3."
Pick two or three that fit the business. A roofer and a salon don't get the same questions.
One card, a long empty bubble after it, slowly filling with the owner's words. A phrase in it underlines itself blue: "nobody calls them back".
Ask one, then listen. You're listening for the gap, in their words. When you hear it, you've found your pitch.
A pile of all seven cards dumped at once on an owner; he backs away.
Don't fire all seven. That's an interview, not a conversation.
Do-this-now: "Pick three questions for the next business in your Calls list."
Look at the next business in your Calls list and pick the three questions you'd ask them.
lessons.read_md:
**The qualifying questions.** Pick two or three that fit the business, and ask them one at a time:

- What kind of work do you do, and where?
- When the phone rings and you can't answer, what happens to that caller?
- How do customers book you today?
- When someone asks about a job and goes quiet, how many times do you follow up?
- How many Google reviews do you have, compared with the competitor you lose work to?
- Do you have past customers you never email?
- Who else makes the decision with you?

Ask one, then listen. You're listening for the gap, said in their own words. Don't run through all seven.

check.q: You're calling a salon that already has an online booking app. Which question fits best?
options: "How do customers book you today?"
"Do you have past clients you never email?"
All seven, so nothing gets missed.
check.why: Pick questions that fit the business. Booking is already covered, so ask about the gap that might be open.

check.q: The owner starts telling a long story about a lost job. What do you do?
options: Let them finish, and listen for the gap in their words.
Start the pitch while they're warmed up.
Cut in with the next question to stay on schedule.
check.why: Their story is the discovery. The words they use are the words your pitch should use.

lessons.title: One answer, one product
lessons.goal: Match what the owner said to the one product that fixes it.
film: The owner's line in a bubble: "The phone rings on a job and I just can't get it." The fourteen product paintings sit in a grid behind, dimmed.
They've told you the gap. Now match it to one thing. Just one.
Lines draw from the bubble to three paintings, which light up: Lineback, Frontdesk, Answer.
Missed calls on a job? Lineback texts them back. Frontdesk answers the call itself. The Answer collection does the text-back plus chat, booking, a business number and payments.
New bubble: "People ask about a job, I reply once, and they vanish." Pursuit lights.
Leads that go quiet: Pursuit, the follow-up that keeps going politely and stops when they reply.
New bubble: "The guy down the road has two hundred reviews." Repute lights; beside it Echo, for "Google shows the wrong hours".
Too few reviews: Repute. A thin or wrong Google listing: Echo.
New bubble: "I've got years of old customers I never contact." Revive and Dispatch light.
Past customers they never contact: Revive to win them back, or Dispatch to email them.

Quick montage, one line each: "Late-night website visitors → Greet." "Back-and-forth booking → Slate." "Personal cell on the truck → Dial." "Chasing invoices → Tap." "Social page gone quiet → Marquee."
Website visitors at night: Greet. Booking back and forth: Slate. Personal cell on the truck: Dial. Waiting to get paid: Tap. A social page gone quiet: Marquee.
Radar lights alone, with a tag: "Only for businesses that sell to other businesses."
Radar finds business customers. Only sell it to a company that wants offices, builders or property managers as customers.
Two gaps in one family: Pursuit and Revive together slide into a "Follow Up" frame.
If they name two gaps from the same family, a collection may fit: Answer, Get Found or Follow Up.
A hand drags Core onto a one-man detailer's card. The card shakes no. Answer slides in instead; tick.
But start with the smallest thing that fixes what hurts most. A client who sees one product working adds more later.
Do-this-now: "On the next card, say the gap in one line, then the one product."
Before your next call, look at "Why them" on the card and say the gap in one line, then the one product that fixes it.
lessons.read_md:
**Match the gap to one product:**

| They say | Lead with |
|---|---|
| Calls go to voicemail on jobs | Lineback (text-back), Frontdesk (answers the call), or the Answer collection |
| Website visitors get no answer at night | Greet |
| Booking is back-and-forth, people no-show | Slate |
| Leads go quiet after one reply | Pursuit |
| Too few reviews | Repute |
| Google listing is thin or wrong | Echo |
| Old customers never hear from them | Revive or Dispatch |
| The business number is their personal cell | Dial |
| They wait weeks to get paid | Tap |
| Their social page has gone quiet | Marquee |
| They want business customers (offices, builders) | Radar, and only for them |

Two gaps from the same family can point to a collection (**Answer**, **Get Found**, **Follow Up**). Plans (Core, Pro, Max) are for
owners who ask to hand off most of the front office. **Start with the smallest thing that fixes what hurts most.**

Don't pitch booking to someone who already has a booking app, and never sell Radar to a business whose customers are households.
**Change** on a card lets you pitch a different product to that business.

check.q: A plumber says, "People ask for a quote, I send one, and half of them never answer." What do you lead with?
options: Pursuit, the follow-up that keeps going and stops when they reply.
Core, so everything is covered.
Radar, to find new customers.
check.why: One gap, one product. The gap is follow-up, and Radar is only for businesses that sell to other businesses.

check.q: A house cleaner wants more homeowners as customers. Can you sell her Radar?
options: Yes, it finds customers in her area.
No. Radar is only for businesses that want other businesses as customers.
Yes, if she buys Core as well.
check.why: Radar finds commercial customers. If that isn't the client, don't sell it.

check.q: A one-van detailer misses DMs and calls. What's the right first offer?
options: Pro, because it's every product at a busy tier.
Every product, priced one by one, so he can choose.
The smallest fix: the Answer collection.
check.why: A small owner who hears a big plan first stops listening. Start small; they add more once one product works.

lessons.title: Who really decides
lessons.goal: Find out who approves, and bring them in instead of pushing the person on the phone.
film: One person on the call, a second chair behind them, empty, with a question mark.
The person on the phone is often not the one who says yes.
Three quick portraits, line drawings: "Mr. Chen, and his daughter." "Karen, and the doctor." "Rosa, and Javier."
Mr. Chen asks his daughter. Karen, the practice manager, needs the doctor to sign off. Rosa and Javier decide together.
Your bubble: "Who else weighs in on something like this? I can send the page to them too."
So ask, kindly. "Who else weighs in on something like this? I can send the page to them too."
The empty chair fills with a second figure. Both names appear on the card's note.
Now there are two people on the card, and your note says so.
Your bubble: "When's a good time to reach you both?" A calendar square lands with both icons on it.
Ask for a time when both of them can listen. Then the second person hears it from you, not secondhand.
A hand pushing a "Yes?" button at the person who can't decide. The button jams. Struck out.
Don't push for a yes from someone who needs a second person. You'll get a no, or a yes that cancels.
Karen's bubble: "Is it HIPAA compliant?" Your bubble: "I can't answer that, and I won't guess. Please email Station at main@station.solutions and ask for the answer in writing."
And when the decider's question is about rules or compliance, never guess. Send it to Station, in writing.
Do-this-now: "Add 'Who else weighs in?' to your question card."
Add "Who else weighs in on something like this?" to the card by your phone.
lessons.read_md:
Ask early, and kindly:

> Who else weighs in on something like this? I can send the page to them too.

Then ask for a time when **both** of them can listen, and note the second person's name and role on the card.

- **Don't push for a yes** from someone who needs a second person.
- **Compliance and legal questions** (health privacy, texting rules, contracts beyond the page): never guess. "I can't answer that,
  and I won't guess. Please email Station at main@station.solutions and ask for the answer in writing."

check.q: Karen, a practice manager, likes it but says the doctor signs off. You:
options: Offer to send the page to both, and ask when's a good time to reach them together.
Tell her it's easier to ask forgiveness than permission.
Ask her to sign up today and tell the doctor later.
check.why: Bring the decider in. A yes from the wrong person usually turns into a cancel.

check.q: She asks, "Is it HIPAA compliant?" You say:
options: "Yes, everything Station does is compliant."
"Probably, most software is these days."
"I can't answer that, and I won't guess. Please email Station at main@station.solutions and ask for the answer in writing."
check.why: Never make a compliance promise. Station answers those in writing.

lessons.title: One true thing you saw
lessons.goal: Spend two minutes on their Google listing and open with one true, specific thing, as a question.
film: A stopwatch set to 2:00. A Google listing scrolls in a browser frame: hours, reviews, photos.
Before you dial, spend two minutes looking at what their customers see.
The cursor circles details one at a time: "Closed Saturday." "23 reviews." "Last photo 2021." "No website."
Hours. Review count. Photos. Whether there's a website. Write down one thing that's true and specific.
Your bubble: "Your Google listing shows closed on Saturdays. Is that right?"
Then ask about it. Don't accuse. "Your Google listing shows closed on Saturdays. Is that right?"
Owner's bubble: "No! We've been open Saturdays for two years." A small blue spark.
Now they're talking about their own business. You didn't pitch anything. They found the gap.
Three lines struck out: "You're losing thousands because of your listing." "Most businesses like yours lose 60% of calls." "Your website is terrible."
Never quote a dollar loss. Never use a statistic. Never insult their site. And never say anything you didn't actually see.
The Calls card's "Why them" line glows: "Rating 4.1, 23 reviews; competitor nearby has 180." A tick appears only after the cursor checks the listing.
The card's "Why them" line gives you a head start. Check it's still true before you say it.
Do-this-now: "Open the next business's Google listing. Write one true thing, as a question."
Open the next business's Google listing. Write one true thing, as a question.
lessons.read_md:
Spend **two minutes** on their Google listing before you call. Look at their hours, review count and rating, photos, and
whether there's a website. Pick **one true, specific thing** and ask about it:

> Your Google listing shows closed on Saturdays. Is that right?

- **Ask, don't accuse.** Let them tell you whether it's a problem.
- **Never quote** a dollar loss, a statistic, or anything you didn't actually see.
- **Never** say their website or listing is bad.
- The card's **Why them** line is a head start. Check it's still true before you say it.

check.q: Which opener uses what you saw the right way?
options: "Your listing is costing you thousands a month."
"Most businesses like yours lose six in ten calls."
"Your listing shows 23 reviews and no photos since 2021. Is that something you've been meaning to get to?"
check.why: One true thing, as a question. Dollar losses and statistics are claims you can't back up.

check.q: The card's "Why them" says they have no website. What do you do before you mention it?
options: Check their listing and search for a site, to make sure it's still true.
Tell them their old site was probably hacked.
Say it straight away. Station already checked.
check.why: Only say what you've seen yourself. Things change, and a wrong fact ends the call.

lessons.title: Their free audit
lessons.goal: Get an owner their free audit with your link, and use it to talk about one gap.
film: The real station.solutions/audit/ page in a browser frame: "What is your front office leaking?"
Some owners want to see it for themselves before they talk. Station has a free audit for exactly that.
The twelve checks tick down a list: "A real website", "After-hours lead capture", "Your reviews", "Your Google listing", "Lead follow-up"...
Twelve checks on what a customer can see from the outside: their website, their Google listing, their reviews, whether anyone can book, ask or pay without calling.
The form fills: name, business, email, city, website. "Free · no card · in your inbox in about a minute."
The owner fills in their name, business, email and website. No card, no call. The report lands in their inbox in about a minute.
Your link in the address bar: "station.solutions/audit/?ref=yourcode". The "?ref=yourcode" glows blue.
Send them to it with your link, your code on the end, so the conversation is tied to you.
A report page. One line marked "We couldn't measure this from outside." A hand tries to circle it in red; the circle won't stick.
Read the report with them. Where it says it couldn't measure something, that isn't a failure. It means it couldn't check. Never call it broken.
The cursor picks one leaking check, "Lead follow-up", and draws a line from it to the Pursuit painting.
Then pick one thing it found. Just one. And connect it to the one product that fixes it.
A struck-out line: "See? You're losing money."
The audit shows what's working and what isn't. It isn't proof they're losing money, so never say it is.
Do-this-now: "Copy your link from any cheat sheet and change the end to /audit/."
Copy your link from any cheat sheet in Products and practice changing the page to slash audit.
lessons.read_md:
Station's **free audit** at station.solutions/audit/ runs **twelve checks** on what a customer can see from the outside: the
website, the Google listing and reviews, and whether people can book, ask or pay without calling. It's free, needs no card or
call, and the report lands in the owner's inbox in about a minute.

- **Send your link:** your code works on any station.solutions page, so send station.solutions/audit/?ref=yourcode.
- **The owner requests it,** with their own email. It's their report.
- **Read it with them,** on a call. Pick **one** thing it found and connect it to the one product that fixes it.
- **"Couldn't measure" isn't a failure.** It means the check couldn't see it from outside. Never call it broken.
- **Never say** the report proves they're losing money.

Whether you get a copy of an owner's audit: Station can confirm.

check.q: An owner wants to "see what's wrong" before talking further. You:
options: Send them station.solutions/audit/ with your code on the end, and offer to go through it on a call.
Run the audit yourself with their email and forward them the result.
Tell them what's wrong from memory.
check.why: The owner requests their own audit with their own email. Your code on the link ties it to you.

check.q: Their report says one check couldn't be measured from outside. What do you tell them?
options: Nothing; skip to the price.
That the audit couldn't see it from outside, so it's worth a look, not that it's broken.
That it's broken and needs fixing right away.
check.why: Can't check isn't the same as failed. Saying otherwise is a claim you can't back up.

lessons.title: A website preview
lessons.goal: Request a free website demo from Station, and know exactly what you do and don't do.
film: An owner's bubble: "Honestly, my website is from 2014."
Sometimes the gap is the website itself.
Your bubble: "Station can build a free demo of your own site, so you can see it side by side. Nothing's charged unless you like it and say yes."
You don't design anything. Station builds a free demo of their own site, by hand. Nothing's charged unless they like it and say yes.
Partner World Leads tab. The cursor opens the business and presses "Request a website". It turns to "Website: asked" with a tick.
In Leads, open the business and press Request a website. It needs a phone, an email or their current website on file.

lessons.read_md:

modules.title: Objections
modules.outcome: Answer every common push-back calmly and truthfully, from the page, without promising, discounting or pushing, and always end on a next step.

lessons.title: The method
lessons.goal: Handle any objection in four moves: acknowledge, one calm question, answer from the page, next step.
film: Owner's bubble lands hard: "That sounds expensive." Your side: a red bubble types fast, "No no, it actually pays for itself because..." and gets struck out.
Here's what an objection sounds like, and here's the wrong answer. Fast, defensive, and a promise you can't keep.
Four ticks draw onto a hairline: "Acknowledge." "One calm question." "Answer from the page." "Next step."
Every objection gets the same four moves.
"Acknowledge" lights. Your bubble: "Fair question."
One. Acknowledge it. "Fair question." "Of course." You're agreeing that it's reasonable to ask, not that they're right.
"One calm question" lights. Your bubble: "Expensive compared with what you're doing now, or more than you'd want to spend on this?"
Two. Ask one calm question, so you know what they actually mean. "Expensive" can mean five different things.
"Answer from the page" lights. The real product page appears in a frame; the price line underlines.
Three. Answer with what's on the page. The real price, what it really does, the trial. Nothing you made up, nothing you hope.
"Next step" lights. A calendar square stamps a date.
Four. End on a next step with a day. Every time.
The ticks fold into the corner. A row of objection cards fans out below, each with two halves: "Say" and "Don't say".
Station has a ready reply for every common objection, and a "don't say" next to each one. The next five lessons go through them all.
The "Don't say" half of every card flashes once: "No promises. No discounts. No urgency."
The "don't say" lines all come down to three things. No promises. No discounts. No false urgency.
Do-this-now: "Say the four moves out loud: acknowledge, question, page, next step."
Say the four moves out loud. Acknowledge, one question, answer from the page, next step.
lessons.read_md:
**Every objection, four moves:**

1. **Acknowledge.** "Fair question." "Of course." It's reasonable to ask.
2. **One calm question,** so you know what they really mean.
3. **Answer from the page:** the real price, what it really does, the trial. Nothing you made up.
4. **Next step,** with a day.

Every ready reply (they're in each product's cheat sheet under **Everything else**) has a **don't say** beside it. They all come
down to three things: **no promises, no discounts, no false urgency.**

check.q: The owner says, "That sounds expensive." What's your first move?
options: Acknowledge it, then ask one calm question about what they mean.
Explain right away that it pays for itself.
Offer a smaller price.
check.why: Acknowledge, then find out what "expensive" means to them. Promises and discounts are never the answer.

check.q: Where does the answer to an objection come from?
options: What another partner told you worked for them.
Whatever you think will keep them on the phone.
The product page and Station's ready replies.
check.why: If it isn't on the page or in the guide, you don't say it. Station can confirm anything else.

lessons.title: "How much?", "Send me info", "I already have a website"
lessons.goal: Answer the three most common early objections and turn each into a next step.
film: Role-play card 1. Owner's bubble: "How much is it?"
First, the one you'll hear on almost every call. "How much is it?"
Your red bubble: "I can get you a deal if you sign up this week." Struck out.
Not this. Never a deal, never a discount, never a price you haven't just checked.

Your blue bubble lands: "Good question. It depends on what you need, because each product is priced on its own, and most are month to month with no contract. For example, missed-call text-back is $197 a month, and the receptionist that answers every call starts at $397 a month."

Good question. It depends on what you need, because each product is priced on its own, and most are month to month with no contract. For example, missed-call text-back is $197 a month, and the receptionist that answers every call starts at $397 a month.
Continue: "Every price is published on station.solutions. What's costing you the most work right now?"
Every price is published on station.solutions. What's costing you the most work right now? Then you can point them at the one that fits.
Role-play card 2. Owner: "Just send me some info." Red bubble: "Sure!" (hang up, no day). Struck out.
Next. "Just send me some info." Where most cold calls die.
Blue bubble: "Happy to. So I send the right thing, what's the main thing you'd want to fix: missed calls, follow-up, reviews, booking or the website?" Then: "I'll check back Thursday."

Happy to. So I send the right thing, what's the main thing you'd want to fix: missed calls, follow-up, reviews, booking or the website? Then send the one page that fits, and name the day you'll check back.
A pile of old price sheets and screenshots gets swept off the desk.
Never old price sheets or screenshots. Only the live product page.
Role-play card 3. Owner: "I already have a website." Red bubble: "Honestly, your site's pretty dated." Struck out.
Last one. "I already have a website." Don't tell them it's bad.

Blue bubble: "That's fine, you can keep it. A lot of what Station does works alongside an existing site, like the chat, the missed-call text-back and reviews. If you ever want to compare, Station can build a free demo of a new site to see side by side. Nothing is charged unless you say yes."

That's fine, you can keep it. A lot of what Station does works alongside an existing site, like the chat, the missed-call text-back and reviews. If you ever want to compare, Station can build a free demo of a new site to see side by side. Nothing is charged unless you say yes.
Do-this-now: "Say the 'send me info' reply out loud, ending with a day."
Say the "send me info" reply out loud, and end it with a day.

"A new site from Station will bring you more customers."

lessons.title: "Is this a scam?", "Do you guarantee it?", "Is it a robot?"
lessons.goal: Answer the trust objections honestly: who you are, what you can't promise, and what the product really is.
film: Role-play card 1. Owner, arms folded: "Is this a scam? Who are you?" Red bubble: "I work for Station, it's totally legit." Struck out.
Owners are right to be suspicious of cold calls. And the wrong answer is to claim you work for Station.

Blue bubble: "Fair question. I'm Sam, an independent partner with Station. Station is Station Automations Group LLC, based in Houston, Texas, and every product and price is published at station.solutions."
Fair question. I'm Sam, an independent partner with Station. Station is Station Automations Group LLC, based in Houston, Texas, and every product and price is published at station.solutions.

I earn a commission if you sign up. There's no contract, and single products start with a 14-day free trial. You can email Station directly at main@station.solutions. If you'd rather I didn't contact you again, just say so.
Owner: "Yeah, take me off your list." The card's "Do not call" button presses itself blue.
If they ask you to stop, stop. Mark them Do not call, that day.
Role-play card 2. Owner: "How many jobs will I get?" Red bubble: "At least five more a month, easy." Struck out.
Next. "Do you guarantee results?" You never promise a number. Not jobs, not calls, not reviews, not rankings.

Blue bubble: "I can't promise a number, because it depends on your business and your market. What I can show you is exactly what the product does, and single products start with a 14-day free trial so you can see it working."

I can't promise a number, because it depends on your business and your market. What I can show you is exactly what the product does, and single products start with a 14-day free trial so you can see it working.

Last. "Is it a robot?" Never say callers can't tell, and never say it doesn't make mistakes.

Blue bubble: "It's an automated assistant. It answers from your business facts, doesn't make up prices, and hands off to you when it's unsure. The receptionist always offers a transfer to a person, and if it ever fails, calls ring your phone. You can read every conversation and change what it says."

It's an automated assistant. It answers from your business facts, doesn't make up prices, and hands off to you when it's unsure. The receptionist always offers a transfer to a person, and if it ever fails, calls ring your phone. You can read every conversation and change what it says.

lessons.read_md:
**"Is this a scam?" / "Who are you?"**

**Don't say** that callers can't tell, or that it never makes mistakes.

check.q: "Who are you, really?" Which part must your answer include?
options: That you're an independent partner and you earn a commission if they sign up.
That you're on Station's team in Houston.
That other businesses on their street have already signed up.
check.why: Independent, and paid on commission. Honesty about both is what makes the rest believable.

check.q: "Will this get me to the top of Google?" You say:
options: You can't promise a ranking or a number, and you'll show exactly what the product does.
Yes, within 90 days.
Most clients reach the top three.
check.why: Nobody can honestly promise a ranking, and Station never does.

check.q: The owner says, "Stop calling me." You:
options: Stop, apologize, and mark them Do not call that day.
Mark them Not interested and try again next month.
Ask once more whether it's timing.
check.why: A request to stop is absolute. Do not call means nobody from Station contacts them again.

lessons.title: "I need to think", "Can you do it cheaper?", "What's the contract?"
lessons.goal: Handle the not-yet objections with patience, no discounts and the real cancellation terms.
film: Role-play card 1. Owner: "I need to think about it." Red bubble: "Prices go up next week, and there are only a few spots left." Struck out.
"I need to think about it." The wrong answer is pressure. No "prices go up tomorrow." No "only a few spots left." It isn't true, and it's against the rules.

Blue bubble: "Of course, take your time. Would it help if I sent you the page so everything's in one place? Is there a question I can answer that would make it easier, like setup time? If it's OK, I'll check back on Thursday."

Of course, take your time. Would it help if I sent you the page so everything's in one place? Is there a question I can answer that would make it easier, like setup time? If it's OK, I'll check back on Thursday.
Role-play card 2. Owner: "Can you do it cheaper?" Red bubble: "I'll knock some off my commission for you." Struck out.
"Can you do it cheaper?" Never share your commission, never invent a special price, never offer a longer trial.

Blue bubble: "I can't change prices. Station sets them, and they're the same for everyone. What I can do is make sure you're on the right thing. If Frontdesk is more than you need, Lineback may do the job."
I can't change prices. Station sets them, and they're the same for everyone. What I can do is make sure you're on the right thing. If Frontdesk is more than you need, Lineback may do the job.
Two price tags side by side: "Frontdesk · $397 a month", "Lineback · $197 a month". Then a collection frame: "Bought together costs less than one by one."
Single products start with a free trial, and there's no contract. And if they want several products, a collection or plan costs less than buying them one by one.
Role-play card 3. Owner: "What's the contract? Can I cancel?" Red bubble: "You can get your money back any time." Struck out.
"What's the contract?" Never say they can get their money back any time. That isn't the policy.

Blue bubble: "There's no long-term contract. It's month to month, and you can cancel any time by emailing main@station.solutions from the account owner's email. Service stays on until the end of the period you've paid for, and months already delivered aren't refunded."

There's no long-term contract. It's month to month, and you can cancel any time by emailing main@station.solutions from the account owner's email. Service stays on until the end of the period you've paid for, and months already delivered aren't refunded.
Continue: "You keep your data and get a full export when you leave. The full policy is on station.solutions under Cancellation."
You keep your data and get a full export when you leave. The full policy is on station.solutions under Cancellation.
Do-this-now: "Find the Cancellation policy on station.solutions and read it once."
Find the cancellation policy on station.solutions and read it once, so you can say it in your own words.
lessons.read_md:
**"I need to think about it."**
> Of course, take your time. Would it help if I sent you the page for [product] so everything's in one place? Is there a question I can
> answer that would make it easier, like setup time or what Station would need from you? If it's OK, I'll check back on [day].

**Don't say:** "the price goes up tomorrow," "only a few spots left," or any other false urgency.

check.q: "I need to think about it." Which reply is right?
options: "Of course, take your time. Would it help if I sent you the page? I'll check back on Thursday."
"No problem, call me if you ever want it."
"I'd decide today. The price goes up next month."
check.why: Be patient, send the page, and set a day. False urgency breaks the rules; no day loses the lead.

check.q: The owner asks you to knock a bit off. You:
options: Offer a longer free trial instead.
Offer to send them part of your commission each month.
Say Station sets the prices and they're the same for everyone, and check they're on the right product.

check.q: "If I don't like it after three months, do I get my money back?" You say:
options: Yes, any time.
It's month to month, they can cancel any time by email, and months already delivered aren't refunded.
Yes, if they tell you first.
check.why: Months delivered aren't refunded. Promising money back is a promise Station doesn't make.

Sorry about that. Some home internet networks and security filters block newer websites. Could you try the link on your phone with Wi-Fi turned off, so it uses mobile data? If it still won't open, tell me what you see and I'll sort it out with Station.

options: He'll need to set it up himself, but it's easy.
