Station sets it up, the messages are pre-written, and he'll book a short onboarding call and share a few business facts.
check.why: Station does the setup, but the owner still books onboarding and gives a few facts. Don't oversell it.

check.q: Your link won't open for an owner. What do you do?
options: Send the same link three more times.
Ask them to try it on their phone with Wi-Fi off, then tell Station what they saw.
Tell them Station's website is down.
check.why: Some networks block newer sites. Mobile data often works, and Station needs the details to fix it.

lessons.title: "Do you do...?", "Can I talk to someone?"
lessons.goal: Handle requests outside the lineup and requests for a person without guessing or giving out a phone number.
film: Role-play card 1. Owner: "Do you do online ordering?" Red bubble: "Yeah, we can do that." Struck out.
"Do you do something that isn't on the shelf?" Never say "yes, we can," and never give a price or a date for it.

Blue bubble: "That isn't one of Station's standard products, so I don't want to promise something Station can't deliver. Let me check with Station and get back to you by Friday. In the meantime, would the Answer collection help?"

That isn't one of Station's standard products, so I don't want to promise something Station can't deliver. Let me check with Station and get back to you by Friday. In the meantime, would the Answer collection help?
The Message Station panel types: "Owner asked for online ordering. Told them I'd get back by Friday."
Then ask Station, and get back to them by the day you said.
Owner: "Does it work with my booking app?" Your bubble: "Station can confirm how it fits. I don't want to guess."
Same for "does it work with" whatever software they use. "Station can confirm how it fits. I don't want to guess."
Role-play card 2. Owner: "Can I talk to someone at Station?" Red bubble: a phone number typed out. Struck out.
"Can I talk to someone?" Of course they can. But never give out a phone number for Station. There isn't one.
Blue bubble: "Of course. I'm happy to get on a call myself. Would Thursday at ten or Friday at two work? If you'd rather talk to Station directly, email main@station.solutions."
Of course. I'm happy to get on a call myself. Would Thursday at ten or Friday at two work? If you'd rather talk to Station directly, email main@station.solutions.
Two doors: "Book a call (your calendar)" and "station.solutions/book/ · free 15-minute intro call with Station".
Book it with Book a call on their card. Or a prospect can book Station's free fifteen-minute intro call at station.solutions slash book.
Do-this-now: "Write your two time options for tomorrow's calls on your card."
Write two time options you can really make for tomorrow, so you're ready when someone asks for a call.
lessons.read_md:
**"Do you do [something not in the lineup]?"**
> That isn't one of Station's standard products, so I don't want to promise something Station can't deliver. Let me check with Station and
> get back to you by [day]. In the meantime, would [closest product] help?

Then message Station. **Don't say** "yes, we can," or give a price or a timeline. For "does it work with [their software]?": "Station can
confirm how it fits. I don't want to guess."

**"Can I talk to someone?"**
> Of course. I'm happy to get on a call myself. Would [two time options] work? If you'd rather talk to Station directly, email main@station.solutions.

Book it with **Book a call** on their card (until your booking calendar is set up, set a call-back time). A prospect can also book Station's
free 15-minute intro call at station.solutions/book/; for a client, pass it on with **Message Station**. **Don't** give out a phone number
for Station, because there isn't one.

check.q: A restaurant asks if Station does online ordering. You say:
options: "Probably, for a small extra fee."
It isn't a standard product, you'll check with Station and get back by a day you name.
"Yes, we can build that for you."
check.why: Never promise or price something off the shelf. Check with Station, and keep the day you named.

check.q: A prospect wants to speak to someone at Station. What can you offer?
options: A call with you, or Station's free 15-minute intro call at station.solutions/book/, or email to Station.
Station's office phone number.
Your Partner Lead's cell number.
check.why: Station has no phone number. Its doors are email and the intro call.

lessons.title: "Not interested" is not "do not call"
lessons.goal: Tell a reflex "not interested" from a real no and a do-not-call request, and log each one right.
film: The phone picks up. Before you finish your name: "Not interested."
Some owners say "not interested" before you've finished your name. That's a reflex, not a decision.
Your blue bubble, calm: "No problem. Is it timing, or you've already got it covered?"
One calm question is fair. "No problem. Is it timing, or you've already got it covered?"
Branch A: Owner: "Timing. Busy season." Your bubble: "Makes sense. Is there a better month to call?" A call-back date stamps onto the card.
If it's timing, ask when's better, and log a call back for then.
Branch B: Owner: "I said not interested." Your bubble: "Understood. Thanks for your time." The cursor presses "Not interested".
If they say it again, stop. Thank them, hang up, and log Not interested. Never ask twice.
Branch C: Owner: "Take me off your list." Your bubble: "Of course. You won't hear from me again." The cursor presses "Do not call". A lock closes on the card.
And if they say "take me off your list" or "don't call me again", that's absolute. Mark Do not call, that same day.
Three outcome cards side by side with plain labels: "Bad lead: wrong number, closed or not a fit." "Not interested: you reached them, they said no." "Do not call: they asked not to be called."
Three buttons, three meanings. Bad lead is a wrong number, a closed business, or not a fit. Not interested is a no. Do not call is a request.
The locked card reappears on a different day in "Found a business yourself?" with a red cross over the Add button.
Do not call means never again. Not even if you find the same business yourself months later.
A struck-out red bubble: "Just thirty more seconds, I promise..."
And no arguing. One question, then respect the answer.
Do-this-now: "Say the one question out loud: 'Is it timing, or you've already got it covered?'"
Say the one question out loud until it sounds friendly. "Is it timing, or you've already got it covered?"
lessons.read_md:
**A reflex "not interested" is not "do not call."**

1. **One calm question is fair:**
   > No problem. Is it timing, or you've already got it covered?
2. **If it's timing,** ask when's better and log **Call back** for then.
3. **If they say it again, stop.** Thank them and log **Not interested**. Never ask twice, never argue.
4. **"Take me off your list" or "don't call me again" is absolute.** Mark **Do not call** the same day. Station then never contacts them either,
   and you never call them again, even if you come across them yourself.

**The three closing buttons:**
- **Bad lead:** wrong number, closed business, or not a fit.
- **Not interested:** you reached them and they said no.
- **Do not call:** they asked not to be called again.

check.q: The owner says "not interested" before you finish your intro. You:
options: Ask one calm question: "Is it timing, or you've already got it covered?"
Hang up and mark Do not call.
Keep going with the pitch so they hear what they're missing.
check.why: A reflex isn't a decision. One calm question is fair; pushing past it isn't.

check.q: You ask your one question and they say "not interested" again. You:
options: Ask a second question to find the real reason.
Mark Call back for next week and try again.
Thank them, hang up, and mark Not interested.
check.why: One question, then stop. Asking twice or calling back after a clear no damages Station's name.

check.q: Months later you find the same business on your own, and they'd asked not to be called. You:
options: Add them as your own lead, since you found them yourself.
Don't call or add them. Do not call means never again.
Call once to check if they've changed their mind.
check.why: A do-not-call request is absolute, however you come across the business.

modules.title: Closing
modules.outcome: Hear the yes coming, close with your link, an email and a dated check-back, and get the sale credited to you without ever taking a payment.

lessons.title: Hearing the yes before they say it
lessons.goal: Spot a buying signal on a call and stop pitching the moment you hear one.
film: A phone held to an ear in a busy kitchen. A speech bubble rises over the noise: "So how would I start?" A blue underline draws under "start".
Halfway through your pitch, the owner asks: "So how would I start?"
The bubble freezes. Small type fades in beside it: "That's not a question." Then: "That's a yes."
That's not really a question. That's a yes that hasn't been said out loud yet.
Five more bubbles stack down the screen on the beat, each with a blue tick: "What's it cost again?" "What happens after I pay?" "Can I cancel?" "How long does setup take?" "My wife does the books."
Listen for these. They ask the price a second time. They ask what happens after they pay, or whether they can cancel. They ask how long setup takes. They bring someone else into it.
A pitch keeps typing out under the bubbles, line after line. A second product painting slides in, then a third. The owner's bubble shrinks and greys out.
The mistake is to keep talking. You hear the yes, and you add one more feature, one more product. And the yes goes cold.
The extra lines delete themselves. One short answer types in: "Month to month. Cancel any time." Then a blue arrow: "Next step."
So when you hear a signal, answer the question in one sentence. Then go straight to the next step.
A bubble: "Sounds interesting." It sits there with no tick. Under it, grey: "No question. No day. Not a yes yet."
Careful with the polite ones. "Sounds interesting" with no question behind it isn't a yes. It's a reason to ask one more question.
A bubble: "Let me ask Javier." Two small name tags appear: "Rosa" and "Javier", joined by a hairline.
And "let me ask Javier" is a real signal, but it means the yes needs two people. You find a time when both of them can look.
Do-this-now: "On your next call, count the signals." A tally mark ticks up in blue.
On your next call, count the signals. You'll hear more of them than you think.
lessons.read_md:
A **buying signal** is the owner telling you they're picturing having it. The common ones:

- They ask the price a second time, or ask what's included.
- They ask **what happens after they pay**, how long setup takes, or what you'd need from them.
- They ask **whether they can cancel**, or about the free trial.
- They bring in someone else: "my wife does the books," "I'd have to ask Javier."

**When you hear one, stop pitching.** Answer the question in one sentence, then go to the next step (lesson 12.2). Adding one more feature or one more product after a yes is how a yes goes cold.

**Not a signal yet:** a polite "sounds interesting" with no question behind it. Ask one more question instead.

**Two people deciding** is a real signal, but don't push the one on the phone for a yes. Ask when both can look, and send the page to both.

check.q: Mid-pitch, the owner asks: "And if it doesn't work out, can I cancel?" What do you do?
options: Finish walking through the rest of the features first, then come back to it.
Tell them they can get their money back any time.
Answer it in a sentence (month to month, cancel any time) and move to the next step.
check.why: A cancel question is a buying signal. Answer it truthfully and close. Refunds aren't "any time".

check.q: Rosa says, "I like it, but Javier decides about money." You:
options: Mark the card Won, since she likes it.
Ask when you can catch them both, and send the page so Javier can read it too.
Push Rosa for a yes now, while she's keen.
check.why: The person on the phone often isn't the one who approves. Bring the decider in, don't go around them.

lessons.title: The close: the page, an email, a day
lessons.goal: Close every interested call by sending the page, getting an email, and naming the day you'll check back.
film: A hand reaches toward a credit card on a counter. A red rule strikes through it. Type: "Not this."
Let's get one thing out of the way. Closing a Station sale never means taking a payment. Ever.
The card fades. The real station.solutions/answer/ page slides in inside a browser frame. Type over it: "This."
You close by sending the page. The price, the trial, what it does and what Station needs: it's all there, in writing.

A script line types, word by word: "I'll send the page with the price so it's in writing. What's the best email?" A blue cursor blinks after the question mark. Then a beat of silence, marked by a small pause icon.
Here's the line. "I'll send the page with the price so it's in writing. What's the best email?" Then stop talking, and let them answer.
An email address types itself into the real Interested card in Calls.
They give you an email. That's the first half of the close.
A calendar strip slides under the card. "Thursday, 10:00" lands on it in blue. Script line: "I'll check back Thursday morning. Does 10 work?"
The second half is a day. "I'll check back Thursday morning. Does 10 work?" A close with no day on it isn't a close. It's a goodbye.
The real "How did it go?" sheet: cursor taps Talked to them, then Interested, then Set a call-back time. Thursday 10:00 fills in, with their local time beside yours.
In Calls, log it: Talked to them, Interested, and set the call-back for the time you both said.
A bubble: "Just send me an email." A second line answers it: "Happy to. So I send the right page, is it the missed calls or the follow-up?" Then "Thursday?"
And when they say "just send me an email", that's still a close. Ask which problem, so you send the right page, and tie it to a day.
A bubble: "Can I just give you my card now?" Reply types: "Station takes payment on its own site. I'll send you the link right now."
If they want to start right now, great. Send your link while you're on the phone. They check out themselves on station.solutions. You never take card details.
Do-this-now: "Write the close line on a card by your phone."
Write the close line on a card and put it by your phone. Say it the same way every time.
lessons.read_md:
**The close is three things:** send the page, get an email, name the day you'll check back.

> I'll send the page with the price so it's in writing. What's the best email? *(stop and let them answer)* I'll check back Thursday morning. Does 10 work?

Then log it in Calls: **Talked to them**, **Interested**, and **Set a call-back time** for the day and time you agreed (or **Book a call** on your booking calendar). An Interested card always needs a next step.

**"Just send me an email"** is still a close. Ask which problem it's about so you send the right page, and tie it to a day: "So I send the right page, is it missed calls, follow-up or reviews? I'll check back Thursday."

**If they want to start now,** send your link while you're on the call. They check out themselves on station.solutions, or through a link Station sends them.

**Never:** take a payment or card details, ask for a decision before they've seen the page, stack two questions, or end the call with no day.

check.q: The owner says, "Sounds good, just send me something." Your best reply?
options: "Sure thing," then hang up and wait for them to reply.
"Happy to. So I send the right page, is it the missed calls or the follow-up? I'll check back Thursday. Does 10 work?"
"Great, I'll send you everything we've got so you can pick."
check.why: Find out what to send and tie it to a day. A vague "sure" with no day is where most calls die.

check.q: The owner says, "Can I just read you my card number now?" You:
options: Take only the last four digits to hold their place.
Say Station takes payment on its own site, and send your link so they can check out themselves.
Write it down carefully and pass it to Station with Message Station.
check.why: You never take payments or card details, not even part of a number. Checkout happens on station.solutions.

check.q: They gave you an email and agreed to Thursday at 10. What do you log in Calls?
options: Talked to them, Interested, and a call-back set for Thursday at 10.
Won: they're buying.
Nothing until they reply to your email.
check.why: They haven't bought yet. Interested always gets a next step, and the call-back reminds you on the day.

lessons.title: Your link, every time
lessons.goal: Send your own referral link on every close, and know what it does and doesn't remember.
film: Two identical product pages side by side. Zoom into the address bars. Left: "station.solutions/frontdesk/". Right: "station.solutions/frontdesk/?ref=yourcode", the last part in blue.
These two pages look the same. Only one of them pays you.
The real Frontdesk cheat sheet in Products. The cursor presses Copy beside "Your link". A small "Copied" tick.
Your link is your partner code on the end of a Station page. Every product's cheat sheet has it, with a Copy button.
The real Interested card in Calls. The cursor presses Copy link.
Interested and Won cards in Calls have Copy link too, for the product you pitched. The code works on any station.solutions page.
A phone opens the link. A small badge pins to the browser: "Your code · 30 days". A calendar flips through thirty days.
When they open it, the site remembers your code in that browser for 30 days, and carries it to checkout.
A second device, a laptop, slides in beside the phone. The badge does not jump across. Grey type: "Same browser only."
But only that browser. If they read it on their phone, then type station.solutions on the office computer a week later, the code isn't there.
The real Calls card with its call log and a Won mark. A shield icon settles over them.
That's why your call log and your Won mark matter. Station's records decide who gets the credit, including between two partners.
The real Write them an email box. A line types: "Good talking today. Should I copy Javier on the page?" No link in it. The reply comes back; a second email goes out with the blue link.
One more rule. Your first email to a business through Partner World can't carry a link. So thank them and ask one short question. When they answer, send your link.
Do-this-now: "Copy your link for the product you pitch most."
Open Products now and copy your link for the product you pitch most.
lessons.read_md:
**Your link** is any station.solutions page with your partner code on the end, for example station.solutions/frontdesk/?ref=yourcode. Find it on every cheat sheet in Products (**Your link**, **Copy**) and on Interested and Won cards in Calls (**Copy link**). Signing up from it is what credits the sale to you.

**What it remembers:** the site keeps your code **in that visitor's browser for 30 days** and carries it to checkout. **It won't follow them to another device.** If they'll sign up on a different computer, send the link where they'll use it.

**Protect your credit:** send your link every time, log every call in Calls (add businesses you found yourself), and mark them Won when they're buying. Station's records decide attribution, including between two partners.

**First email rule:** with **Write them an email**, your first email to a business can't carry a link. Thank them and ask one short question; send your link once they answer.

check.q: Dave opens your link on his phone Monday. On Friday he types station.solutions into his office computer and signs up there. What did your link carry?
options: Everything. The code follows him to any device for 30 days.
Nothing to that computer. The code stays in his phone's browser, so your logged calls and your Won mark are your backup.
Everything, as long as he signs up within a week.
check.why: The code lives in the browser that opened the link. Station's records decide, so log the calls and mark Won.

check.q: You're closing on Frontdesk. Which do you send?
options: station.solutions/frontdesk/?ref=yourcode, copied from the cheat sheet or the card.
A screenshot of the price, so they don't have to click anything.
station.solutions/frontdesk/, because Station will work out who sent them.
check.why: The code on the end of the link is what credits the signup to you. Screenshots go stale and carry no code.

check.q: You're writing your first email to a business through Write them an email. What goes in it?
options: A short thank-you and one question. Your link goes in the next email, once they answer.
Your link, so they can sign up straight away.
Nothing. Send it from your personal email instead, so you can include the link.
check.why: First emails to a business can't carry a link. Getting round the rule with another address breaks it.

lessons.title: Mark it Won, then tell Station
lessons.goal: Mark a sale Won, tell Station what they're buying, and get a client you closed yourself into your book.
film: The owner's bubble: "OK, let's do it." A blue path starts from it, toward a small book labelled "Your book".
They said yes. Now make sure it lands in your book.
The real "How did it go?" sheet. Cursor taps Talked to them, then Won: they're buying. The card asks for their email; it fills in.
One. In Calls, mark them Won: they're buying. The card asks for their email, and gives you Copy link and Write them an email. Send your link.

The real Help tab. Message Station opens; a message types: "Won: Dave's Heating, Answer collection. Dave Ruiz, dave@... Wife does the books. Wants calls forwarded from his own number." Send to Station.
Two. Tell Station what they're buying with Message Station, so the order can be accepted into your book. Add what you learned: hours, the decision maker, worries, anything they think you promised.
The real Money tab. A row slides into "Wins Station is checking": "Dave's Heating".
On a business Station sent you, Won goes to Station to check. You'll see it on Money under Wins Station is checking until Station confirms it and matches it to their signup.
The row moves from Wins Station is checking up into Your clients, once a payment line appears.
Once they pay, the client shows under Money.
Cursor hovers over "Marked Won by mistake? Change it" on the card. A small clock; then the link greys out and "main@station.solutions" appears.
Marked Won by mistake? Change it works until Station confirms the win. After that, email main@station.solutions.

A gym owner at a hardware-store counter, shaking hands. Then the real Clients tab: cursor presses Add a client. Fields fill: business name, the email they pay Station with, what they bought, a note. The row reads "Waiting for Station".

Closed a business you found yourself, say a gym owner you met at the hardware store? Add it to your list and mark it Won. Then on Clients, press Add a client, with the email they'll pay Station with and what they bought. It shows Waiting for Station until Station accepts or declines.
What's new on Home: "Station accepted Iron Lane Gym."
Station's answer lands under What's new on Home, and in your email.
Do-this-now: "Won. Link. Message Station. Every time."
Won, your link, Message Station. Every sale, the same three steps.
lessons.read_md:
**Every sale, three steps:**
1. **Mark them Won** in Calls (**Talked to them**, then **Won: they're buying**). Add their email and send your link.
2. **Message Station** with what they're buying, so the order can be accepted into your book. Add what you learned: hours, services, the decision maker, their worries, and anything they expect you promised.
3. **Check Money.** On a business Station sent you, the win shows under **Wins Station is checking** until Station confirms it and matches it to their signup. The client shows under Money once they pay.

**Marked Won by mistake?** **Change it** on the card works until Station confirms the win. After that, email main@station.solutions.

**A business you found yourself:** add it to your list first (**+ Add a business you found yourself**) and mark it Won. Then on Clients, press **Add a client** with the business name, **the email they pay Station with**, what they bought, and a note if you like. It shows **Waiting for Station** until Station accepts or declines, and the answer lands under **What's new** on Home and in your email. You can send up to five a day. A business already in another partner's book can't be added, and your own or your family's business is never eligible.

A client is in your book only once Station accepts the order.

check.q: You marked a business Station sent you Won yesterday. Where do you see it while Station checks?
options: On Clients, straight away.
Nowhere until your first payout.
On Money, under Wins Station is checking.
check.why: Station confirms the win and matches it to their signup first. The client appears under Money once they pay.

check.q: Station has already confirmed a win you marked on the wrong business. What now?
options: Press Change it on the card.
Email main@station.solutions.
Leave it. It will sort itself out when nobody pays.
check.why: Change it only works until Station confirms. After that, Station has to fix it.

check.q: You closed a gym owner you met at the hardware store. He was never on your list. What do you do?
options: Nothing. Station will see the signup and credit you.
Add him to your list and mark him Won, send your link, Add a client with the email he'll pay with, and tell Station what he's buying.
Ask him to email Station saying you sent him.
check.why: Station's records decide. A business Station hasn't accepted doesn't put a client in your book.

lessons.title: "What happens after I pay?"
lessons.goal: Tell a new client exactly what happens next, without promising a date or doing any of it yourself.
film: A bubble: "OK. So what happens after I pay?" A blue underline under "after".
Almost every new client asks this. Here's the answer, in order.
An inbox: an email from Station slides in, "Thanks, here's your receipt", with a receipt attached.
First, Station emails a thank-you with their receipt.
A second email: "Your Station account". A login card unfolds out of it.
Their Station account is set up, and the login details come by email.
The real station.solutions/onboarding/ page in a browser frame. A time slot gets picked.
Then they book a short onboarding call, where Station walks them through the account and connects their phone and calendar.
A checklist builds down the right side: "Hours." "Services and prices." "Google Business Profile link." "Social handles." "A brand colour."
Tell them what to have handy: their hours, services and prices, their Google Business Profile link, social handles and a brand colour.
A text-message icon with a small stamp: "Carrier registration · about 2 business days". A note under it: "Legal name, EIN, address."

If they're getting anything that texts, Station files the carrier registration. It takes about two business days, and the carriers control it. They'll need their legal business name, EIN and address, exactly as the IRS has them.
A calendar with a date circled. A red rule strikes through the circle. Type: "No go-live date. Ever."
What you never say is a go-live date. And you never say you'll set it up yourself.
A final line: "I'm your contact throughout." A small partner badge beside it.
And you finish with: "I'm your contact throughout."
Do-this-now: "Learn the answer by heart."
Learn it by heart. You'll say it at the end of every yes.
lessons.read_md:
When they ask what happens after they pay, say:

> After checkout, you get a thank-you email from Station with your receipt, and your Station account is set up, with login details sent by email. Then you book a short onboarding call where Station walks you through the account and connects your phone and calendar. Have your hours, services and prices, your Google Business Profile link and your brand colours handy. If you're getting anything that texts, Station files the carrier registration, which takes about 2 business days. I'm your contact throughout.

Good to know:
- Single products and collections start with a **14-day free trial**. Plans (Core, Pro, Max) are billed at checkout.
- Each product page states its own time to go live. Anything that texts waits on carrier registration first, and **the carriers control the timing**. If the business has no EIN, tell Station.

**Never say** a go-live date, "live today" for anything that texts, or that you'll do the setup yourself.

check.q: A new Lineback client asks, "So it'll be texting my missed callers by Monday?" You say:
options: "I'll set it up myself this weekend so it's ready."
"Yes, Monday for sure."
Texting starts after carrier registration, about 2 business days, and the carriers control it. Station keeps them posted.
check.why: Never promise a go-live date, and never do setup yourself. Texting always waits on the carriers.

check.q: What should a new client have ready for their onboarding call?
options: Their customer list, emailed to you first.
Their hours, services and prices, Google Business Profile link, social handles and a brand colour.
Their Google password, so Station can get in quickly.
check.why: Station never needs passwords (Google access comes through Google's own invite), and customer lists go to Station, never to you.

lessons.title: The custom website path
lessons.goal: Send an owner who wants a custom website down the right path, and mark it Won only when Station says so.
film: A tired website on an old laptop: a stretched logo, a copyright from years ago. The owner's bubble: "Honestly, I hate our website."
Some owners don't want a missed-call text. They want a new website.
The real Custom website cheat sheet in Products. Cursor presses Copy beside Your link: "station.solutions/custom/?ref=yourcode".
There's a separate path for that. Copy your link from the Custom website cheat sheet. It goes to station.solutions/custom/.
The real station.solutions/custom/ page in a browser frame. Questions scroll by; a small timer reads "about 5 minutes".
The owner answers about five minutes of questions there.
A demo site builds itself on paper, section by section. A calendar strip: "2 to 3 business days".
Station builds a free demo of their site by hand, and emails it within two to three business days.
A price tag flips over to show no number, just "Priced to the project".
It's priced to the project. There's no set price, so you never quote one. Nothing is charged until they've seen the demo and said yes.
The real "How did it go?" sheet: Interested, then a call-back set. A grey note under the Won button: "Not yet."
On the call, mark them Interested, with a call-back. Not Won.
An email from Station lands: "They said yes." Only now does the cursor press Won.
You mark it Won only when Station tells you they've said yes. You earn 40% of the website's setup fee, once, when they pay it.
Two cards side by side: "Custom website: quoted" and "Free website with Core or Pro: up to 5 pages, built after the first paid month".

Don't mix it up with the free website that comes with the Core and Pro plans. That one's built after their first paid month clears. A custom website is its own project, and collections get 50% off it.
Do-this-now: "Copy your Custom website link now."
Copy your Custom website link now, so it's ready when someone says they hate their site.
lessons.read_md:
**When an owner wants a custom website:**
1. Send your link from the **Custom website** cheat sheet: station.solutions/custom/?ref=yourcode, so the demo is credited to you.
2. Mark the call **Interested**, with a call-back.
3. The owner answers about **5 minutes of questions**. Station builds a **free demo by hand** and emails it within **2 to 3 business days**, then quotes the project.
4. **Mark it Won only when Station tells you they've said yes.** You earn 40% of the website's setup fee, once, when they pay it.

You can also use **Request a website** on a business in Leads, as long as Station has their phone, email or current website. It shows **Website: asked ✓** once it's sent.

**Never** quote a price for the build or for hosting & care. Both are quoted by Station. Send a demo only to someone who asked for it or agreed to receive it. You can share station.solutions/portfolio/, but don't call any site in it a client or a reference unless Station says so.

The **free website** that comes with the Core and Pro plans is different: up to 5 pages, built after the client's first paid month clears, never during a trial. Collections get **50% off a custom website** instead, and Station quotes it.

check.q: The owner asks, "Roughly what will a new website cost me?" You say:
options: The price of the Core plan, since that includes a website.
A ballpark, based on what the last website client paid.
It's priced to the project, so there's no set price. Station builds a free demo first, and nothing's charged unless they say yes.
check.why: Never quote a custom website. The free demo and Station's quote answer it properly.

check.q: She answered the questions through your link on Monday. Station emails her the demo on Thursday. When do you mark Won?
options: Monday, when she answered the questions.
Thursday, when the demo goes out.
Only when Station tells you she's said yes.
check.why: A demo isn't a sale. Station tells you when the owner says yes.

check.q: You think a bakery's site looks dated, but the owner never asked about it. Can you have Station email them a demo?
options: Yes, as long as your link is on it.
No. Send a demo only to someone who asked for it or agreed to receive it.
Yes, a free demo is a nice surprise.
check.why: An unasked-for demo is unsolicited marketing. Ask first; send it once they've said yes to seeing one.

modules.title: After the sale & the rules
modules.outcome: Look after a new client from checkout on, hand every problem to Station the same business day, grow your book at published prices, and follow every rule that keeps you, the client and Station safe.

lessons.title: What Station does after checkout
lessons.goal: Explain what Station does after a client pays, and what each product needs from the client.
film: Dave in his van, phone in hand. A checkout confirmation glows on screen: "You're in." Then the van goes quiet.
Dave just checked out. Here's everything that happens next, and who does it.
A blue path draws across paper with six stops. Stop 1 lights: "Checkout · station.solutions".
One. He paid on station.solutions, or through a link Station sent him. You never take payments.
Stop 2: a receipt slides out of an email. A small loop arrow beside it: "every renewal too".
Two. Station emails a thank-you with the receipt, and another receipt at each renewal.
Stop 3: a login card unfolds. Behind it the client's Station account, products switching on one by one with their wording already filled in.

Stop 4: the real station.solutions/onboarding/ page. A slot gets picked.

The path fades. A grid of the product paintings, each turning over to show what it needs: Repute "Google invite, never a password". Dispatch "their own list, never a bought one". Tap "their own processing account".

Do-this-now: "Open each cheat sheet you sell. Read what the client needs."

lessons.read_md:
**What Station does, in order:**
1. **Checkout** on station.solutions, or through a link Station sends. You never take payments.
2. **Receipt:** a thank-you email with the receipt, and another at every renewal.
3. **Account:** the client's own Station account, login details by email. Products switch on with pre-written wording they can edit.
4. **Onboarding call**, booked at station.solutions/onboarding/. Station connects their phone and calendar.
5. **Carrier registration** for anything that texts (Lineback, Dial, and the text parts of Slate, Pursuit and Repute), filed with the legal business name, EIN and address exactly as the IRS has them. About 2 business days; the carriers control it. No EIN? Tell Station.
6. **Product setup:** Station sets up each product.

**What each product needs from the client:**
- **Storefront:** form answers, a domain (or Station registers one), logo, photos, services.
- **Greet:** the chat code on their site or site access (nothing if Station built it), and their common questions.
- **Slate:** services with real durations, working hours, their calendar.
- **Lineback and Dial:** legal name, EIN, address, and where calls forward.
- **Frontdesk:** business facts, what it may and may not say, call forwarding, calendar, a test call.
- **Pursuit:** nothing; they can review the messages.
- **Repute and Echo:** Google profile access through Google's invite, never a password. Echo also needs photos.
- **Dispatch and Revive:** their own customer list, never a bought list.
- **Radar:** who they want as customers.
- **Tap:** their own card-processing account, set up by them.
- **Marquee:** social accounts they connect themselves, logo and job photos. Managed also needs their ad account.

**Where changes go:** wording, in their account under **Settings, then Your Words**. Everything else, the **Help** page in their account or main@station.solutions. A Station-built site they now run themselves: station.solutions/site-help/.

check.q: A new Repute client asks, "Should I just send you my Google password?" You say:
options: Yes, but only by text, not email.
No. Station gets access through Google's own invite, and never needs a password.
Yes, send it to you and you'll pass it on.
check.why: You never ask for or handle a client's passwords. Google access comes through Google's invite.

check.q: A new Lineback client's business has no EIN. What do you do?
options: Tell Station, because carrier registration needs one.
Nothing. Texting will work without it.
Tell them to use your EIN for now.
check.why: Carrier registration uses the legal name, EIN and address. Station decides how to handle a business without one.

check.q: A client wants their missed-call text to sound friendlier. Where does that change happen?
options: They wait for their next onboarding call.
In their own Station account, under Settings, then Your Words.
You log in and change it for them.
check.why: The client owns their wording and can change it any time. You never log into a client's account.

lessons.title: Your after-sale checklist and the Clients tab
lessons.goal: Do the six things a partner does after every sale, and use the Clients tab to look after your book.
film: A sticky note on a fridge: "Call Dave back." Crossed out. Then: "Done?" Then a big blue "Not done."
You closed it. You're not done. Here's what a good partner does after the sale.
A checklist builds, one line per beat. Line 1: "Won + your link." Line 2: "Message Station what you learned."
One, mark them Won and send your link. Two, tell Station what you learned: hours, services, worries, the decision maker, and anything they think you promised.
Line 3: "They book onboarding, and know what to bring."
Three, make sure they book their onboarding call and know what to have ready.
Line 4: "Talk with them on Clients." The real Clients tab opens beside it: a client row with its latest message and a "2 new" count.
Four, once they're paying, talk with them on the Clients tab.
Line 5: "Problem? Station, same business day." An arrow from a client bubble to Message Station.
Five, if they bring you any question or problem, Station handles it. You pass it on the same business day.
Line 6: "Notes current. Check in after a few weeks." A calendar page flips three weeks ahead and gets a blue dot.
Six, keep your notes current, and check in after the first few weeks.
Inside Clients: cursor presses Send email. Subject line shows the partner's name. A small eye icon: "Station sees every message." Then Add a note, and Interested in: "Repute".

On Clients, Send email replies by email from Station, with your name in the subject, and Station keeps the thread. Add a note with business facts only. Save Interested in, so you remember what to raise next.
Cursor presses Book Station support. A time is picked on Station's calendar.
If they need Station on a call, Book Station support picks a time on Station's own calendar. Station handles the call. You tell the client when it is.
Do-this-now: "Set a check-in three weeks after every sale."
After every sale, set yourself a check-in three weeks out. That's where the next sale comes from.
lessons.read_md:
**After every sale:**
1. Mark them **Won** in Calls and send your link. Tell Station what they're buying with **Message Station**.
2. Tell Station what you learned: hours, services, concerns, the decision maker, and anything they expect you promised.
3. Make sure they **book their onboarding call** and know what to have ready.
4. Once they're paying, talk with them on the **Clients** tab, including about adding products at published prices.
5. If they bring you a question or a problem, tell them Station will handle it and pass it on **the same business day**. Don't try to fix it yourself.
6. Keep your notes and lead status current, and **check in after the first few weeks**.

**The Clients tab:** a client shows up once a business you brought in is paying Station, or once Station accepts one you added.
- **Send email** replies by email from Station, with your name in the subject. Station keeps the thread and sees every message. There's no texting. If Station has no email for the client yet, Send email stays off; Message Station to add one.
- **Add a note** with business facts only (for example, "ask for Maria after 2"). Save **Interested in** a product to remember to raise it. Only you and Station see your notes.
- **Book Station support** books a call on Station's own calendar. Station handles it; you tell the client when.

Never log into a client's account. Never ask for or handle their passwords, bank details, card numbers or ID.

check.q: Three weeks after the sale, Dave hasn't heard from you. What's the right move?
options: Check in on the Clients tab: how's it going, and is anything not working?
Call and pitch him Core straight away.
Leave it. Station looks after clients now.
check.why: Checking in after the first few weeks is part of your job. It's how you hear about problems early and what to offer next.

check.q: Which note belongs on a client in Partner World?
options: "Office manager is Maria, best after 2. Interested in reviews."
"Login: dave@... password Summer24."
"Card ends 4417, expires next spring."
check.why: Notes are business facts only. Card details and passwords never go anywhere near you.

lessons.title: Hand it to Station, the same business day
lessons.goal: Know every situation that goes straight to Station, and write a hand-off Station can act on.
film: A client bubble at 4:52 pm: "My texts stopped sending??" A clock beside it ticks toward 5.
It's almost five. A client says their texts stopped. What now?
The bubble slides across a hairline to Station's side and turns blue: "Handled." Type: "Same business day."
You don't fix it. You don't wait until Monday. You pass it to Station the same business day.

A long list builds down the screen, quickly, one line per half-beat: "Something's broken." "A charge or an invoice." "Refund, credit, chargeback." "Cancel, downgrade, pause." "A complaint, a lawyer, a regulator." "A discount, a longer trial, an annual plan." "A website or hosting & care quote." "Not in the catalogue." "No EIN, or a carrier problem." "Keeping or moving a number." "A link won't open." "A leak or a login problem." "Wants someone other than you." "Anything you're unsure about."

Here's the list. Anything broken. Any charge, refund or chargeback. Cancel, downgrade or pause. A complaint, or the word lawyer. A discount or a longer trial. Any quote. Anything not on the shelf. No EIN. Phone numbers. A link that won't open. A data leak or a login problem. A client who wants someone else. And anything you're unsure about.
The list compresses into one line: "Asking is always better than guessing."
If you're unsure, that's on the list too. Asking is always better than guessing.
The real Help tab: Message Station. Then an email draft with the subject typing in: "Partner DR214 — Dave's Heating — texts stopped".
Use Message Station, or email main@station.solutions. Those are Station's only contacts. There's no phone number. If you email, the subject line is: Partner, your code, the business, the topic.

The email body fills in six short lines, each with a tick: "Me: name + code." "Them: business, contact, email." "What they said, in their words." "What I told them." "Urgent: broken today." "What I need: a fix."

In the message: your name and code. The business, the contact and their email. What they said, in their words. What you've already told them. How urgent it is. And what you need back: an answer, a quote, a fix or a call.
Back to the client bubble. A reply types: "Thanks for telling me. Station handles this, and I've passed it on just now."
Then tell the client: Station will handle it, and you've passed it on.
Do-this-now: "Save the subject line as a template."
Save that subject line somewhere you can paste it. You'll use it every week.
lessons.read_md:
**Hand off right away when:**
- Something is broken in a client's account or product.
- A client asks about a charge, invoice, receipt or card.
- A client asks for a refund or credit, or mentions a chargeback.
- A client wants to cancel, downgrade or pause.
- A client complains, is upset, or mentions a lawyer, a legal problem or a regulator.
- Someone asks for a discount, a custom price, a longer trial or an annual plan.
- Someone wants a website quote or a hosting & care quote.
- Someone asks for something not in the catalogue, or about contract terms beyond what's on the site.
- A business has no EIN, or has a carrier registration problem.
- Someone asks about keeping or moving a phone number and you're not sure.
- A link or page won't open for someone.
- You suspect a data leak or a login problem (tell Station within 72 hours).
- A client asks to work with someone other than you.
- Anything you're unsure about. Asking is always better than guessing.

**How:** **Message Station** on the Help tab, or email **main@station.solutions**. Those are the only contacts; there's no phone number. Subject line: **Partner [yourcode] — [business name] — [topic]**. Include your name and code; the business, the contact's name and email; what they asked, in their words; what you've told them; how urgent it is (broken today, this week, whenever); and what you need back (an answer, a quote, a fix or a call).

Then tell the client Station will handle it and that you've passed it on. On a billing question, don't guess what the charge is or promise a refund. If they mention disputing it with their bank, ask them to contact Station first, and tell Station.

check.q: A client says, "I'm going to dispute this charge with my bank." You:
options: Tell them it's probably the usual monthly fee.
Promise them a refund so they don't dispute it.
Ask them to contact Station first, and pass it to Station right away.
check.why: Billing is Station's. Never guess at a charge or promise a refund, and a chargeback threat is urgent.

check.q: On Friday afternoon, a client asks you for a longer free trial for her sister's salon. You:
options: Leave it until Monday's batch of messages.
Pass it to Station today. Only Station can agree a longer trial.
Agree to an extra two weeks, since it's family of a client.
check.why: Trials and discounts are Station's call, and hand-offs go the same business day.

check.q: Which subject line is right for an email hand-off?
options: URGENT!!! Please help
Question about a client
Partner DR214 — Dave's Heating — texts stopped
check.why: Your code, the business and the topic let Station find the account and act without writing back to ask.

lessons.title: Grow your book: land, then expand
lessons.goal: Offer the next product at published prices, at the right moment, with no pressure.
film: A single product painting, Lineback, sits on paper with a small green "working" dot. Weeks tick by on a hairline beneath it.
You started Dave on one thing. It's working. Now what?
A check-in bubble types: "How's it going? Is anything not working?" Dave's reply: "Texts are great. Still missing the after-hours calls though."
You check in. And you listen for the next gap. He tells you himself.
The Frontdesk painting slides in beside Lineback and clicks into place. Its price tag reads "$397 a month", taken from the live page.
Now there's a reason to mention Frontdesk, the receptionist that answers every call. At the price on its page. Nothing else.
The real My Services screen in a client's Station account, previewing the charge before he confirms.
He adds it himself from My Services in his Station account, which shows the charge first, or from the product page. You tell Station about it with Message Station.
A row of three paintings stacks into one collection card. Small type: "A collection or plan usually costs less than the products separately."
If a client ends up wanting several products, a collection or plan usually costs less than buying them one by one. Show them the page.
A pushy line types out: "Only a few spots left at this price!" A red rule strikes it through.
What you never do: pressure. No "only a few spots left", no "the price goes up Friday". If he says not now, note it and ask again another day.
A bubble: "Who does your plumbing? Your accountant? Who printed your van?" Three business names appear and drop into Calls as "Your lead".
One more way your book grows. Once a client is happy, ask who they work with. Specific questions work better than "know anyone?". Those become businesses you found yourself.
Do-this-now: "On every client, save one Interested in."
For every client on your Clients tab, save one Interested in. That's your next conversation.
lessons.read_md:
**Land with one product. Expand when the client shows you the next gap.** A client who sees one thing working adds more later, and you earn on each one.

- **Check in** after the first few weeks: how's it going, and is anything not working? Listen for the next problem in their words.
- **Offer only at published prices**, checked on station.solutions before you say them.
- The client adds a product from **My Services** in their Station account (it previews the charge first) or from the product page. Tell Station about the upsell with **Message Station**.
- If a client outgrows one product, they upgrade just that product for the difference. If they want several, a **collection or plan** usually costs less than buying them separately.
- Save **Interested in** on the client so you remember what to raise.

**No pressure, ever.** No false urgency, no "only a few spots left", no "the price goes up Friday". If they say not now, note it and check back another time.

**Ask for introductions.** A happy client knows other owners. Ask specific questions ("Who does your plumbing? Your accountant?"). Add those businesses to Calls yourself and call them by the normal rules. Never ask a client for their customer list.

check.q: A Lineback client says the texts are great but she still loses calls after hours. Best move?
options: Mention Frontdesk at the price on its page, and send the page if she wants to look.
Pitch Max, so she never needs to add anything again.
Offer Frontdesk at a little less, since she's already a client.
check.why: Expand on the gap she named, at published prices. Discounts are never yours to give.

check.q: A client says, "Not right now," when you mention Repute. You:
options: Note it on Clients as Interested in Repute, and raise it another time.
Tell him the price is going up next month.
Mention it in every email until he says yes.
check.why: No false urgency and no pressure. A calm "not now" is often a "later".

check.q: A happy client offers to email you her whole customer list "so you can find more people like me." You:
options: Accept it and pass it to Station later.
Thank her and decline. Ask instead which businesses she works with, and add those yourself.
Accept it and call the ones that look like businesses.
check.why: You never collect a client's customer list. Introductions she names are fine; her list is not.

lessons.title: When a client wants to cancel
lessons.goal: Handle a cancel request calmly, pass it to Station straight away, and never work against Station after.
film: A client bubble: "I think I want to cancel." The client's card on Clients, a small pause in the music.
Sooner or later a client says this. Here's what you do.
A reply types: "I'm sorry to hear that. Can I ask what's not working?"
First, ask what's not working. Sometimes it's a setting Station can fix, or a different product fits better.
The reply continues: "If you still want to cancel, email main@station.solutions from the account owner's email. Service stays on until the end of the period you've paid for."
If they still want to cancel, they email main@station.solutions from the account owner's email, and Station confirms it. Service stays on to the end of the period they've paid for.
Message Station opens: "Dave's Heating wants to cancel. Reason: slow season." An arrow: "Straight away."
And you tell Station straight away.
Two lines struck through in red: "Stay and I'll get you a month free." "You'll get a refund."
Never pressure them. Never promise a refund or a credit. That's Station's call.
A website card with two paths: "Keep the site: $1,250 once" and "Hosting & care: quoted by Station".
If a plan with a free website ends, the site comes off Station hosting at the end of the paid period. Unless they take a hosting and care plan Station quotes, or pay the one-time $1,250 to keep it.
A calendar running twelve months. Type: "Never steer a Station client to a competitor."
And one rule that outlasts the client, and even your agreement. For twelve months after you leave, you never encourage a Station client to cancel, and never move them to a competing product.
Do-this-now: "Save the cancel reply in your notes."
Save the cancel reply where you can find it. You'll want it to sound calm on the day.
lessons.read_md:
When a client in your book wants to cancel:

> I'm sorry to hear that. Can I ask what's not working? Sometimes it's a setting that can be fixed, or a different product fits better. If you still want to cancel, email main@station.solutions from the account owner's email and Station will confirm it. Service stays on until the end of the period you've paid for.

**Then tell Station straight away.** Don't pressure them, and don't promise a refund or a credit.

**Good to know:** there's no long-term contract. Months already delivered aren't refunded, and the client gets a full export of their data when they leave. If their plan's free website comes off Station hosting, they keep their domain, words and photos; they can take a hosting & care plan Station quotes, or pay a one-time **$1,250** to keep the built site (you earn 40% of it, once). Cancelling hosting on its own is at station.solutions/cancel-hosting/.

Your commission on that client stops once they stop paying. Money already earned stays yours.

**Never work against Station.** While your agreement runs and for 12 months after it ends, you never encourage a client you dealt with through Station to cancel, downgrade or not renew, never move them to a competing product, and never steer a Station prospect to a competitor.

check.q: A client says she wants to cancel. Which reply follows the rules?
options: Ask what's not working, explain she emails main@station.solutions from the owner's email, and tell Station straight away.
Tell her she'll get this month refunded.
Offer her a free month out of your commission to stay.
check.why: Listen, point to how cancelling works, and hand off. Credits, refunds and side deals are never yours.

check.q: You leave the program in June. In September, a former client asks if you can move her to another company's text-back tool. You:
options: Decline. For 12 months after you leave, you don't move Station clients to competing products.
Help, as long as she cancels Station herself.
Help, since you're not a partner any more.
check.why: The non-solicitation rule lasts 12 months after the agreement ends, for every client you dealt with through Station.

lessons.title: The rules: brand, prices, promises, disclosure
lessons.goal: Describe Station, its prices and yourself accurately, and disclose your commission every time you recommend it.
film: Four words stack on paper like a sign: "Brand." "Prices." "Promises." "Disclosure."
Four sets of rules keep you, the client and Station safe. They're short.
"Brand" lifts out. Under it: "Station." "Your Station account." "Station's platform." A row of blank logo shapes slides in and is struck through.
Brand. Say Station, your Station account, or Station's platform. Never name any software company behind Station's products.
A badge reads "Station employee". A red rule strikes it. A search-ad box with "Station" in it is struck through too.
Don't pretend to be Station or an employee. Don't bid on Station's name in search ads. And when your agreement ends, stop using Station's name and logo.
"Prices" lifts out. The live station.solutions price for Frontdesk sits under a magnifying glass: "$397 a month", with a small "checked today".
Prices. Quote only what's published on station.solutions, and check it before you quote.
Struck through, one by one: "Discount." "Credit." "Rebate." "A bit of my commission." "Custom website price." "Hosting & care price." "A price for the app."

No discounts, credits, rebates or custom prices, and never a share of your commission. No price for a custom website, hosting and care, or anything not in the catalogue. The mobile app is free, so it never gets a price.
"Promises" lifts out. Struck through: "You'll rank first." "Ten more jobs a month." "Texting live today." "Only three spots left."
Promises. No guarantees of results, rankings, calls, reviews, jobs or earnings. No timelines Station hasn't approved. Never same-day texting. And no false urgency.
"Disclosure" lifts out. A phone shows a social post with your link; a line types into the caption: "I earn a commission if you sign up through my link."
Disclosure. Whenever you recommend Station in public, a post, a review, a comment or a video, say clearly that you earn a commission. The FTC requires it.
A phone call card: "Hi, it's Sam, an independent partner with Station." Then later: "I earn a commission if you go ahead."
And on a call, say you're an independent partner, and say you're paid a commission before you ask for anything.
Do-this-now: "Write your disclosure line into your social bio drafts."
Write your disclosure line now, so it's there before your first post.
lessons.read_md:
**Brand**
- Say "Station," "your Station account" or "Station's platform." Never name any software vendor behind Station's products.
- Use Station's name, logo and approved materials only to promote Station, and stop when the agreement ends.
- Don't impersonate Station or suggest you're an employee. You can't sign anything, accept payments or make commitments for Station.
- Don't bid on Station's name in paid search ads.

**Prices**
- Quote only prices published on station.solutions, checked before you quote.
- No discounts, credits, custom prices, rebates or side incentives (including sharing your commission) without Station's written consent.
- Never quote a custom website build, hosting & care, or anything not in the catalogue. The mobile app is free; never quote a price for it.

**Promises**
- No guarantees of results, rankings, calls, reviews, jobs or earnings.
- No timelines, custom work, features, credits or discounts Station hasn't approved in writing. Never promise same-day texting.
- No false urgency.

**Disclosure**
- Whenever you recommend Station publicly (a post, review, comment or video), say clearly that you earn a commission. For example: "I earn a commission if you sign up through my link." The FTC requires it.
- On calls, say who you are ("an independent partner with Station") and that you're paid a commission before you ask for anything.

check.q: You post a short video recommending Station with your link. What must it include?
options: A disclosure only if someone asks in the comments.
A clear line that you earn a commission if they sign up through your link.
Nothing extra. It's your personal account.
check.why: The FTC requires a clear disclosure on every public recommendation, in the post itself.

check.q: An owner asks which company's software is behind the receptionist. You say:
options: Name the company, since it's a well-known brand.
It's Station's platform, set up and supported by Station.
"I'll tell you off the record."
check.why: Never name any vendor behind Station's products, on or off the record.

check.q: A friend suggests running a search ad on "Station Solutions" to catch people looking for it. You:
options: Do it, but only in your own city.
Do it, as long as the ad uses your link.
Don't. Partners never bid on Station's name in paid search.
check.why: Bidding on Station's name is barred by the agreement, whatever link the ad uses.

lessons.title: The rules: calls, texts and email
lessons.goal: Call, text and email only in the ways the law and your agreement allow.
film: A hand dials a number on a phone keypad, one digit at a time. Type: "By hand."
Every call you make for Station is dialled by hand. One at a time.
An autodialer box and a "press 1" recording icon slide in and get struck through. "TCPA" in small type beside them.
No autodialers, no recorded messages. Calls follow the TCPA and state telemarketing rules.
A clock face with the hours shaded blue: "9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone". The real Calls card: the call button greys out at 8:01 pm their time.
Call only 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone. Partner World shows their local time and switches the call button off outside those hours.
A bubble: "Take me off your list." The real card: cursor presses Do not call. A lock icon. Type: "Same day. For good."
When someone asks not to be called again, mark them Do not call the same day. Then nobody calls them. Not you, not Station, even if you come across them again.
A record button on a phone, struck through.
And never record a call with a business.
A text bubble with a check mark: "They said yes to texts." Beside it a stack of fifty identical texts, struck through. "STOP" types in and every bubble stops.
Texts go only to people who've agreed to hear from you, one person at a time. Never a mass text. Honor STOP, or any request to stop, immediately.
An email with three highlighted parts: an honest subject, the sender's real name, an unsubscribe line. "CAN-SPAM" in small type.
Email follows CAN-SPAM: an honest subject and sender, and an easy way to opt out. Write one to one. Never a mass email.
The real Write them an email box. Station's additions appear at the bottom: your name, Station's postal address, an unsubscribe line.
Once Partner World's email is on for you, every email to a lead goes through Write them an email. Station adds your name, its postal address and an unsubscribe line, and replies come back to Station.
A client's texting product with a stamp: "A2P registration approved". Below it: "Only to their own customers who gave them their number." "A past purchase isn't consent."

For clients, texting through Station starts only after carrier registration is approved. It only goes to the client's own customers who gave the business their number. A past purchase alone isn't consent to text, which is why Revive starts with email.
Do-this-now: "Unsure if a call is allowed? Ask Station first."
And if you're ever unsure whether a call or a text is allowed, ask Station first.
lessons.read_md:
**Calls** follow the TCPA and state telemarketing rules:
- Dial by hand. No autodialers and no recorded messages.
- Call only **9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone**. Each Calls card shows their local time and turns the call button off outside those hours.
- Respect do-not-call requests and do-not-call lists. When someone asks not to be called again, mark them **Do not call** the same day. Neither you nor Station contacts them after that, even if you come across them again yourself.
- Never record a call.

**Texts** go only to people who've agreed to hear from you, **one person at a time**. Never mass-text. Honor **STOP**, and any request to stop, immediately. Station doesn't currently have its own texting number.

**Email** follows **CAN-SPAM**: an honest subject and sender, and an easy opt-out. Write one to one; never send a mass email. Once Partner World's email is switched on for you, send every email to a lead with **Write them an email**. Until then you may email from your own address, as long as you say you're a Station partner and follow these rules.

**No spam:** no unsolicited bulk email, texts or calls, ever.

**Client texting** through Station's products starts only after carrier registration (A2P 10DLC) is approved. It goes only to the client's own customers who gave that business their number. A past purchase alone isn't consent to text, which is why Revive is email-first.

If you're unsure whether a call or text is allowed, check with Station first.

check.q: Twenty owners didn't pick up today. Can you text them all a short note with your link?
options: Yes, as long as each text is sent separately.
No. Text only people who've agreed to hear from you, one at a time, and never mass-text.
Yes, if you include "Reply STOP to opt out."
check.why: An opt-out line doesn't create consent. No agreement to texts means no text.

check.q: Linda asks if Station can text all 1,200 past clients in her spreadsheet. What's true?
options: Yes, they're her clients, so it's allowed.
A past purchase alone isn't consent to text, so past clients get email. Texts go only to people who agreed to them.
Yes, once carrier registration is approved.
check.why: Carrier registration lets texting start; it doesn't create consent. That's why Revive is email-first.

check.q: A business you called last month said, "Don't call me again." You find it again today on Google. You:
options: Don't call. Do not call is for good, even when you find them again yourself.
Email them instead.
Call, since it's been a month.
check.why: A do-not-call request covers every channel and every partner, permanently.

lessons.title: The rules: data, privacy, and what gets a partner removed
lessons.goal: Protect client and lead data, and know the conduct that ends a partnership.
film: A laptop on a kitchen table, Partner World open. A family member walks past behind it.
Partner World holds real people's names, numbers and businesses. They're trusting you with them.
One line, big: "Station work only."
Use client and lead details only for your Station work.
Struck through on the beat: "Sell it." "Share it." "Export it." "Copy it into a spreadsheet." "Use it for another business."
Never sell, share or bulk-export them. Never copy them into a personal spreadsheet, contact list or mailing list. Never use them for another business. Partner World has no export, on purpose.
A login screen. A padlock clicks shut. "Keep your login private."
Keep your Partner World login private, and keep your devices secure.
A clock with "72 hours" on it.
If you think client or lead data has leaked, tell Station within 72 hours.
A door closing: "If the agreement ends". Three lines under it: "Stop using it." "Delete copies." "Confirm in writing if asked."
If your agreement ends, stop using the data, delete any copies, and confirm in writing if Station asks.
A red strip builds across the screen: "Spam." "Misrepresentation." "Fake or self-referrals." "Fraud." "Misuse of data." "Breaking the agreement." "Damaging the brand."
And here's what gets a partner suspended or removed: spam, lying to a business, fake or self-referrals, fraud, misusing data, breaking the agreement, or damaging Station's brand.
Under the strip: "Unpaid commission can be forfeited." The green balance on Money drains to grey.
For any of those, unpaid commission can be forfeited.
Do-this-now: "Check: is anything from Partner World saved anywhere else?"
Right now, check your phone and computer. If anything from Partner World is saved anywhere else, delete it.
lessons.read_md:
**Client and lead data**
- Use client and lead details only for your Station work.
- Never sell, share or bulk-export them, never copy them into a personal CRM, spreadsheet or mailing list, and never use them for another business. Partner World has no export.
- Keep your Partner World login private, and use reasonable security on your devices.
- If you think client or lead data has leaked, **tell Station within 72 hours**.
- When the agreement ends, stop using the data, delete any copies, and confirm in writing if asked.
- Don't collect a client's customer list yourself. The client gives it to Station.
- Never log into a client's account, and never ask for or handle their passwords, bank details, card numbers or ID.

Anything you learn about Station that isn't public (how its tools work, its pricing internals, its clients) is confidential, during and after your agreement.

**What gets a partner removed:** Station can suspend or remove a partner, and forfeit unpaid commission for cause, for **spam, misrepresentation, fake or self-referrals, fraud, misuse of client data, breach of the agreement, or conduct that damages Station's brand**.

check.q: You'd like to keep a spreadsheet of your leads' phone numbers so you can call from your car. Is that OK?
options: No. Lead details stay in Partner World; copying them into a personal spreadsheet breaks the agreement.
Yes, as long as you delete it when you leave.
Yes, if the spreadsheet has a password.
check.why: No copies outside Station's systems, however well protected. Partner World works on your phone.

check.q: You leave your phone in a cab, signed in to Partner World. What do you do?
options: Tell Station within 72 hours, so the login can be dealt with.
Nothing, if the phone has a lock screen.
Wait to see if anyone uses it.
check.why: A possible leak or login problem goes to Station within 72 hours, every time.

check.q: Which of these can get you removed, with unpaid commission forfeited?
options: Taking a week off from calling.
Asking Station a question you could have looked up.
Signing up your brother's business through your link.
check.why: Family businesses are never eligible. A self-referral is cause for removal. There's no quota.

quiz.q: A roofer you've just met asks, "So you're with Station?" Which answer is right?
options: "I'm an independent partner with Station. Station builds, sets up and supports everything, and I'm your contact."
"I'm a Station account manager, so I can sort out your account for you."
"Yes, I'm on Station's sales team."
"Not really. I just resell some software."

quiz.q: A client in your book texts: "The booking page shows last month's hours. Can you just log in and fix it?" You:
options: Ask for her login. It's a two-minute fix.
Note it and pass it on with the rest of your messages at the end of the week.
Tell her Station will handle it, and pass it on with Message Station the same business day.
Tell her to work it out from the help pages.

quiz.q: A plumber has paid $397 a month for Frontdesk every month and is now in month 14. You have 6 clients. What do you earn on him this month?
options: $158.80, because Frontdesk is a top-pay product.
Nothing. Commission ends after the first year.

options: $118.80, paid after the 30-day hold.
$118.80, on the day they sign up.
Nothing. The 14-day free trial earns nothing; commission starts when the first real payment clears.
Half of $118.80, because it's a trial.

quiz.q: Which of these earns you commission?
options: A top-up pack a client buys ahead.
A client's monthly hosting & care.
A client's extra texts over their allowance.
A client's one-time $1,250 payment to keep the website that came with their plan.

options: "Other dental offices use it, so it must be."
"It's fine, as long as you don't type health information into it."

"I can't answer that, and I won't guess. Please email Station at main@station.solutions and ask for the answer in writing."

Ask when you can reach them both, and email the page with the price so she can read it with him.

quiz.q: An owner buying Lineback asks: "So it'll be texting my missed callers tomorrow?" You say:
options: "Yes, it's live the same day."
Texting starts after carrier registration, about 2 business days, and the carriers control the timing.

options: Sell it. She asked for it.

quiz.q: A new Answer client asks when Station will build the free website that comes with it. You say:

After the first paid month clears, never during the trial.

quiz.q: A client wants her missed-call text to say "Hi from Joe's" instead of the full business name. What happens?
options: You log in and change it for her.
She changes it herself in her Station account, under Settings, then Your Words.

quiz.q: A happy client wants to add Repute. How does she do it?

You add it for her in Partner World.

From My Services in her Station account, which previews the charge first, and you tell Station with Message Station.

quiz.q: A business Station sent you reads "Yours till" a date three days from now. You haven't reached them. What keeps it yours?
options: Adding a note to the card.
Nothing. It's yours until you close it.
Logging a call on it. Every logged call gives you another 14 days from that call.
Marking it Interested without calling.

quiz.q: It's 8:15 pm on Saturday where the business is, and 7:15 pm where you are. Why is the Call button grey?
options: It's outside calling hours in the business's own time zone: 9 am to 8 pm, Monday to Saturday, in the business's own time zone.
You've hit your daily call limit.

options: Add them to your list as Your lead.

options: "No, I'm calling the owner about missed calls. When's the best time to catch him?"
Leave the price with her.

options: Your name, that you're an independent partner with Station, and that you'll try again. No price.
Station's phone number so they can call back.
The price and your link.

quiz.q: Twenty owners didn't pick up today. Can you text each of them a short note with your link?
options: Yes, if each text says "Reply STOP to opt out."
No. Text only people who've agreed to hear from you, one at a time.
Yes, as long as each text is sent separately.

options: That you're a Station employee, so people trust it.

options: Keep only the ones who were interested.
